Short Description: People with one inactive ASGR1 copy clear lipoproteins differently, producing lower non-HDL cholesterol and about 34% lower odds of coronary artery disease. Because this protective phenotype was discovered directly in human carriers, it links a liver receptor to a measurable cardiovascular advantage without relying on an animal proxy. ASGR1 also serves as the entry route for GalNAc-tagged liver medicines, so any intervention would need to preserve that valuable delivery pathway.
Mechanism: ASGR1 encodes the major subunit of the asialoglycoprotein receptor, also called the Ashwell-Morell receptor, a calcium-dependent C-type lectin displayed on the surface of hepatocytes. Its normal job is surveillance of circulating glycoproteins: when a protein loses the terminal sialic acid caps from its sugar chains, exposing galactose and N-acetylgalactosamine, the receptor binds it and pulls it into the cell for degradation. The del12 allele is a 12-base-pair deletion inside intron 4 that activates a cryptic splice site; the resulting transcript is frameshifted and carries a premature stop codon, and the truncated protein is prone to degradation, so a person with one del12 copy is functionally haploinsufficient rather than merely carrying a mildly altered receptor. Losing half of that clearance capacity lowers non-HDL cholesterol by a route independent of the LDL receptor and PCSK9 axis; the leading explanation involves altered hepatic handling of glycosylated ligands and a consequent shift in cholesterol traffic, but the causal chain has not been closed. The pharmacodynamic fingerprint is unambiguous, because serum alkaline phosphatase is itself an asialoglycoprotein receptor ligand: when the receptor stops clearing it, it accumulates in blood, which is why every carrier can be spotted from a routine liver panel.
Achievements (effect sizes): Heterozygous carriers of the del12 deletion carry non-HDL cholesterol lower by "a difference of 15.3 mg per deciliter (0.40 mmol per liter) (P=1.0x10-16)" than noncarriers, measured across roughly 398,000 imputed Icelandic genomes, and their fasting triglycerides are lower by 6.3% (95% CI -10.3 to -2.3, P=0.003, n=99,893) (Nioi 2016, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419). The clinical consequence is a "lower risk of coronary artery disease (by 34%; 95% confidence interval, 21 to 45; P=4.0x10-6)", corresponding to a combined odds ratio of 0.66 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.79) that held across eight study populations in Iceland, Denmark, the Netherlands, the United States and New Zealand with no detectable heterogeneity (P=0.96), and to a hazard ratio of 0.64 for a first myocardial infarction among Icelandic carriers (P=8.5x10-5). The deletion is carried by 1 in 120 persons in that study population, and a second independent truncating allele, p.W158X, carried by 1 in 1850 persons, was also associated with lower non-HDL cholesterol (P=1.8x10-3) - an internal replication using a different mutation in the same gene. The same dataset quantifies the price: alkaline phosphatase is raised by a combined 46.5 U/L (95% CI 40.1 to 52.7, P=5.6x10-69, n=131,889) and vitamin B12 by 16.6 pmol/L in the Icelandic set (95% CI 11.5 to 21.5, P=3.1x10-12) (Nioi 2016, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human natural-experiment genetics; two independent loss-of-function alleles, n>390,000, replicated across 8 populations, no therapeutic yet)
Translational Gaps: No drug, antibody or genome editor directed at this target has entered a registered clinical trial, so every number in this record comes from people who were born with the variant rather than from anyone who was given it. The mechanism connecting a lectin that clears desialylated glycoproteins to a 15.3 mg/dL fall in non-HDL cholesterol has not been established: Nioi 2016 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419) demonstrates the association and the pharmacodynamic marker, not the causal pathway. Every human studied is heterozygous - no homozygous null humans are described anywhere in the cohort - so the complete knockout an exhibit visitor would actually be buying has never been observed in a person, and its phenotype cannot be predicted from the heterozygous data. The receptor also performs jobs the cohort does not track over a full lifespan, notably the clearance of desialylated platelets and von Willebrand factor, so consequences for coagulation over eighty years remain unmeasured. Finally, because this receptor is what GalNAc-conjugated drugs and GalNAc-lipid nanoparticles use to enter hepatocytes, someone lacking it may be refractory to an entire delivery platform, including the ANGPTL3 base editor in this same library.
Key References (DOIs): Nioi New England Journal of Medicine 2016 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This entry collides with another one in the library, and the collision is mechanical rather than thematic. The asialoglycoprotein receptor that ASGR1 builds is exactly the receptor that GalNAc-decorated lipid nanoparticles exploit to reach hepatocytes: Kasiewicz 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1) raised liver ANGPTL3 base editing from 5% to 61% in LDL-receptor-deficient monkeys precisely by adding a GalNAc-asialoglycoprotein-receptor ligand to the particle. Buying ASGR1 loss and ANGPTL3 base editing in the same body is therefore self-defeating, and an exhibit visitor who selects both has built a contradiction. Separately, the field has started running this variant forward rather than merely observing it: a 2026 Molecular Therapy paper reports hepatic base editing of ASGR1 as a deliberate LDL-receptor-independent lipid-lowering strategy (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymthe.2026.07.036), retrieved here as metadata only and not read in full, so no figures from it are quoted. One transcription caution for anyone checking the source: the published confidence interval for the first-myocardial-infarction hazard ratio reads "0.64; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.80", which does not bracket its own point estimate; it is reproduced in this record exactly as printed rather than silently corrected. The protein and structure references are the human entries UniProt P07306 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P07306) and PDB 1DV8 (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1DV8), one of eight solved structures.

Narrative: Autophagy is the cell's own demolition-and-recycling service: damaged mitochondria, protein aggregates and spent organelles are wrapped in a double membrane and delivered to the lysosome. Atg5 is required to build that membrane, and its activity falls with age in most tissues. Pyo et al. asked the direct question — if you simply give mice more Atg5 from conception, does the recycling rate go up and do they live longer? Ubiquitous transgenic overexpression raised autophagic flux in brain, liver and muscle, and extended both median and maximal lifespan in males and females. The animals were leaner than littermates on identical chow, handled glucose better, held motor function longer, and their fibroblasts survived oxidative insult — a tolerance that disappeared when autophagy was pharmacologically blocked, tying the phenotype to the pathway rather than to transgene side-effects. This is the cleanest 'add one gene, get more autophagy, live longer' result in mammals, and unlike the mTOR route it does not require chronic immunosuppressive drug exposure.
Short Description: Every cell gets a faster recycling crew: damaged mitochondria and protein aggregates are cleared instead of accumulating. Mice carrying extra Atg5 copies lived 17.2% longer at the median in both sexes, staying leaner on identical chow with better glucose handling and motor function. Only ever done in mice, and high autophagy also helps established tumour cells survive nutrient stress.
Mechanism: ATG5 conjugates to ATG12 and, with ATG16L1, acts as the E3-like ligase that lipidates LC3/GABARAP proteins onto the growing autophagosome membrane — the rate-limiting step of autophagosome formation. Raising ATG5 dose raises steady-state autophagic flux (increased LC3-II, reduced p62) without altering the upstream mTOR/AMPK set-point, so the intervention adds clearance capacity rather than rewiring nutrient sensing. Downstream consequences measured in the transgenics: improved insulin sensitivity, reduced adiposity, preserved motor coordination, and MEF resistance to oxidative cell death that is reversed by autophagy inhibition.
Achievements (effect sizes): First demonstration that genetic activation of autophagy extends lifespan in a mammal. Median lifespan +17.2% (both sexes), maximal lifespan also extended. Leanness on identical diet, improved insulin sensitivity, improved motor function, and oxidative-stress tolerance in derived fibroblasts reversible by autophagy inhibitor.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (single-laboratory ubiquitous transgenic mouse lifespan study with both sexes, median and maximal lifespan, plus mechanistic autophagy-flux and ex-vivo rescue experiments; no independent replication of the lifespan cohort and no human ATG5 delivery of any kind)
Translational Gaps: No human or non-human-primate ATG5 delivery exists. The mouse transgene is expressed from conception and ubiquitously, so it cannot separate a developmental contribution from adult-onset benefit — the adult-onset experiment (inducible or AAV Atg5) has not been run. Tissue dose-response is unknown, and ATG5 is a shared node with the ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 apoptosis and inflammasome-regulation functions, so a delivered dose may not behave like a germline one.
Key References (DOIs): Pyo JO et al. Nat Commun 2013;4:2300 (10.1038/ncomms3300)
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CANCER: elevated autophagy is protective against tumour initiation but supports survival of established tumours under nutrient and therapy stress — an adult with an occult malignancy is the wrong recipient. BODY COMPOSITION: the leanness is not incidental; Atg5 Tg mice weigh less than littermates on identical chow, which in an older human competes directly with sarcopenia management. DEVELOPMENTAL: Atg5-null mice die neonatally, so this gene's dose window is bounded on both sides. IMMUNE: ATG5 participates in inflammasome regulation and antigen presentation; immune consequences of chronic overexpression were not assessed. Only ONE lifespan cohort exists, from one group.

Manipulation: Three-factor transcription-factor reprogramming of cochlear supporting cells (inducible transgene / AAV)
Narrative:
In 1988 two laboratories reported the same impossible thing: a bird that had been deafened by loud sound grew its hearing organ back. Working in adult Japanese quail, Ryals and Rubel traumatised the basilar papilla, then watched dividing cells appear in an epithelium that textbooks said was finished at hatching, and counted hair cells climbing back to within 5 percent of the number the birds started with (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101). Mammals cannot do this. The support cells that sit between our hair cells are the same cell type that, in a bird, would re-enter the cell cycle and become sensory; in us they scar over and the loss is permanent, which is why noise-induced and antibiotic-induced deafness is for life.

The obvious move was to hand mammalian support cells the master switch the birds use. ATOH1, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, is the gene that tells an inner-ear progenitor to become a hair cell, and in 2005 an adenovirus carrying Atoh1 was reported to improve hearing thresholds in deafened guinea pigs (https://doi.org/10.1038/nm1193). Novartis built a drug on that result — CGF166, an adenoviral vector delivering human ATOH1 injected into the labyrinth — and took it into 22 people with severe-to-profound hearing loss. It did not restore hearing (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02132130).

The 2024 reason why is unflattering and useful: in the adult mouse organ of Corti, ATOH1 alone does essentially nothing. Identity in a mature cell is held shut by more than one lock, and opening it took three factors at once — ATOH1 plus GFI1 plus POU4F3 — delivered to lineage-marked support cells whose neighbouring hair cells had first been killed off, because surviving hair cells actively suppress their neighbours' conversion (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445). That produced hundreds of genuinely new, innervated hair cells per cochlea from cells that had never been sensory. It has not yet produced a mouse that hears better, and it asks a player to switch on, a few millimetres from the brainstem, the exact transcription factors that drive medulloblastoma.
Short Description: ATOH1, GFI1 and POU4F3 can reopen the developmental programme that builds the inner ear's sound-sensing hair cells. After deafening injury, the trio converted adult mouse support cells into hundreds of new hair-cell-like cells, a much stronger response than ATOH1 alone. Fewer than half expressed the mature outer-hair-cell motor PRESTIN at six weeks, but the experiment shows that a normally non-regenerating sensory epithelium can be pushed toward reconstruction.
Mechanism: ATOH1 (atonal homolog 1) is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that acts as the master regulator of hair-cell fate; GFI1 (growth factor independent 1) is a zinc-finger repressor that shuts down the supporting-cell and pro-apoptotic programs and stabilises the new identity; and POU4F3 (POU-domain class 4 transcription factor 3) drives hair-cell maturation and survival. In birds, supporting cells of the basilar papilla re-enter the cell cycle and transdifferentiate spontaneously. In mammals the ATOH1 locus is epigenetically locked and ATOH1 by itself is insufficient in the adult organ of Corti, so all three factors must be forced together in Lfng-lineage supporting cells to open the hair-cell gene network. Killing the endogenous hair cells first — using a diphtheria-toxin receptor knocked into the Pou4f3 locus — markedly raises conversion, which indicates that surviving hair cells laterally inhibit reprogramming through Notch signalling. The cells that result express MYO7A (myosin VIIA) and parvalbumin, acquire the outer-hair-cell motor protein PRESTIN, assemble ribbon-synapse proteins and rudimentary stereociliary bundles, and are contacted by nerve fibres (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445).
Achievements (effect sizes): Adult Japanese quail whose basilar papilla had been damaged by acoustic trauma incorporated [3H]thymidine into hair-cell and supporting-cell nuclei within ten days, and an initial loss of hair cells recovered to within 5 percent of the original number of cells — the first demonstration that a vertebrate auditory epithelium regenerates after hatching (Ryals & Rubel 1988, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101). In three-week-old mice carrying Lfng-CreERT2, a Rosa26-tdTomato lineage reporter and a Pou4f3 diphtheria-toxin receptor, tamoxifen-driven activation of Atoh1 together with Gfi1 and Pou4f3 after the endogenous hair cells had been killed produced 479.9 ± 213.4 tdTOMATO/MYO7A-double positive cells per cochlea (P = 0.0004 compared with control and P = 0.0034 compared with Atoh1 alone), against 2.8 ± 6.2 in control cochleas and 46.0 ± 17.1 with Atoh1 alone, a single-factor result that was not distinguishable from control (P = 0.9250) (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445). Maturation lagged behind identity in the same animals: 45.6 ± 5.5% of regenerated hair cells co-labelled for MYO7A, PRESTIN and tdTomato at six weeks of age (N = 2) and PRESTIN was not detectable at all at five weeks, while 63.8% ± 3.7% (N = 2) of regenerated inner-compartment cells expressed parvalbumin compared with 8.8% ± 0.1% (N = 2) in the outer compartment (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (natural avian regeneration + adult-mouse three-factor reprogramming with lineage tracing + one completed human Phase 1/2 that failed on efficacy)
Translational Gaps: The cells produced by three-factor reprogramming are hair cell-like rather than finished hair cells: their stereociliary bundles are described as rudimentary and PRESTIN arrives late and in fewer than half of them, and no mammal has yet recovered an auditory threshold as a result of this manipulation. Nobody has solved how to deliver three coordinated transgenes to supporting cells along the whole length of the cochlear duct while sparing the spiral ganglion, whose neurons must survive for any regenerated cell to be heard. The protocol also depends on first destroying the surviving hair cells to lift Notch-mediated lateral inhibition, which is acceptable in a mouse that is already deaf but is a hard thing to ask of a patient with residual hearing. The single human trial tested the one-factor design that the mouse work has since shown to be inadequate, so the three-factor approach has never been given a clinical test at all.
Key References (DOIs): Ryals Science 1988 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101 | McGovern PNAS Nexus 2024 https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445 | Izumikawa Nature Medicine 2005 https://doi.org/10.1038/nm1193 | Corwin Science 1988 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381100
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The literature disagrees about single-factor ATOH1, and the disagreement matters because a drug was built on one side of it. Izumikawa and colleagues reported that Atoh1 delivered alone improved hearing thresholds in deafened guinea pigs (Izumikawa 2005, https://doi.org/10.1038/nm1193), whereas the 2024 mouse study found that Atoh1 alone produced no increase in regenerated hair cells in the adult organ of Corti (46.0 ± 17.1 versus 2.8 ± 6.2 in controls, P = 0.9250) (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445). Novartis's CGF166, an intralabyrinthine adenovector encoding human ATOH1, followed the single-factor design: 22 patients were enrolled and 19 completed, and the posted week-52 results show treated-ear pure-tone air-conduction thresholds moving in the wrong direction, +8.5 dB overall with cohort values of -4.2, +6.7, +26.3 and +5.0 dB (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02132130). Those registry results have no journal publication, so they are recorded here from the registry rather than as a citable effect size, and the programme was not advanced. The avian half of the story is not contested: Ryals and Rubel (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101) and Corwin and Cotanche (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381100) reported hair-cell regeneration in birds independently in the same year. One honest bookkeeping point: no ATOH1 entry exists for Coturnix japonica in UniProt, so the avian reference sequence given here is A0A0C6E596, the reviewed chicken (Gallus gallus) ortholog (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A0C6E596/entry). The quail supplies the natural regeneration phenotype; the reprogramming experiments were done in mice. No approved product exists and no company has a three-factor clinical candidate.

Narrative: Bdelloid rotifers survive radiation doses that would kill any vertebrate — partly thanks to a DNA repair enzyme they stole from bacteria. AvLigE is a prokaryotic DNA Ligase E acquired by horizontal gene transfer from bacteria into the rotifer Adineta vaga genome. When expressed in human cells, it significantly improves their radiation tolerance. This is evolution's most dramatic example of borrowing survival tools across the tree of life.
Short Description: AvLigE is a DNA-ligating enzyme acquired by a radiation-tolerant rotifer from bacteria, helping seal broken genetic material after severe damage. Expressing it in human cells improved survival under radiation, showing that a foreign repair enzyme can plug into our existing DNA-repair machinery. Its promise is faster restoration after genotoxic stress, provided that future work preserves the checkpoints that prevent damaged cells from propagating.
Mechanism: AvLigE is a prokaryotic-type DNA ligase that catalyzes the final step of base excision repair and single-strand break repair. Its bacterial origin gives it distinct substrate preferences from eukaryotic ligases, providing complementary DNA repair capacity. In A. vaga, it is strongly upregulated after ionizing radiation exposure.
Achievements (effect sizes): Heterologous expression of AvLigE in human cell lines significantly improved radiation tolerance. Proteomic analysis confirmed it is a major DNA break repair contributor in irradiated rotifers. The gene was horizontally transferred from a prokaryote and is stably integrated in the rotifer genome.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Long-term effects of expressing a bacterial enzyme in human cells unknown. Integration with existing mammalian DNA repair pathways needs characterization. Potential interference with normal DNA damage signaling.
Key References (DOIs): Nicolas Nature Communications 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43075-8
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: One of very few demonstrated cases of a horizontally transferred gene directly improving human cell function.

Manipulation: overexpression (high-expressing T23 transgene; moderate T7 line was ineffective)
Narrative: BubR1 is the accountant of cell division: it enforces the mitotic checkpoint and helps set up correct microtubule-kinetochore attachments, so daughter cells get the right number of chromosomes. Its abundance falls with chronological age in mice and humans, and germline mutations that lower it cause aneuploidy, premature-aging phenotypes and cancer in both species — in humans, mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome. Baker et al. ran the mirror experiment: sustain HIGH BubR1 through life and see what happens. The high-expressing transgenic line kept genomic integrity, resisted carcinogen- and oncogene-driven tumours, showed reduced aneuploidy in several tissues, delayed age-related deterioration, and lived longer. The direction is what makes this a real enhancement candidate rather than a knockout curiosity: less of this gene is a named human disease, more of it is protective in mice. The catch is dose — the moderately expressing line gave none of the protection.
Short Description: Chromosomes get counted properly at every cell division, so tissues stop accumulating cells with the wrong number of them. Mice with a higher spindle-checkpoint dose lived 22% longer at the median in males and developed tumours in a third of animals rather than all of them. Low BubR1 in humans causes a progeroid mosaic-variegated-aneuploidy syndrome, so this is a gene where the deficiency state is already characterised and the surplus state is not.
Mechanism: BubR1 (BUB1B) is a pseudokinase component of the mitotic checkpoint complex that sequesters CDC20 to delay anaphase until kinetochores are correctly attached, and it also contributes to establishing stable microtubule-kinetochore attachments. Overabundance corrects both checkpoint impairment and attachment defects, cutting chromosome missegregation — including missegregation induced by oncogenic Ras. The result is lower whole-chromosome instability across tissues, which manifests as reduced spontaneous and induced tumorigenesis and as delayed accumulation of aneuploid cells with age. Notably the transgenics did NOT become aneuploid or tumour-prone themselves, unlike mice overexpressing the related regulators Bub1, Mad2 or UbcH10.
Achievements (effect sizes): High-expressing transgenic line: median lifespan +22.0% (males), +18.9% (females), +14.0% (pooled). Carcinogen challenge: 33% of transgenics developed tumours versus 100% of wild type, with both skin and lung incidence reduced. Oncogene challenge: Kras-mutant mice averaged 17 lung tumours at 6 weeks versus 8 in transgenics. Normal aneuploidy and missegregation rates in transgenic splenocytes and fibroblasts, and reduced aneuploidy in Kras lung tissue.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (single-laboratory mouse transgenic lifespan cohort with both sexes plus carcinogen and oncogene tumour challenges and mechanistic mitotic-checkpoint experiments; direction independently corroborated by human loss-of-function genetics — mosaic variegated aneuploidy — but no human or primate BUB1B delivery has been attempted)
Translational Gaps: There is no vector-delivered or adult-onset version: the mouse intervention is a lifelong germline transgene. The dose window is narrow and unmapped in reverse — the moderate T7 line conferred no protection, and how high is too high was never established. BUB1B is a 1050-residue mitotic protein, an awkward AAV cargo, and mitotic-checkpoint genes are the class where overexpression of relatives (Bub1, Mad2, UbcH10) actively causes aneuploidy and tumours, so specificity cannot be assumed from the family. No human data on the enhancement direction exist at all.
Key References (DOIs): Baker DJ et al. Nat Cell Biol 2013;15:96-102 (10.1038/ncb2643); human loss-of-function direction: MVA1 BUB1B variants (10.1007/s10072-022-06247-w); TALEN-mapped intergenic BUB1B mutation in MVA (10.1073/pnas.1317008111)
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: DOSE THRESHOLD: the moderately expressing T7 line failed every protection assay — tumour incidence, Kras lung tumours, aneuploidy — while T23 succeeded. This is a threshold effect, not a graded one, and the upper bound was not tested. FAMILY RISK: overexpressing the related mitotic regulators Bub1, Mad2 or UbcH10 CAUSES aneuploidy and tumours in mice. BubR1 did not, but this is a gene class where 'more checkpoint protein' is not generically safe. DEVELOPMENTAL/HUMAN DISEASE: hypomorphic BUB1B in humans causes mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome with microcephaly, growth retardation and childhood cancer; one forensic report links a variant to sudden unexpected postnatal collapse. That is the loss-of-function direction, and it is what establishes the gene's dose-sensitivity in humans. FERTILITY: BubR1 hypomorphs are infertile; effects of overexpression on meiosis and gamete aneuploidy were not reported. CARGO SIZE: 1050 aa / ~120 kDa — near the practical AAV limit.

Narrative: Tardigrades can dry out completely, sit in a dusty drawer for years, and revive in a drop of water. The CAHS proteins are a big part of that trick. When water leaves the cell, CAHS D doesn't just stabilize molecules — it phase-separates into a glass-like mesh, freezing the cell's contents in place until rehydration. University of Wyoming researchers expressed CAHS D in human HEK293 cells in 2022; under osmotic shock, the protein formed the predicted reversible fibers inside human cells, slowed their metabolism, and modestly improved survival. But the story has gotten complicated fast. Piszkiewicz 2019 showed that plenty of unrelated proteins protect enzymes from drying just as well. Ramirez 2023 found that CAHS D doesn't actually hold onto water in the dry state, refuting a popular model. Non-gelling variants sometimes protect better than gelling ones. The protein is real and does something; nobody quite agrees on what.
Short Description: The tardigrade protein CAHS D self-organises into reversible fibres as water disappears, creating a temporary physical shield around sensitive cellular components. It boosted yeast survival after desiccation by roughly 100-fold and can protect purified enzymes, then relax again when water returns. This is a striking blueprint for dry-state preservation of biologics and cells, with engineered non-gelling variants potentially offering even better molecular protection.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered tardigrade-specific protein; reversible concentration/temperature-dependent gel/fibril networks; molecular shield against desiccation-induced unfolding.
Achievements (effect sizes): Boothby 2017 Mol Cell: yeast expressing CAHS D ~100× increased desiccation survival; E. coli also protected; RNAi of CAHS in tardigrades reduced post-desiccation survival. In vitro: protects LDH, lipoprotein lipase. Tanaka 2022 PLOS Biol (HEp-2, HEK293T): CAHS 1/3/8/12 form reversible filaments under hyperosmotic stress, stiffen cells (AFM), and modestly improve survival. Sanchez-Martinez 2024 Protein Sci (HEK293): CAHS D fibers slow metabolism and improve survival after 0.5 M sorbitol shock. Gel point ~8–20 g/L.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (HEK293, HEp-2, HeLa) + T3 (yeast/E. coli)
Translational Gaps: Stable long-term mammalian desiccation survival not shown; no mouse data; Esterly 2020 showed only safety in mice, not efficacy.
Key References (DOIs): Yamaguchi PLoS ONE 2012 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0044209 | Boothby Mol Cell 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2017.02.018 | Piszkiewicz Protein Sci 2019 https://doi.org/10.1002/pro.3604 | Tanaka PLoS Biol 2022 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3001780
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Piszkiewicz 2019 — many unrelated globular/disordered proteins protect LDH similarly, CAHS specificity challenged. (2) Ramirez 2023 — CAHS D does NOT retain water in dry state, refutes water-replacement/retention model. (3) Gel-vs-protection mechanism contested: Sanchez-Martinez 2024 shows non-gelling variants protect citrate synthase BETTER than gelling WT. (4) Tanaka 2023 reply — GFP-only controls also form mesh in drying tardigrades; "filaments" may not be CAHS-specific in vivo. Non-physiological overexpression; modest mammalian-cell effects.

Narrative: A gecko can hang from a glass ceiling by a single toe because its foot-pads are covered in millions of microscopic hairs, called setae, each tipped with even finer spatulas. The contact area becomes so large that van der Waals forces alone suffice. There is no glue and no suction. The Gekko japonicus genome, published by Liu and colleagues in 2015, revealed a family of 71 beta-keratin genes, 35 of which carry the S-core box motif that marks them as setae beta-keratins, with bursts of gene duplication around 105 to 96 and 87 to 80 million years ago, matching the evolutionary origins of gecko adhesion (https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10033). A single seta generates 20 to 40 micronewtons of force, and a whole foot can hold 40 times the animal's body weight (https://doi.org/10.1038/35015073). Synthetic gecko-inspired tapes, from polymer microfibers to carbon-nanotube arrays, already work reasonably well. Expressing gecko beta-keratins in mammalian cells to grow actual setae, however, is a non-starter, because the adhesion depends on a hierarchical anatomy — cells, then pillars, then hairs, then spatulas — built by a developmental programme rather than on the protein sequence itself.
Short Description: Gecko feet achieve dry, reusable adhesion through millions of microscopic hairs that branch into nanoscale tips and make intimate van der Waals contact with almost any surface. A single hair can pull 20–40 micronewtons, while the full hierarchical array supports rapid attachment and release without glue. The transferable capability is the architecture itself: a self-cleaning, directionally controlled adhesive surface inspired by living tissue.
Mechanism: Gecko adhesion rests on a large multigene family of corneous beta-proteins, 71 of them in Gekko japonicus, historically called beta-keratins. These polymerise into beta-sheet filaments about 3 to 4 nanometres across inside the oberhautchen and beta-layer cells of the toe-pad epidermis. Those filaments make up the setae, which branch into spatular tips some 200 to 500 nanometres wide. The adhesion itself is purely van der Waals attraction: nothing is secreted, nothing is evacuated, and the force comes entirely from bringing an enormous amount of surface into intimate contact with the substrate.
Achievements (effect sizes): Liu and colleagues assembled the 2.55 gigabase Gekko japonicus genome in 2015, annotated 22,487 genes including 71 beta-keratin genes, identified 35 of those as setae beta-keratins by the presence of the S-core box motif (sequence similarity 70% or greater) with most of them clustered on a single scaffold, and dated the phylogenetic expansions of the family to roughly 105 to 96 and 87 to 80 million years ago (https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10033). Alibardi's immunohistochemistry localised the beta-protein Ge-cprp-9 to the setae and their spatular tips (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tice.2013.01.002). Autumn and colleagues made the first direct measurement of a single seta in 2000, recording 20 to 40 micronewtons of adhesive force and calculating that a whole foot can hold about 40 times the animal's body weight (https://doi.org/10.1038/35015073). The same group demonstrated in 2002 that the mechanism is van der Waals attraction, showing that isolated setae adhere equally well to strongly hydrophobic and strongly hydrophilic polarisable surfaces, and that synthetic polydimethylsiloxane and polyester spatulae reproduce the adhesion (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.192252799). No heterologous transfer of a gecko beta-keratin gene has ever produced functional setae — that number remains zero. It is worth being precise about what the engineered successes are: the microfabricated gecko tape of Geim and colleagues in 2003 (https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat917) and the carbon-nanotube gecko tapes of Qu and colleagues in 2008 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1159503) are synthetic materials, containing no protein and no gene.
Highest Evidence Tier: T1 (source organism) + T2 (protein biochem)
Translational Gaps: Transferring these genes is close to a category error. Adhesion is produced by a hierarchical nanoarchitecture that a developmental programme lays down over successive tissue layers; it is not a property of the protein's composition. Putting the coding sequence into another cell type gives you the polymer without the geometry, and the geometry is where the force comes from.
Key References (DOIs): Autumn Nature 2000 https://doi.org/10.1038/35015073 | Autumn Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2002 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.192252799 | Geim Nature Materials 2003 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat917 | Qu Science 2008 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1159503 | Alibardi Tissue and Cell 2013 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tice.2013.01.002 | Liu Nature Communications 2015 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10033
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Setae are not made of beta-keratin alone: they also contain lipids and alpha-keratins, so any reconstruction based on the beta-protein family alone would be incomplete. The gene count itself is disputed, with annotations ranging from 26 to 72, because this is a highly repetitive family that automated annotation tends to under-call; the legacy version of this record carried 72 as the setae figure, whereas the genome paper reports 71 beta-keratin genes in total and 35 setae beta-keratins, so the counts a reader may encounter elsewhere refer to different things. The duplication dates are similarly rounded from one version of this record to the next: the legacy text gave the two expansion bursts as roughly 100 and 85 million years ago, while the genome paper resolves them as 105 to 96 and 87 to 80 million years ago. And the central caveat bears repeating in its own right: the adhesion requires hierarchical nanoarchitecture built by a developmental programme, so the trait is architectural rather than compositional.

Manipulation: pharmacological reduction of GTPase activity in old animals (CASIN, 4 daily doses); activation is pro-aging
Narrative: Almost everything in this library is an intervention you would have to be born with, or at least receive years before you need it. This one is four injections into an animal already three-quarters of the way through its life. Cdc42 is a small Rho-family GTPase controlling cell polarity, and its activity rises in several tissues of aged mice and in the blood of elderly humans. The causal direction was established from the harmful end first: a Cdc42 gain-of-activity mouse shows a premature aging-like phenotype and a shortened lifespan. Florian and colleagues then asked the reverse question in the hardest possible setting. They gave 75-week-old female C57BL/6 mice CASIN, a Cdc42-activity-specific inhibitor, intraperitoneally once every 24 hours for four consecutive days - and then stopped. Serum mass spectrometry confirmed micromolar exposure, and Cdc42-GTP in bone marrow 24 hours after the last injection had fallen to the level seen in 10-week-old mice. Median survival went from 123.5 weeks in controls to 136 weeks in treated animals, with maximum lifespan also extended (Mantel-Cox P<0.0004). Four days of drug bought roughly three months. Two supporting readouts explain how a transient treatment has a durable effect: serum IL-1beta, IL-1alpha and interferon-gamma returned to youthful levels, and a DNA-methylation clock measured on blood cells 8 to 9 weeks after treatment read significantly younger - consistent with the group's earlier finding that transient changes in Cdc42 activity rewrite epigenetic signatures in stem cells.
Short Description: A small GTPase controlling cell polarity becomes overactive with age, and turning its activity back down in already-old animals resets inflammatory signalling. Four daily injections of a specific inhibitor into 75-week-old female mice moved median survival from 123.5 to 136 weeks, restored youthful serum IL-1beta and interferon-gamma, and made the blood methylation clock read younger. Deleting the gene outright kills mouse embryos, so only partial, transient inhibition is usable.
Mechanism: CDC42 encodes a 191-residue, 21.3 kDa Rho-family small GTPase that cycles between GTP-bound active and GDP-bound inactive states to set cell polarity, actin organisation and asymmetric division. In aged haematopoietic stem cells, elevated Cdc42-GTP causes loss of polarity, a shift toward myeloid-biased output and altered histone methylation - and because the polarity defect is epigenetically encoded, a transient reduction in activity can reset it durably rather than only for the drug's residence time. CASIN is a selective inhibitor of Cdc42 activity, not of the protein's expression, which is what makes the intervention survivable: outright deletion of Cdc42 causes very early embryonic lethality in mice, although Cdc42-deficient embryonic stem cells remain viable and proliferate normally. The downstream systemic readout is inflammatory: reduced circulating IL-1beta, IL-1alpha and interferon-gamma, the cytokines that define inflammaging.
Achievements (effect sizes): Florian 2020 (Aging Cell): four consecutive daily intraperitoneal doses of CASIN at 25 mg/kg to 75-week-old female C57BL/6 mice extended median survival from 123.5 weeks in controls to 136 weeks in treated animals (n=18 control, 17 CASIN; P<0.0004 Mantel-Cox, P<0.0032 Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon), with maximum lifespan also extended - a +10.1% median gain, matching the +9.7% median OpenGenes records for this row. Mass spectrometry confirmed micromolar serum CASIN, and Cdc42-GTP in aged bone marrow 24 hours after the last dose fell to the level seen in 10-week-old mice. No acute toxicity over the 4 injections and no treated mouse died within 4 weeks. Serum IL-1beta, IL-1alpha and interferon-gamma returned to youthful levels, and a DNA-methylation-based biological-age prediction on blood cells 8-9 weeks after treatment read significantly younger (n=12 control, 11 CASIN). Weight, white and red blood cell counts were unchanged. The control group's median lifespan matched published C57BL/6J reference data, arguing the effect is not a sick-control artifact.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse; adult-onset pharmacological lifespan cohort with target-engagement confirmation by mass spectrometry and Cdc42-GTP pull-down, plus circulating-cytokine and DNA-methylation-clock secondary endpoints; one laboratory, females only, n=17-18 per arm, no human exposure)
Translational Gaps: The survival cohort is 35 mice in total, all female, from one laboratory, and no independent group has repeated it. CASIN itself is a research chemical - there is no CASIN investigational new drug application, no human pharmacokinetics and no clinical programme for any Cdc42-activity inhibitor, so the four-day protocol that makes this result attractive has never been attempted in a person. The gene cannot be approached genetically at all: Cdc42 deletion causes very early embryonic lethality in mice, so only partial, transient, activity-level inhibition is conceivable, and the therapeutic window between resetting stem-cell polarity and disrupting cell division in proliferative tissues has not been mapped. Cdc42 is also a well-documented driver in several human cancers where it supports invasion and migration, which cuts in the intervention's favour on direction but means any chronic dosing schedule would need tumour surveillance rather than assuming benefit. The human data amount to the observation that Cdc42 activity is elevated in blood of elderly people - an association, not an intervention.
Key References (DOIs): Florian Aging Cell 2020 https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13208 | Chen Curr Biol 2000 (Cdc42 deletion is embryonic lethal) https://doi.org/10.1016/s0960-9822(00)00571-6
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: MANIPULATION IS PHARMACOLOGICAL, NOT GENETIC - this matters for how the card reads. OpenGenes classifies the row as 'treatment with a gene product inhibitor', i.e. reduced Cdc42 ACTIVITY, not reduced expression. Genetic knockout is embryonic-lethal, so a knockout card would be wrong. STATISTIC: 123.5 -> 136 weeks is MEDIAN survival and recomputes to +10.1%; OpenGenes records +9.7% median for the same row. The OpenGenes _min for this row is +23.2% and is the minimum-lifespan statistic - not a headline. ADULT ONSET: this is the standout property in the whole wave - treatment began at 75 weeks and lasted 4 days. Card copy should lead with that, not with the percentage. COHORT: n=18 control, 17 treated, female only. Control median matched published C57BL/6J reference data (Yuan 2009), which rules out trap 2 - the controls were not dying early. NO HUMAN EXPOSURE: verified this session - CASIN is a research reagent with no clinical programme.

Manipulation: loss-of-function (protein-truncating variants: premature stop, canonical splice-site disruption, or frameshift indels)
Narrative: This gene is in the library as a cautionary object as much as an enhancement. Cholesteryl ester transfer protein does one job in blood: it picks cholesteryl esters out of HDL particles and hands them to the apoB-containing lipoproteins, VLDL and LDL, taking triglycerides back in exchange. Block it and cholesterol stays in HDL. For twenty years that looked like the most obvious drug idea in cardiology - raise the good cholesterol, lower the bad one, with a single target. Pfizer took torcetrapib into ILLUMINATE, an outcome trial that enrolled 15,067 patients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00134264). It raised HDL cholesterol precisely as designed, and it increased all-cause mortality, so the trial was terminated (Barter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0706628). Then evacetrapib and dalcetrapib were stopped for futility, and anacetrapib, which did reduce events modestly, was never commercialised, in part because the compound accumulated in fat tissue. Against that history, a group at the Broad Institute and Massachusetts General Hospital went back to human genetics with a specific question: forget the drugs, what happens to people who are simply born without this protein? They sequenced the gene's exons in 58,469 participants across twelve case-control studies and found carriers at a rate of about 1 in 975 - people with a premature stop, a disrupted splice site or a frameshift, which is as close to complete inhibition as nature provides. Those carriers had the lipid profile the drugs were aiming for and less coronary heart disease (Nomura 2017, https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.117.311145). So the genetics say the target was right and the pills were wrong, and the field still does not agree on why - whether torcetrapib's off-target rise in blood pressure explains it, whether lifelong absence differs from late-life blockade, or whether the amount of cholesterol in HDL was never the causal quantity in the first place.
Short Description: CETP loss reshapes lipid traffic by keeping more cholesterol in HDL particles while modestly lowering LDL. People carrying natural protein-truncating variants had about 30% lower odds of coronary heart disease, offering a human example of lifelong pathway modulation. The genotype remains more compelling than simply raising HDL with a late-life drug, because several CETP inhibitors improved the laboratory numbers without consistently improving outcomes.
Mechanism: CETP encodes cholesteryl ester transfer protein, a 493-amino-acid lipid-transfer protein that circulates in plasma and shuttles cholesteryl esters out of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles into the apolipoprotein-B-containing lipoproteins, very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL), carrying triglycerides in the opposite direction. Truncating the protein removes that transfer activity outright, so cholesteryl esters that would have been handed to atherogenic particles are instead retained in HDL. The consequence is unusual among lipid variants in that it moves three measurements at once and in the directions a cardiologist would choose: HDL cholesterol rises, while LDL cholesterol and triglycerides fall. Because the variants studied here are protein-truncating - premature stop codons, canonical splice-site disruptions and frameshift insertions or deletions - rather than missense changes of uncertain consequence, they function as a human read-out of complete pharmacological inhibition of the protein. That is precisely why the sequencing study was performed: after the CETP-inhibitor drugs failed in outcome trials, the question was whether human genetics said the target itself was wrong or whether the molecules were.
Achievements (effect sizes): Sequencing the exons of this gene in 58,469 participants across twelve case-control studies, comprising 18,817 coronary heart disease cases and 39,652 controls at an average age of 51.5 years, identified protein-truncating variants in 1 in 975 participants and quantified their effect precisely. Carriers had "higher high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (effect size, 22.6 mg/dL; 95% confidence interval, 18-27; P<1.0x10-4)", along with "lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (-12.2 mg/dL; 95% confidence interval, -23 to -0.98; P=0.033), and lower triglycerides (-6.3%; 95% confidence interval, -12 to -0.22; P=0.043)" (Nomura 2017, https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.117.311145). The clinical endpoint moved in the expected direction: "CETP PTV carrier status was associated with reduced risk for CHD (summary odds ratio, 0.70; 95% confidence interval, 0.54-0.90; P=5.1x10-3)", a figure that incorporates an additional Japanese-specific truncating variant genotyped in a further 27,561 participants across three case-control studies of 14,286 cases and 13,275 controls. The honest reading of these numbers notes their asymmetry: the HDL effect is large and overwhelmingly significant, whereas the LDL and triglyceride arms are only marginally so, with the LDL confidence interval extending to -0.98 mg/dL - effectively null at its boundary - and the coronary-disease result comes from case-control odds rather than from a randomised trial in carriers.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human protein-truncating-variant genetics, n=58,469 sequenced plus 27,561 genotyped; no gene-directed therapeutic, and the pharmacological phenocopy has a history of failed and harmful outcome trials)
Translational Gaps: The central question this record cannot answer is why human loss of the protein looks protective while drugs that inhibit it did not deliver. Several explanations remain live and the field has not chosen between them: torcetrapib had an off-target effect that raised blood pressure through aldosterone, lifelong absence from conception may not be equivalent to blocking the protein for a few years in late life, and the concentration of cholesterol in HDL may never have been the causal quantity - HDL particle function may matter more than how much cholesterol it carries. No gene-editing or gene-therapy program targets this gene, so no one has ever been given this genotype; every number here comes from people born with it. The effect sizes for LDL cholesterol and triglycerides are only marginally significant, and the coronary-disease benefit rests on an odds ratio derived from case-control comparison rather than from any randomised trial in carriers, which means the enhancement's headline claim has never been tested prospectively in anyone.
Key References (DOIs): Nomura Circulation Research 2017 https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.117.311145 | Inazu Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis 2025 https://doi.org/10.5551/jat.rv22037 | Barter New England Journal of Medicine 2007 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0706628
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The pharmacological history attached to this target is the most important thing in this record, and it points the other way from the genetics. Torcetrapib, tested in the ILLUMINATE outcome trial, raised HDL cholesterol as designed but increased all-cause mortality and was terminated; evacetrapib in ACCELERATE and dalcetrapib were stopped for futility despite large HDL gains; anacetrapib in REVEAL achieved only a modest event reduction and was not commercialised, partly because the compound accumulated in adipose tissue. Those trial papers were not retrieved for this record, so they are named as context and no numbers are quoted from them - the direction of their outcomes is what matters here. Obicetrapib, from NewAmsterdam Pharma, is the current late-stage candidate, with recent reports describing attenuated kidney-function decline in high-cardiovascular-risk patients and interest in Alzheimer's prevention; that literature (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajpc.2026.101532 and https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jlr.2026.101029) was retrieved as metadata only, and again no figures from it are asserted. Homozygous deficiency of this protein is comparatively common in Japan and produces marked hyperalphalipoproteinemia whose long-term consequences remain under active debate (Inazu 2025, https://doi.org/10.5551/jat.rv22037). Two further caveats on population specificity: a 2025 Atherosclerosis paper examines truncating variants and coronary risk specifically among heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia patients, a group in which the effect may differ (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atherosclerosis.2025.120417, metadata only), and a separate genome-wide association study reports protective variation at this locus in cardiovascular resilience (https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.123.031459). Reference identifiers are UniProt P11597 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P11597) and PDB 2OBD (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/2OBD), one of three solved structures.

Narrative: The Egyptian mongoose attacks cobras with impunity, and the molecular secret fits in a single amino acid change. Snake alpha-neurotoxins kill by binding the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) at the alpha-1 subunit, paralyzing the diaphragm and causing death by suffocation. Drabeck and colleagues showed in 2015 that mongooses, honey badgers, hedgehogs, and pigs have independently acquired amino acid substitutions at position 187 in the toxin-binding site of CHRNA1 that prevent alpha-neurotoxin binding through two mechanisms: introduction of an N-glycosylation motif (F187N in mongooses, adding a bulky sugar that blocks the toxin) or a positive charge (Y187R in honey badgers, electrostatically repelling the toxin). In 2022, Drabeck expanded the survey to find at least 13 independent instances of convergent venom resistance across all mammals — one of the most frequently convergently evolved traits known. Crucially, these single amino acid changes do not impair normal acetylcholine signaling. The receptor still conducts neurotransmission perfectly. This makes CHRNA1 F187N an ideal base editing target: one nucleotide change, minimal off-target risk, and the adaptation has been validated by natural selection in over a dozen independent mammalian lineages.
Short Description: Mongooses and other venom-resistant mammals carry receptor changes that prevent cobra-like alpha-neurotoxins from blocking the nerve-to-muscle signal. Evolution has independently arrived at related solutions at least 13 times, suggesting a robust way to preserve breathing and movement during otherwise paralysing envenomation. The protection is exquisitely targeted to toxins that bind nicotinic acetylcholine receptors rather than a universal antidote to every venom.
Mechanism: The F187N substitution introduces an N-linked glycosylation sequon at the alpha-neurotoxin binding site of the nAChR alpha-1 subunit. The attached N-glycan sterically blocks alpha-bungarotoxin and cobra neurotoxin binding. Alternative Y187R introduces positive charge that electrostatically repels cationic toxin. Both leave acetylcholine binding and channel gating intact.
Achievements (effect sizes): Drabeck 2015 Toxicon: convergent nAChR mutations in mongoose (F187N), honey badger (Y187R), hedgehog, pig — two distinct biochemical resistance mechanisms. Drabeck 2022 Biol Lett: 13 independent convergent evolution events across mammals under positive selection. Chandrasekara 2025: 25 additional instances in Australian skinks, binding assays confirming resistance.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mammalian natural variants + functional binding assays)
Translational Gaps: No engineered base-editing demonstration — all evidence from natural variants. In-vivo venom challenge in edited animals not performed. Protection specific to alpha-neurotoxins — does not cover hemotoxic, cytotoxic, or phospholipase venoms.
Key References (DOIs): Drabeck Toxicon 2015 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.toxicon.2015.03.007 | Drabeck Biol Lett 2022 https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2022.0361
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Protects ONLY against alpha-neurotoxins (elapid snake venom) — not viper hemotoxins, bee venom, or other mechanisms. Practical utility is narrow: relevant for people in cobra/krait/mamba habitats or military/fieldwork in tropical regions. The beauty is evolutionary validation — nature has run this exact experiment 13+ times and the edit always works without breaking the receptor.

Narrative:
Bowhead whales live past 200 years in Arctic water, reach more than 80,000 kilograms, and are not especially cancer-prone despite having vastly more cells and vastly more time in which those cells can go wrong. Firsanov and colleagues set out to find why, and the answer they found inverts the usual expectation.

They first asked how many oncogenic hits bowhead fibroblasts need to transform. The answer was fewer than human fibroblasts need, not more. The whale is not protected by extra tumour suppressor barriers. What its cells do have is better repair: enhanced double-strand break repair capacity and fidelity, and lower mutation rates than other mammals. Screening DNA repair proteins across species by immunoblot, quantitative mass spectrometry and transcriptome sequencing turned up the cold-inducible RNA-binding protein CIRBP as markedly abundant in bowhead fibroblasts and tissues, while it was largely undetectable in other mammals apart from humpback whale, with moderate levels in dolphins. Putting bowhead CIRBP into human cells enhanced both non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination, reduced micronuclei formation, promoted DNA end protection and stimulated end joining in vitro; the legacy version of this record quantified those gains as roughly 1.6-fold and the whale's protein abundance as roughly 100 times the human and mouse level, figures that summarise the paper's panel data rather than sentences in its text. Overexpressing CIRBP in Drosophila extended lifespan and improved survival after irradiation (2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09694-5).

The strategy this describes is meticulous proofreading rather than armour plating. The whale cell is not hard to break. It is very good at fixing what breaks, and fixing it correctly the first time instead of leaving a scar.
Short Description: Bowhead-whale CIRBP makes repair of DNA double-strand breaks more accurate, a compelling feature in an animal that maintains a vast body for more than two centuries. In human cells the whale protein improved repair performance by about 1.6-fold, and it also extended survival in fruit flies. The result points to better repair quality—not merely faster patching—as a route to keeping long-lived tissues genetically stable.
Mechanism:
CIRBP is a small stress-response RNA-binding protein of roughly 18 kilodaltons, built from an RNA recognition motif and a glycine-rich domain. At a double-strand break it accumulates in the chromatin fraction, an enrichment that Firsanov and colleagues showed is sensitive to RNase A treatment, indicating that its recruitment depends on RNA. Once there it promotes loading of the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer onto DNA ends, protects double-stranded DNA from exonuclease degradation, and stimulates end joining, which places it upstream in the non-homologous end joining pathway alongside the XRCC4-DNA ligase IV step. It also binds poly(ADP-ribose), linking it to the earliest damage-signalling events.

The bowhead advantage is a matter of protein abundance rather than a novel catalytic activity. Human and bowhead CIRBP differ by five carboxy-terminal amino acid residues. Substituting those five residues from the whale into human CIRBP increased its protein abundance, and the reciprocal substitution into the whale protein decreased it. The humanised-to-whale swap did not reach full bowhead expression levels, which led the authors to conclude that synonymous changes to the messenger RNA coding sequence also contribute to higher translation efficiency (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09694-5).
Achievements (effect sizes):
Firsanov and colleagues reported that CIRBP is markedly abundant in bowhead whale fibroblasts and tissues, measured by western blot, by label-free liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry on fibroblasts from twelve samples per species and on nuclear liver extracts from three biological replicates per species, and by transcriptome sequencing. In the same panel it was largely undetectable in other mammals except humpback whale, with moderate levels in dolphins. The legacy version of this record summarised the difference as approximately 100 times higher protein abundance in bowhead than in human or mouse, and the repair gain in human cells as approximately 1.6-fold for both non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination; both figures are readings of the paper's quantified panels rather than values stated in its running text, and I have kept them here in that form rather than dropping them. By contrast, Ku70, Ku80 and DNA-PKcs were more abundant in human cells than in the whale, which the authors interpret as a human-specific adaptation.

Expressing bowhead CIRBP in human fibroblasts enhanced both non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination frequencies, measured with GFP reporter constructs, and reduced the percentage of binucleated cells carrying micronuclei three days after 2 Gy of gamma irradiation. Purified recombinant bowhead CIRBP stimulated end joining in vitro, promoted Ku binding to a labelled double-stranded DNA substrate, and protected a 20-base-pair duplex from T7 exonuclease digestion. Knocking CIRBP down in bowhead fibroblasts with small interfering RNA reduced repair, closing the loop in the whale's own cells.

Bowhead fibroblasts themselves resolved double-strand break foci faster than human cells after bleomycin, were more resistant to bleomycin and etoposide in clonogenic assays, and formed fewer micronuclei after gamma irradiation. Sequencing of repair junctions indicated higher non-homologous end joining fidelity in the whale than in humans and other mammals, alongside lower mutation rates.

Overexpression of CIRBP in Drosophila extended adult survival, with 1,357 flies for the bowhead construct and 1,730 for the human construct, and improved resistance to irradiation. Bowhead CIRBP also inhibited anchorage-independent growth in soft agar and slowed tumour progression in xenografts of transformed human fibroblasts (2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09694-5).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 + T3 (Drosophila whole-organism longevity) + T2
Translational Gaps: No transgenic mouse lifespan or cancer study has been done, so the longevity claim rests on Drosophila and the repair claim on cultured human cells. Delivery to a human would require adeno-associated virus or lipid nanoparticle packaging, neither of which has been attempted for this gene. The safety question is specific and known: the same protein released into the extracellular space acts as a pro-inflammatory damage-associated molecular pattern, so raising CIRBP levels systemically has a defined mechanism by which it could cause harm.
Key References (DOIs): Firsanov Nature 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09694-5 | Qiang Nature Medicine 2013 https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.3368
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
The central paradox is that bowhead fibroblasts require fewer oncogenic hits to transform than human fibroblasts do (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09694-5). The whale's cancer resistance therefore cannot be explained by stronger tumour-suppressive barriers, which is the mechanism most often proposed for Peto's paradox, and instead has to be explained by repair fidelity. This matters for anyone reasoning about human application: importing a whale repair protein does not import a whale-like resistance to transformation, and the two properties are separable.

CIRBP has genuinely opposed roles depending on where it is. Inside the nucleus it supports accurate repair. Released from stressed cells, extracellular CIRP acts as a pro-inflammatory damage-associated molecular pattern in haemorrhagic shock and sepsis (Qiang 2013, https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.3368), and it also has ischaemia-reperfusion injury and pro-tumorigenic roles reported in hepatocellular carcinoma and breast cancer. Whether raising it helps or harms is therefore context-dependent in a way that is not resolved.

The causal attribution is not airtight either. CIRBP is one among many differentially expressed proteins in the bowhead comparison, and RPA2 is also elevated. The authors' knockdown and overexpression experiments make the case for CIRBP contributing, but they do not exclude other contributors to the whale's repair phenotype.

The two clinical trial records attached to this gene are observational measurements of the human protein, not interventions. One assesses serum and tissue CIRBP levels in patients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06260189) and the other examines the correlation between donor CIRBP and transplanted kidney function as a predictor of delayed graft function (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06641622). Nobody is administering CIRBP to a human.

Manipulation: Overexpression (transgenic; maintains youthful expression level against the normal age-dependent decline)
Narrative:
CISD2 sits on the mitochondrial outer membrane, and the amount of it falls as a mouse ages. That decline matters in both directions, which is unusual and is what makes this gene worth having in the record.

Delete it and the mouse ages early. Tsai's group showed that Cisd2-deficient mice suffer mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction with autophagic cell death, and that these events precede the first visible failures — nerve and muscle degeneration — assembling into a premature-ageing phenotype. Homozygous nulls lost around 22% of median lifespan in females and 21.8% in males; heterozygotes were shortened too, so one functional copy is not enough. The same work identified CISD2 as the causative gene for Wolfram syndrome 2 in humans and argued the syndrome is in part mitochondrial (Chen 2009, https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.1779509).

Then they did the harder experiment. Holding CISD2 at a persistent youthful level by transgenic expression extended both median and maximum lifespan — 19.3% mean in males, 18.8% in females — and did so, in the authors' words, without apparent deleterious side effects. Skin, skeletal muscle and neurons all aged more slowly, mitochondria were protected from age-associated damage and functional decline, and the age-associated fall in whole-body energy metabolism was attenuated (Wu 2012, https://doi.org/10.1093/hmg/dds210).

The gene lies on human chromosome 4q, in the interval where an early linkage study mapped a component of human longevity. That is motivation rather than evidence — 4q is a large piece of chromosome — and the authors present it as such.

What makes CISD2 a strong entry is the symmetry: loss shortens life and causes a human disease, restoration to youthful levels extends it, and both arms carry mitochondrial and tissue-level phenotypes rather than a bare survival curve. What makes it incomplete is that both arms come from the same laboratory.
Short Description: A small protein on the mitochondrial outer membrane keeps those mitochondria intact, and the body makes progressively less of it with age. Holding it at youthful levels extended mouse median and maximum lifespan by about 19% while slowing degeneration of skin, muscle and neurons — one Taiwanese laboratory, no vector or drug. Humans who inherit two broken copies get Wolfram syndrome 2: juvenile optic atrophy and diabetes.
Mechanism: CISD2 (also NAF-1) is a 135-residue CDGSH iron-sulfur domain protein anchored in the mitochondrial outer membrane and in endoplasmic-reticulum membranes, binding a labile [2Fe-2S] cluster through redox-sensitive coordination. It participates in iron-sulfur cluster handling and in the control of calcium flux and autophagy at the mitochondria-ER interface. Its loss causes mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction with autophagic cell death, with nerve and muscle failing first, consistent with their dependence on mitochondrial supply. Sustaining the protein at youthful levels protects mitochondria from age-associated damage and functional decline and attenuates the age-associated fall in whole-body energy metabolism, which places the gene on the mitochondrial-integrity and macroautophagy hallmarks rather than among the antioxidant enzymes.
Achievements (effect sizes):
Loss of function. Cisd2 deficiency in mice caused mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction accompanied by autophagic cell death, preceding nerve and muscle degeneration and producing a premature-ageing phenotype; the work also established CISD2 as the causative gene for Wolfram syndrome 2 in humans (Chen 2009, https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.1779509). Per-cohort survival losses recorded in OpenGenes: homozygous nulls -22.3% median in females and -21.8% in males, a mixed-sex cohort at -27.9% median, and another heterozygous cohort at -20.4% median with a bone phenotype; heterozygotes -16.0% median in females and -8.1% in males, so a single functional copy does not suffice.

Gain of function. A persistent level of CISD2 achieved by transgenic expression extended median and maximum lifespan without apparent deleterious side effects, ameliorated age-associated degeneration of skin, skeletal muscles and neurons, protected mitochondria from age-associated damage and functional decline, and attenuated the age-associated reduction in whole-body energy metabolism (Wu 2012, https://doi.org/10.1093/hmg/dds210). Per-cohort figures: +19.3% mean and +19.4% median lifespan in males, +18.8% mean and median in females, with the maximum-lifespan gain reaching +28.7% in the female cohort.

The two arms are internally consistent — same gene, same laboratory, opposite manipulations, opposite outcomes, mitochondrial phenotypes in both — and the gain-of-function arm is the rarer and more valuable one, because it is a restoration to youthful expression rather than a supraphysiological load.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (bidirectional mammalian in-vivo lifespan with mitochondrial and multi-tissue endpoints; single laboratory lineage) + T8 for the human loss-of-function phenotype (Wolfram syndrome 2)
Translational Gaps: Both the loss- and gain-of-function lifespan arms come from the same group at National Yang-Ming University, and neither has been independently replicated. There is no CISD2 gene therapy, no vector, and no compound that raises CISD2 expression in a human; the only registered human study touching the gene is the Wolfram syndrome registry (NCT02841553), which observes patients who have lost it rather than supplying it. The human genetic evidence runs entirely in the loss direction, so we know what human deficiency looks like and nothing about human excess. The chromosome 4q longevity linkage that motivated the work is a broad interval and has not been resolved to this gene. Because the intervention is defined as maintaining a youthful level, its translation also depends on a dosing window nobody has mapped: the mouse experiment did not test expression above the youthful set point, and CISD2/NAF-1 is overexpressed in several human cancers where it supports tumour-cell survival.
Key References (DOIs): Chen Genes Dev 2009 https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.1779509 | Wu Hum Mol Genet 2012 https://doi.org/10.1093/hmg/dds210
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN THE RECORD AND BOTH BELONG. Eight mouse cohorts: two gain-of-function cohorts extend lifespan (+19.3% mean males, +18.8% mean females), six loss-of-function cohorts shorten it (-8.1% to -27.9% median). The enhancement claim rests on the two overexpression cohorts; the six negative rows are the loss-of-function arm and are recorded with positive='false'.

HUMAN DISEASE TRADEOFF, NAMED. Biallelic loss of CISD2 causes Wolfram syndrome 2: juvenile optic atrophy, diabetes mellitus, defective platelet aggregation with bleeding tendency, and neurodegeneration. The direction of the enhancement (more, not less) is therefore not contradicted by human genetics — but the gene is a Mendelian disease locus and any manipulation touches it.

CANCER TRADEOFF. CISD2/NAF-1 is overexpressed in several human cancers, where the protein supports tumour-cell survival and resistance to apoptosis. The mouse gain-of-function study reported no deleterious side effects but was not a tumour study, and it deliberately restored youthful rather than supraphysiological levels. Expression above the youthful set point is not covered by the mouse data.

SINGLE LABORATORY. Both arms are from Tsai's group; no independent replication of either the shortened or the extended survival curve.

CHROMOSOME 4q. The human longevity linkage on 4q is cited by the authors as motivation for studying the gene. It is a large interval and has not been resolved to CISD2. Do not present it as a human longevity association for this gene — the OpenGenes record contains no longevity-association rows for CISD2.

THE MAXIMUM-LIFESPAN COLUMN. The largest single number in the gain-of-function record is +28.7% maximum lifespan in females. The headline used on the card is the mean/median figure of about 19%.

Narrative: Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time — one hemisphere stays awake, so they never stop swimming or breathing. The molecular question is whether this is hardwired into the genes of their circadian clock. Yin et al. in 2025 took the cetacean-specific amino-acid changes and dropped them into zebrafish Clock and Bmal1 proteins, then bred transgenic larvae: the mutant fish slept significantly less, stayed alert longer, and upregulated wake-promoting glutamate signaling while downregulating the sleep-promoting GABA and acetylcholine networks. That's a real result — a cell-autonomous piece of the sleep rewiring — but it's also a toe in the water, not a leg. The actual dolphin genes have never been knocked into a mammal. Zebrafish don't have unihemispheric sleep, and hemispheric asymmetry is almost certainly a brain-network property, not something you can install in a cell culture. The clock mutations look like one ingredient in a much larger recipe.
Short Description: Cetacean-style substitutions in CLOCK and BMAL1 strengthened circadian transcription and shifted neural signalling toward wakefulness. Zebrafish larvae carrying the altered proteins slept less, had shorter sleep bouts and woke more often, providing a functional demonstration of reduced sleep drive. Dolphin-like half-brain sleep still depends on specialised neural circuitry, but these variants reveal a molecular ingredient that can tune the sleep–wake balance.
Mechanism: bHLH-PAS circadian transcription factors; cetacean-specific substitutions alter nuclear localization and TF activation.
Achievements (effect sizes): Yin 2025 PLOS Genet: cetacean-specific substitutions introduced into ZEBRAFISH Clocka/Bmal1a backbone. Luciferase per1b promoter reporter: Clocka-mut and Bmal1a-mut significantly enhanced transactivation. Nuclear localization increased; Co-IP showed stronger heterodimer (p=0.0184). Zebrafish larvae overexpressing mutants (n=40–46) had significantly reduced sleep, shorter bouts, more wake bouts (p<0.0001). Transcriptome: ↑glutamatergic wakefulness genes; ↓GABAergic/cholinergic sleep genes.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (zebrafish whole-organism)
Translational Gaps: Mouse knock-in; EEG/hemispheric resolution study; unihemispheric sleep is not a cell-autonomous phenotype.
Key References (DOIs): Yin PLoS Genet 2025 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011598
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: NOT the actual dolphin gene — mutations introduced on zebrafish backbone at homologous positions; zebrafish don't exhibit USWS; no mammalian validation. Same group's Bai 2024 SLEEP: BMAL2 (not BMAL1) K204E/K346Q enhances PER2 activation in zebrafish — three different clock genes (CLOCK, BMAL1, BMAL2) all claimed to adapt, overlapping claims unresolved. USWS is widely viewed as network/neuroanatomical, not cell-autonomous.

Narrative: The deathstalker scorpion's sting contains a 36-amino-acid peptide called chlorotoxin that evolution designed to kill — but oncologists are using it to find and treat brain tumors. Chlorotoxin selectively binds chloride channels and matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) on the surface of glioma cells with remarkable specificity, while ignoring normal brain tissue. Mamelak and colleagues ran Phase I/II clinical trials in 2006 using iodine-131-labeled synthetic chlorotoxin (TM-601) injected directly into brain tumors of 18 glioma patients: the peptide bound to tumor periphery with long retention, one patient achieved partial response, and two were disease-free beyond 30 months. A next-generation version, tozuleristide (BLZ-100), conjugates chlorotoxin with a near-infrared fluorescent dye for real-time surgical tumor visualization. Patil and colleagues reported in 2019 that BLZ-100 was safe at doses up to 30 mg IV with fluorescence detected in both high- and low-grade gliomas. This is one of the most clinically advanced venom-derived peptides in medicine — a scorpion protein repurposed to paint cancers visible under a surgeon's lamp. The FDA granted orphan drug designation for pediatric brain tumor imaging.
Short Description: Chlorotoxin turns a 36-amino-acid scorpion peptide into a precision guide for glioma surgery and targeted treatment. A radioactive form concentrated around brain tumours in an 18-person study, while fluorescent tozuleristide made both high- and low-grade gliomas visible during surgery at doses up to 30 mg intravenously. It is a vivid example of venom chemistry repurposed to find malignant tissue that is difficult to distinguish from healthy brain.
Mechanism: Chlorotoxin is a 36-aa cystine-knot miniprotein with 4 disulfide bonds. It binds MMP-2 and chloride channels (ClC-3) overexpressed on glioma cell surfaces, inhibiting cell migration and invasion. Glioma selectivity correlates with annexin A2 expression. Conjugated to I-131 for targeted radiotherapy or ICG for fluorescence-guided surgery.
Achievements (effect sizes): Mamelak 2006 J Clin Oncol: Phase I/II 131I-TM-601 in 18 glioma patients — well tolerated, tumor-specific binding, 1 PR, 2 disease-free >30 months. Patil 2019 Neurosurgery: BLZ-100 Phase I safe at 30 mg IV, fluorescence in gliomas, no DLTs. Fu 2007: recombinant CTX IC50 ~0.28 μM in glioma vs ~8 μM in normal astrocytes.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (Phase I/II human clinical trials)
Translational Gaps: Glioma selectivity mechanism incompletely understood. Full regulatory approval not yet achieved. IV systemic delivery crosses BBB with limited efficiency. Non-brain tumor applications less validated.
Key References (DOIs): Mamelak J Clin Oncol 2006 https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2005.05.4569 | Patil Neurosurgery 2019 https://doi.org/10.1093/neuros/nyz125 | Fu Neurosci Lett 2006 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neulet.2006.10.056
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: While chlorotoxin is a scorpion venom component, the therapeutic versions are synthetic peptides — no actual venom production is involved. BLZ-100/tozuleristide (Blaze Bioscience) is the most clinically advanced chlorotoxin conjugate. The binding mechanism via annexin A2 and MMP-2 is still debated — specificity correlates with but may not be perfectly selective for malignant tissue.

Manipulation: Overexpression of the secreted isoform (human transgene)
Narrative:
Most chaperones live inside cells and spend ATP. Clusterin does neither. It is secreted into blood and cerebrospinal fluid, works without any energy source, and its job is to catch proteins that have started to unfold in the extracellular space and hold them in a soluble complex before they can aggregate. It is the extracellular arm of proteostasis, and the space it patrols is exactly where amyloid forms.

The cleanest gain-of-function test was done in flies. Kim and colleagues put the human secreted clusterin coding sequence into Drosophila under GAL4 control and found the protein in adult homogenates and larval haemolymph. Flies expressing it ubiquitously or in motor neurons lived significantly longer than uninduced controls, and were more tolerant of heat shock, wet starvation and oxidative stress, with lower whole-body reactive oxygen species (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2012.03.087). The largest single OpenGenes row is a 32.5% mean-lifespan gain in motor-neuron-expressing males, 32.9 to 43.6 days.

The mammalian half of the story arrived from a different direction. De Miguel and colleagues at Stanford found that plasma from running mice, infused into sedentary mice, reduces brain inflammation, and that clusterin is one of the proteins that goes up. Intravenously injected clusterin binds brain endothelial cells and lowers neuroinflammatory gene expression in both an acute-inflammation model and an Alzheimer's model, and people with cognitive impairment who exercised for six months had higher plasma clusterin (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04183-x). That is protein infusion, not gene delivery — a distinction this card keeps.
Short Description: A secreted chaperone circulates in blood, grips proteins that have begun to unfold and holds them soluble before they can clump, and coats brain blood vessels to damp inflammatory signalling. Flies carrying the human gene lived 32.5% longer on average, from 32.9 to 43.6 days, though maximum lifespan moved only 11.9%. Injected as protein it calms inflamed mouse brains, but the gene has never been delivered to a mammal and this locus carries a common Alzheimer's risk allele.
