Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Part of a multi-gene iron management system; isolated overexpression may not recapitulate full benefit.

Manipulation: Overexpression (moderate; human G6PD transgene under its own endogenous promoter)
Narrative:
Most antioxidant experiments add an enzyme that destroys a reactive molecule. This one adds the enzyme that pays for the destruction.

Every major antioxidant system in the cell — thioredoxins, glutaredoxins, peroxiredoxins, and the maintenance of catalase in its active form — ultimately runs on the reducing power of NADPH, and the enzyme that sets NADPH availability is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase at the head of the pentose phosphate pathway. Nóbrega-Pereira and colleagues in Manuel Serrano's group built a mouse carrying a human G6PD transgene under its own endogenous promoter, deliberately keeping the overexpression moderate rather than maximal, and followed cohorts to death on standard chow.

The animals had higher NADPH, lower ROS-derived damage, and better protection from age-associated functional decline. Median lifespan rose in females by 3.45 months, 13.7%; in males it did not move, and maximum lifespan was unchanged in both sexes. The healthspan effects also split by sex: old transgenic males had better glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, old transgenic females better rotarod performance (Nóbrega-Pereira 2016, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10894).

The part that earns this gene its place is the cancer arm, because G6PD is a textbook worry. The enzyme is overexpressed in many human tumours and has been proposed to be pro-oncogenic, so the obvious objection to raising it is that you are feeding tumour biosynthesis. The authors tested that directly and did not find it: the transgene had no effect on tumour development, in a wild-type background or when crossed onto p53-null, Atm-null, MMTV-PyMT and Emu-Myc tumour-prone backgrounds. Detailed histopathology of the deceased animals found no difference in the profile of pathologies.

A single moderate-overexpression cohort with a female-only median gain is not a large longevity result. As a demonstration that supplying reducing power is safer than it looks, with the cancer question actually asked, it is a clean one.
Short Description: Every antioxidant system in the body runs on reducing power, and one enzyme at the head of the pentose phosphate pathway sets how much of it is available. Mice with a moderate extra copy had higher NADPH, less oxidative damage, and a female median lifespan 3.45 months longer at 13.7%, while maximum lifespan did not change at all. Males got the metabolic benefits but no extra lifespan whatsoever.
Mechanism: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (515 residues) catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of the pentose phosphate pathway, oxidising glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone and reducing NADP+ to NADPH. NADPH is the terminal electron donor for the thioredoxin, glutaredoxin and peroxiredoxin systems and is required to keep catalase in its active form, so G6PD activity sets the ceiling on the cell's capacity to reduce oxidised protein thiols and clear peroxides — it does not scavenge a radical itself but supplies the currency that every thiol-based defence spends. Moderate overexpression under the endogenous promoter raises steady-state NADPH and lowers ROS-derived damage without the compartment mistargeting or supraphysiological load that defeated single-enzyme antioxidant experiments.
Achievements (effect sizes):
Nóbrega-Pereira and colleagues generated a transgenic mouse with moderate overexpression of human G6PD under its endogenous promoter and followed cohorts with wild-type littermates for their entire lifespan on standard chow. Transgenic animals had higher NADPH levels, lower levels of ROS-derived damage, and partial protection from age-associated functional decline. Median lifespan of G6PD-Tg females increased significantly by 3.45 months, or 13.7%; there was no significant increase in males, and no effect on maximal lifespan in either sex. Detailed histopathological analysis of the deceased mice found no significant difference in the profile of pathologies developed. Healthspan endpoints separated by sex: old transgenic males showed improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, old transgenic females improved rotarod performance as an index of neuromuscular fitness (Nóbrega-Pereira 2016, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10894).

The cancer arm is the notable negative. G6PD has been proposed to be pro-oncogenic on the basis of its overexpression in several tumour types and in-vitro work, and overexpression under an actin promoter increases fibroblast proliferation. The authors tested tumour onset in the transgenic line in a wild-type background and on p53-null, Atm-null, MMTV-PyMT and Emu-Myc tumour-prone backgrounds, and found the transgene had no effect on tumour development in any of them.

The OpenGenes record additionally captures the male cohort as a lifespan decrease of -1.3% median, which is the non-significant male result from the same study and should be read as no effect rather than harm.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mammalian in-vivo lifespan and healthspan cohort with a tumour-susceptibility arm across four tumour-prone backgrounds; single laboratory, female-only median effect) + T7 for the human deficiency phenotype
Translational Gaps: No human has received a G6PD transgene, and there is no vector or expression-raising drug. The human literature on this gene is almost entirely about its deficiency: G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide, causes haemolysis on oxidative challenge, and is routinely genotyped or assayed before primaquine and tafenoquine dosing for malaria (NCT02216123, NCT02389374, NCT04698980) and in newborn screening panels (NCT05687474). That tells us what too little looks like in a human and nothing about a moderate excess. The mouse result is also narrow: a single laboratory, one cohort, median-only, females-only, with no change in maximum lifespan — so the effect is best described as a healthspan and early-mortality shift rather than a change in the rate of ageing. The sex split is unexplained. Finally, moderation was designed into the construct by using the endogenous promoter; the cancer-neutral result cannot be extrapolated to a strong promoter, and the authors note that actin-promoter G6PD overexpression does increase fibroblast proliferation.
Key References (DOIs): Nóbrega-Pereira Nature Communications 2016 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10894
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
FEMALE-ONLY, MEDIAN-ONLY. The 13.7% figure is the female median lifespan gain (3.45 months). Males showed no significant increase, and maximal lifespan was unchanged in both sexes. The OpenGenes row recording -1.3% median for males is the non-significant male arm of the same study, not an independent harmful result; it is entered with positive='false' to keep the record honest but should be read as no effect.

CANCER QUESTION WAS ASKED AND ANSWERED, WITHIN LIMITS. G6PD is proposed to be pro-oncogenic and is overexpressed in many human tumours. This study found no effect of the transgene on tumour development in a wild-type background or on p53-null, Atm-null, MMTV-PyMT or Emu-Myc backgrounds, and no difference in the pathology profile at death. That is a stronger safety result than most antioxidant genes carry. It applies to MODERATE overexpression under the endogenous promoter; the paper notes that G6PD overexpression under an actin promoter increases fibroblast proliferation, so a strong promoter is a different experiment.

HUMAN DEFICIENCY IS THE FAMOUS DIRECTION. G6PD deficiency is the most common human enzymopathy and causes drug- and infection-triggered haemolysis; it is screened before primaquine/tafenoquine antimalarial dosing. All registered human trials in the record measure or genotype the enzyme in the deficiency context. None supplies the gene, so all human rows are intervention='observational' or natural_variant.

SEX SPLIT UNEXPLAINED. Lifespan gain in females, metabolic gain (glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity) in males, neuromuscular gain (rotarod) in females. No mechanism was offered.

SINGLE LABORATORY, SINGLE COHORT. Serrano group, 2016; no independent replication.

FLY CONTEXT. G6PD overexpression extends longevity and raises maximum lifespan in Drosophila; the mouse result is weaker than the fly result, which is the usual direction and should not be used to inflate the mammalian claim.

Narrative:
The Antarctic yeast Glaciozyma antarctica lives in permanently frozen sea ice and produces a powerful antifreeze protein to do it. The relevant activity is not the one most people associate with antifreeze. Two properties are usually measured in these proteins: thermal hysteresis, the gap the protein opens between the melting and freezing points of a solution, and ice recrystallisation inhibition, the ability to stop small ice crystals from merging into large ones during temperature fluctuation. GaAFP is strong at the second, which is the property that actually matters for preserving cells and tissue, because freeze-thaw damage comes mostly from large crystals growing at the expense of small ones rather than from the initial freezing event. Fish antifreeze proteins, by contrast, are better known for lowering the freezing point.

Majewska and colleagues found that the Antarctic yeast strain 186, identified as Glaciozyma martinii, secretes a glycosylated ice-binding protein of roughly 27 kilodaltons with ice recrystallisation inhibition activity, the first evidence of antifreeze protein secretion by this species. The native strain makes very little of it and needs at least fourteen days of refrigerated culture, so they cloned the homologous gene from the closely related Glaciozyma antarctica into a pPICZB vector and expressed it in Pichia pastoris strain GS115. The resulting recombinant protein, GaAFP, is 261 amino acids and 26.57 kilodaltons, a value the legacy record rounds to 26.6 kDa, carries a 20-amino-acid signal peptide that lets the yeast secrete it, and showed ice recrystallisation inhibition activity along with a cryoprotective effect in frozen food (2025, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459).
Short Description: The Antarctic-yeast protein GaAFP prevents small ice crystals from merging into larger, tissue-ripping structures during temperature fluctuations. Recombinant 26.6-kDa protein protected frozen vegetables and improved yeast survival after 35 days at −20°C, demonstrating useful cryoprotection at only 0.1–0.2 mg/mL. Its strength is ice-recrystallisation control, a property well suited to food, cell and biomaterial preservation.
Mechanism: GaAFP binds ice crystal surfaces through a flat ice-binding face. Adsorption onto the crystal surface pins the growth front locally, so the ice can only advance by curving between the bound protein molecules, which is energetically unfavourable and slows growth. In practice this manifests primarily as ice recrystallisation inhibition, the suppression of the process by which large crystals grow at the expense of small ones during temperature fluctuation, rather than as strong thermal hysteresis. Hashim and colleagues measured thermal hysteresis of 0.1 degrees C in the Glaciozyma antarctica culture filtrate and 0.08 degrees C for recombinant Afp1 refolded from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies, values comparable to those reported for bacteria and fungi and far below the levels at which thermal-hysteresis-driven protection would dominate (2012, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-012-0494-4). The practical consequence is that GaAFP protects cells and tissues at concentrations where a thermal hysteresis protein would be doing very little.
Achievements (effect sizes):
Hashim and colleagues identified the antifreeze protein gene from a genome sequence survey of Glaciozyma antarctica. The complementary DNA encoded a 177-amino-acid protein with 30% similarity to a fungal antifreeze protein from Typhula ishikariensis. Expression peaked within six hours of growth at minus 12 degrees C. Expressed in Escherichia coli the recombinant protein formed inclusion bodies, was denatured in urea and refolded in vitro, and retained antifreeze activity with a thermal hysteresis of 0.08 degrees C, against 0.1 degrees C for the native culture filtrate (2012, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-012-0494-4).

Majewska and colleagues expressed a synthetic Glaciozyma antarctica gene in Pichia pastoris GS115, obtaining a secreted, 261-amino-acid, 26.57 kilodalton protein, 26.6 kDa when rounded, with a predicted glycosylation site, at optimal yield with 28 degrees C cultivation and 1% methanol induction twice daily over 72 hours. Vegetables and fruit pre-soaked in 0.1 milligrams per millilitre GaAFP and then frozen at minus 20 degrees C kept intact cell structures under microscopy, without the visible ruptures seen in untreated samples, and blueberries retained their pigment. In drip loss testing across five replicates, carrots showed a clear protective effect that was comparable to 0.5 molar glycerol and significantly different from the untreated control, improving with longer soaking time; the legacy version of this record quantified the effect as a 40-60% reduction in drip loss, a figure I could not locate in this paper or in any other source, and which is preserved here as the record's own claim rather than as a published measurement; kohlrabi gave similar results except at the shortest four-hour soak; blueberries showed no clear difference between conditions, which the authors attribute to the intact peel acting both as a barrier to water loss in controls and as a barrier to protein penetration in treated fruit. Frozen baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, held at minus 20 degrees C for 35 days showed increased cell survival with GaAFP at 0.1 and 0.2 milligrams per millilitre. The authors also assessed cytotoxicity against Caco-2 and HT-29 human colon adenocarcinoma lines and RAW 264.7 mouse macrophage-like cells at 50 to 400 micrograms per millilitre and concluded the protein is non-cytotoxic. This was the first demonstration of yeast-derived antifreeze proteins as food cryoprotectants (2025, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps:
Food-grade regulatory approval has not been obtained for this protein. Only type III antifreeze proteins from psychrophilic fish are currently approved for consumption, cleared as an ice cream additive by the European Food Safety Authority in 2008 and by the Food and Drug Administration in 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459), so there is a regulatory path but GaAFP has not walked it.

Pichia pastoris production has been optimised at laboratory scale and needs to be scaled to industrial volumes.

The clinical claim is entirely unmade. Benefit for cryopreservation of human organs and tissues has not been demonstrated; the published cryoprotection data cover carrots, kohlrabi, blueberries and baker's yeast.
Key References (DOIs): Majewska PLOS ONE 2025 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459 | Hashim Extremophiles 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-012-0494-4
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
This gene complements the existing fish antifreeze protein and antifreeze glycoprotein entry in the library through a distinct mechanism: ice recrystallisation inhibition rather than thermal hysteresis. The two are not interchangeable, and the distinction is the whole argument for including both.

The organism attribution needs care. The protein secreted by the Antarctic strain that Majewska and colleagues isolated is GmAFP from Glaciozyma martinii; GaAFP is the recombinant product of a synthetic gene taken from the related species Glaciozyma antarctica and expressed in Pichia pastoris, because the native strain produces too little protein too slowly to work with (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459). The performance data therefore describe a recombinant yeast-produced protein, not a purified native secretion.

The cryoprotection result is not uniform across substrates. It held for carrot and kohlrabi and did not hold for blueberry, and for kohlrabi it failed at the shortest soaking time. A protein that works on cut hard vegetables and not on intact soft fruit is telling us something about penetration, and that has direct implications for whether it could reach the interior of a whole organ.

Manipulation: overexpression (single-copy human hNAG-1/hGDF15 transgene, two independent founder lines)
Narrative: GDF15 is the body's malaise signal. Damaged mitochondria, cellular stress and many drugs raise it, and it acts on one receptor — GFRAL, in the hindbrain — to suppress appetite and drive weight loss. Wang et al. made mice carrying a single extra human GDF15 copy in two independent lines and followed them to death. Female transgenics lived significantly longer in both lines, with the gap widening dramatically on a high-fat diet: on ordinary chow the median gain was 19.5% and 12.8%, but on 60% fat it reached 23.6% and 43.6%, because the wild-type controls on that diet died early and the transgenics did not. The mice were smaller, carried less fat, had lower serum IGF-1, insulin and glucose, better insulin sensitivity and higher energy expenditure, with reduced signalling through the IGF-1/mTOR axis. The awkward fact is the direction of every clinical programme: AV-380, visugromab and NGM120 all BLOCK GDF15 or its receptor, because in cancer patients this hormone causes cachexia. Nobody is developing GDF15 as a therapy to give people; three companies are developing drugs to take it away.
Short Description: A hindbrain-acting hormone suppresses appetite, burns off fat mass and lowers circulating IGF-1 and insulin. Female mice with one extra copy gained 19.5% median lifespan on ordinary chow and 43.6% on 60% fat, and the axis is an active clinical obesity target. Every clinical programme exists to BLOCK it because it drives cancer cachexia, and it works by making you eat less: the mice stayed permanently smaller.
Mechanism: GDF15 is a divergent secreted member of the TGF-β superfamily that signals through GFRAL-RET in the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius of the hindbrain — anatomically an aversion and nausea circuit, not a metabolic one. Chronic elevation reduces food intake and adipose mass and raises energy expenditure and oxidative metabolism. In the transgenics this was accompanied by lower serum IGF-1, insulin and glucose, improved insulin sensitivity, and reduced phosphorylation of IGF-1/mTOR pathway components including p70S6K and PI3K/Akt — the same axis that caloric restriction and growth-hormone-axis mutants work through. Mechanistically, therefore, this is a hormonally-enforced caloric-restriction mimetic rather than a cell-autonomous longevity gene.
Achievements (effect sizes): Two independent founder lines, both showing significantly increased mean and median lifespan in females. On low-fat diet: +19.5% and +12.8% median. On high-fat diet: +23.6% and +43.6% median (line 1398 median 110.6 vs 77.0 weeks in wild type). Reduced body and adipose weight, lowered serum IGF-1, insulin and glucose, improved insulin sensitivity, increased oxygen utilisation and energy expenditure, and reduced IGF-1/mTOR signalling.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (two independent transgenic mouse lines with full survival curves on two diets from one laboratory, plus metabolic and signalling mechanism; females only for lifespan; no human has received GDF15 therapeutically and all human clinical development targets its inhibition)
Translational Gaps: Lifespan was measured in females only — the male transgenics had elevated serum hNAG-1 but no reported survival curve, so a sex-specific effect cannot be excluded. The headline high-fat numbers are partly rescue of diet-induced early death in the controls rather than extension of a normal lifespan, and the low-fat figures are the fairer comparison. No human has received GDF15 as a gene or protein for any indication, and there is no dose-finding or safety data in the supplementation direction. The GFRAL receptor sits in a nausea circuit, so appetite suppression and aversion are not separable side effects — they are the mechanism.
Key References (DOIs): Wang X et al. Aging (Albany NY) 2014;6:690-704 (10.18632/aging.100687); direction-opposing clinical programmes: AV-380 NCT05865535; visugromab CTL-002 NCT04725474; NGM120 NCT04068896
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: THE TRADEOFF IS THE MECHANISM: GDF15 causes anorexia and weight loss through a hindbrain aversion circuit. There is no version of this intervention that gives the metabolic benefit without the appetite suppression — in an older adult that collides directly with sarcopenia and frailty. CACHEXIA: elevated GDF15 is the driver of cancer cachexia, which is why AV-380 (Phase 1b in cachectic cancer patients with elevated GDF-15), visugromab and NGM120 are all antagonists. A GDF15-supplementation card sits opposite the entire clinical literature and the record must say so. SEX: lifespan data are FEMALE ONLY. HFD CONFOUND: the +43.6% figure comes from a cohort whose wild-type controls were dying early on 60% fat (median 77.0 vs 94.9 weeks in the other line's controls). Quote the +19.5% low-fat number as the headline; the HFD number is diet-rescue. BIOMARKER STATUS: GDF15 is used clinically as a marker of mitochondrial disease, heart failure and chemotherapy toxicity — elevated GDF15 in a patient is normally bad news, and that framing is now widespread in the literature. PREGNANCY: GDF15 is strongly implicated in hyperemesis gravidarum; raising it in a person who might become pregnant is contraindicated on current evidence.

Narrative:
Green fluorescent protein was isolated from the crystal jellyfish in 1962 by Osamu Shimomura, cloned in 1992, demonstrated as a reporter gene by Martin Chalfie in 1994 (Chalfie 1994, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295), and has since been used to light up creatures from E. coli to marmosets. It won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and rewrote experimental biology: you can now watch a specific gene switch on, follow a single protein as it moves, or track a tumour as it grows, simply by fusing GFP to it and shining blue light. The protein needs no substrate and no cofactor — only molecular oxygen, which it uses to fold its own chromophore into existence.

There are fluorescent pigs, rabbits, mice, zebrafish, monkeys, and at least one glow-in-the-dark cat. The honest caveat is that GFP is emphatically a laboratory reporter and not a therapeutic. Its green emission barely penetrates tissue, and it is mildly immunogenic in humans, which is why adoptive cell therapies quietly dropped it. Human clinical imaging moved long ago to positron-emission tomography tracers that can be read through the whole body.
Short Description: Green fluorescent protein lets a cell generate bright green light under blue illumination using only the protein itself—no added chemical fuel. It has functioned across organisms from bacteria to transgenic marmosets, transforming biology by making gene expression, cell migration and neural activity directly visible. Its deepest capability is not decoration but a self-contained optical tag that follows living cells through time.
Mechanism: Green fluorescent protein is a 238-amino-acid polypeptide that folds into a barrel of 11 beta strands. Buried at the centre of that barrel, the tripeptide serine 65 - tyrosine 66 - glycine 67 cyclises and oxidises autocatalytically to form the chromophore, so the protein manufactures its own fluorophore from its own backbone. The only external requirement is molecular oxygen; no cofactor, substrate or accessory enzyme is needed, which is precisely why the gene works in essentially any organism it is transferred into.
Achievements (effect sizes): GFP became the universal reporter almost immediately after Chalfie and colleagues showed that the gene alone was sufficient to make E. coli and Caenorhabditis elegans fluoresce (Chalfie 1994, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295); it now works routinely in E. coli, yeast, plants, C. elegans, Drosophila, zebrafish and every standard human cell line. Okabe and colleagues generated the 'green mice', which express enhanced GFP ubiquitously from a CAG promoter and remain a standard source of donor cells for transplantation studies (Okabe 1997, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-5793(97)00313-X). Transgenic GFP pigs were produced in 2006. Sasaki and colleagues went furthest, producing transgenic common marmosets that expressed GFP and transmitted the transgene through the germline to their offspring — the first transgenic non-human primates to do so (Sasaki 2009, https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08090). Transgenic cats were made carrying GFP co-expressed with the antiviral restriction factor TRIMCyp, which rendered their cells resistant to feline immunodeficiency virus (Wongsrikeao 2011, https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1703). On the photophysics, enhanced GFP has a molar extinction coefficient of approximately 56,000 M-1 cm-1 and a quantum yield of 0.6, which is bright enough for single-cell detection, and the photostable c3GFP mutant reported in 2020 is stable enough to survive stimulated emission depletion super-resolution imaging.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human cells routinely); T5 across multiple mammalian species; T7 ex-vivo only (not approved in vivo in humans)
Translational Gaps: The in-vivo clinical reporter role has already been ceded to other systems. Herpes simplex virus thymidine kinase imaged with the positron-emitting tracer [18F]FHBG, the sodium-iodide symporter, prostate-specific membrane antigen and the E. coli dihydrofolate reductase / trimethoprim pair all report from deep tissue, which green fluorescence cannot do. GFP is not approved for in-vivo use in humans and there is no pathway under which a green fluorophore would outperform these tracers in a patient.
Key References (DOIs): Chalfie Science 1994 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295 | Okabe FEBS Letters 1997 https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-5793(97)00313-X | Sasaki Nature 2009 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08090 | Wongsrikeao Nature Methods 2011 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1703
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: GFP belongs in this database as a reporter rather than an enhancement; it tells you what a cell is doing and changes nothing about what the cell can do. Its green emission does not penetrate tissue, so anything deeper than a few millimetres is invisible. Chromophore maturation depends on molecular oxygen, which makes the signal unreliable in hypoxic tissue such as a tumour core. The fluorophore photobleaches under sustained illumination. Most consequentially for anyone thinking about human use, GFP is mildly immunogenic in humans and was cleared out of adoptive cell therapy protocols for that reason. Human clinical imaging uses positron-emission tomography reporters, not GFP.

Manipulation: loss-of-function (E180 splice mutation, homozygous); growth hormone receptor deficiency
Narrative: In the valleys of Loja and El Oro in southern Ecuador there lives an extended set of families whose members reach an adult height of about 118 cm. They were identified in the clinic the ordinary way, by severe short stature with very low IGF-1, and then genotyped: homozygous for a splice mutation at codon 180 of the growth hormone receptor. Growth hormone circulates in their blood normally. Their cells simply cannot hear it. Jaime Guevara-Aguirre's institute in Quito followed them for more than two decades, and in collaboration with Valter Longo's lab in Los Angeles published what remains one of the most striking natural experiments in human ageing: across the monitored cohort there was one non-lethal malignancy and no diabetes at all, in a population whose own relatives - the best possible controls, sharing their genes, diet, water and village - ran 17% cancer and 5% diabetes (Guevara-Aguirre 2011, https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845). The mechanism reads as a list of the pathways lifespan researchers had already found in yeast, worms and mice: with growth hormone signalling abolished, hepatic IGF-1 collapses, RAS, PKA and TOR signalling fall, and the antioxidant enzyme SOD2 rises. Serum from these subjects, applied to human breast epithelial cells under oxidative stress, produced fewer DNA breaks but more apoptosis - damaged cells being deleted rather than kept. And yet the cohort does not live longer, and the reason is a hard lesson about what protection from disease buys you. Of 30 deaths over the age of ten, 21 came from convulsive disorders, alcohol toxicity, accidents and liver cirrhosis. A genotype that removes cancer and diabetes does nothing about the world you live in. Longo has proposed this receptor as a drug target for healthy lifespan extension; three decades after the cohort was described, nothing has reached a trial in that direction.
Short Description: Laron syndrome reveals what lifelong reduction of growth-hormone signalling does in humans: it produces a much smaller body alongside striking protection from diabetes and cancer. Across 22 years, an Ecuadorian cohort of 90 affected people recorded no diabetes and only one non-lethal cancer, versus 5% and 17% in relatives. The tradeoff is defining—adult height averaged 118.5 cm—making this a powerful natural experiment rather than a simple longevity recipe.
Mechanism: GHR encodes the 638-amino-acid growth hormone receptor, the cell-surface protein that binds circulating growth hormone and transduces its signal inward. The Ecuadorian E180 allele is a splice mutation that, in the words of the source, "results in a protein that lacks 8 amino acids in its extracellular domain and is possibly misfolded and degraded". Homozygotes therefore cannot transduce the growth hormone signal at all, and the immediate consequence is that hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) collapses, because that production is the liver's main response to growth hormone. What follows is a lifelong, whole-body attenuation of the growth hormone / IGF-1 / insulin axis: downstream RAS, protein kinase A (PKA) and target-of-rapamycin (TOR) signalling all fall, while the mitochondrial antioxidant superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) rises. This is the same conserved pro-ageing pathway whose attenuation extends lifespan in yeast, nematodes and mice, which is why the cohort attracted longevity researchers rather than only endocrinologists. The proposed anti-cancer arm is a shift in how damaged cells are handled: serum taken from deficient subjects and applied to human mammary epithelial cells under hydrogen peroxide stress reduced DNA breaks but increased apoptosis, meaning damaged cells are eliminated rather than retained and allowed to accumulate mutations.
Achievements (effect sizes): Twenty-two years of monitoring an Ecuadorian growth-hormone-receptor-deficient cohort against 1,606 unaffected first- to fourth-degree relatives produced "only one non-lethal malignancy and no cases of diabetes, in contrast to 17% cancer and 5% diabetes prevalence in the controls", and the diabetes absence was quantified exactly: "we estimated the prevalence of diabetes in the GHRD cohort as 0/90 = 0%, with 95% exact Clopper-Pearson Confidence Interval: 0% - 4%" (Guevara-Aguirre 2011, https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845). Cause-of-death analysis extended the finding to mortality: "cancer was not a cause of death in GHRD subjects of any age group; however, it accounted for 20% of deaths in the relatives". The metabolic phenotype behind this is extreme insulin sensitivity, with fasting insulin of 1.4 microunits per millilitre against 4.4 in unaffected relatives and a HOMA-IR insulin-resistance index of 0.34 against 0.96. The same literature quantifies the cost and the limits with equal precision. Adult height is 118.5 +/- 9.5 cm in 21 affected subjects against 153.2 +/- 7 cm in 23 control relatives (p<0.0001), with weight 43.9 kg against 70.4 kg and head circumference 51.8 against 54.5 cm (Guevara-Aguirre 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medj.2024.03.022). Vascular mortality is not improved - "relative mortality from vascular diseases (combining cardiac disease and stroke) appears to be similar (33% of deaths in relatives vs 30% of deaths in GHRD subjects)" - and no lifespan extension was measured, because of 30 deaths above age ten, 21 came from convulsive disorders, alcohol toxicity, accidents, cirrhosis and other non-age-related causes (https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845). A later follow-up did find carotid plaque in 7% of affected subjects against 36% of controls, though with only 14 versus 11 people assessed the difference was not significant (p = 0.1333), alongside a significantly lower left carotid intima-media thickness (p = 0.0106).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human natural experiment; 22-year prospective cohort with n=90 for the diabetes estimate, 1,606 relative controls, plus an independent 2024 cardiovascular follow-up)
Translational Gaps: The cohort is small and geographically confined to two Ecuadorian provinces, and the cancer-incidence finding rests on the absence of events rather than on a measured rate, which by construction carries wide intervals - the diabetes estimate of 0% spans 0% to 4%. No lifespan extension has been demonstrated, and cannot be from this cohort, because 70% of deaths came from causes that have nothing to do with ageing; whether removing cancer and diabetes would translate into longer life in a safer environment remains untested. There is no route to this phenotype in an adult body. Partial pharmacological suppression of the growth hormone / IGF-1 axis is possible - the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant exists and is licensed for acromegaly - but it has never been trialled for cancer or diabetes prevention, and doing so would trade against the documented consequences of adult growth hormone deficiency. It also remains unresolved whether the protection requires the deficiency to be present from development onward, as it is in these families, or whether an intervention started in mid-life could capture any of it.
Key References (DOIs): Guevara-Aguirre Science Translational Medicine 2011 https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845 | Guevara-Aguirre Med 2024 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medj.2024.03.022 | Guevara-Aguirre BMJ Case Reports 2020 https://doi.org/10.1136/bcr-2019-231737
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The registry direction here is worth stating plainly, because it inverts this library's framing. Every interventional trial found in these families runs the opposite way: NCT00571727 (Ipsen, mecasermin, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00571727) and NCT00368173 (Insmed, recombinant IGF-1 with IGFBP-3, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00368173) both administer IGF-1 to children in order to reverse the deficiency and restore height. Neither tests the enhancement; the clinical world treats this genotype as a disease to be corrected, and neither trial administers or edits the gene itself. The one same-direction human intervention is pharmacological rather than genetic: pegvisomant, a growth hormone receptor antagonist, was used in a University of California insulin-sensitivity study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02023918), which again measures rather than installs the genotype and was not aimed at longevity. A further caution for anyone reading the lipid panel of this genotype: the 2024 follow-up found affected subjects have elevated LDL cholesterol yet lower carotid intima-media thickness (Guevara-Aguirre 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medj.2024.03.022), so their blood work looks worse than their arteries do. Obesity is also part of the clinical picture rather than absent from it, with body mass index 31 against 30.1 in relatives and 57% versus 52% above a BMI of 30. Finally, the non-medical cost is documented in the same literature: people with genetic syndromes of severe short stature in developing countries face social branding and stigma (Guevara-Aguirre 2020, https://doi.org/10.1136/bcr-2019-231737). Reference identifiers are UniProt P10912 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P10912) and PDB 1A22 (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1A22), one of eleven solved structures.

Narrative: The Venus' flower basket sponge (Euplectella aspergillum) builds an intricate glass skeleton at ambient temperature and pressure — a feat human engineering cannot match. Glassin is the silica-precipitating protein that templates this process, directing dissolved silicic acid into precisely organized nanoscale glass fibers with fiber-optic-grade optical clarity. This biological glass factory operates where industrial synthesis requires extreme heat.
Short Description: Glassin helps glass sponges assemble silica at room temperature and neutral pH, replacing harsh industrial conditions with protein-guided mineral growth. Recombinant glassin can produce amorphous silica nanoparticles, while the sponge's complete silica fibres also conduct light. This points toward biologically manufactured optical and structural materials, with the protein serving as a gentle nucleator rather than the entire finished skeleton.
Mechanism: Glassin contains a unique silica-condensing domain that catalyzes polycondensation of silicic acid. The protein self-assembles into filaments that template hierarchical silica deposition, creating structures with superior mechanical properties to synthetic glass fibers — combining strength, flexibility, and optical waveguide capability.
Achievements (effect sizes): Recombinant glassin produces amorphous silica nanoparticles at room temperature and neutral pH. Sponge spicules show fiber-optic light transmission with better flexibility than industrial optical fibers.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Scaling recombinant production for industrial application. Multi-protein cooperation in vivo may be required for full structural hierarchy. Biocompatibility for medical implants needs validation.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Most advanced bio-glass material known. Potential applications in optical sensors, bone scaffolds, and room-temperature glass manufacturing.

Narrative: The naked mole-rat is virtually immune to cancer and lives 10x longer than similar-sized rodents. Its fructose metabolism pathway is uniquely altered — GLUT5 transporter and ketohexokinase (KHK) show reduced expression, effectively blocking fructose-driven lipogenesis and metabolic syndrome. This natural metabolic rewiring may explain the species' remarkable resistance to obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disease.
Short Description: The naked mole-rat's fructose-handling programme suggests a way to uncouple sugar use from liver-fat production. In mice, inhibiting ketohexokinase cut liver fat by about 80%, and a KHK inhibitor has reached Phase 2 testing for metabolic liver disease. The capability is selective metabolic rerouting: preserve useful energy handling while reducing the fructose flux that feeds steatosis.
Mechanism: Downregulated GLUT5 limits cellular fructose uptake. Reduced KHK activity prevents fructose phosphorylation and subsequent de novo lipogenesis, uric acid production, and ATP depletion. Together they block the fructose-driven metabolic syndrome cascade.
Achievements (effect sizes): Naked mole-rats show no age-related metabolic decline. KHK inhibitors in mice reduce hepatic steatosis by 80%. Pfizer KHK inhibitor PF-06835919 reached Phase 2 clinical trials for NASH.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Species-specific metabolic context may limit direct translation. KHK inhibition in humans needs careful monitoring for hereditary fructose intolerance-like effects.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab3896
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: KHK pharmaceutical inhibitors already in clinical development independently of NMR biology.

Narrative: Greenland sharks swim through Arctic depths for 272 to 392 years — some individuals were alive before the American Revolution. Julius Nielsen dated them by radiocarbon-dating their eye lenses in 2016, making them the longest-lived vertebrates known. In 2024, a preprint from Alessandro Cellerino's group reported a 6.45-Gb genome assembly: 81 duplicated genes enriched for DNA double-strand-break repair, three copies of RAD51, expanded NF-κB signaling, and a unique lysine insertion in the C-terminus of p53 that AlphaFold predicts would extend an alpha-helix. All of it, so far, is comparative genomics — no one has expressed the shark p53 variant in a cell, knocked it into a mouse, or done any functional assay whatsoever. The shark is essentially unculturable; you cannot easily get primary cells. It's the most tantalizing longevity genome we have, and simultaneously the one furthest from any experiment a lab could actually run next Tuesday.
Short Description: The Greenland shark combines extreme longevity—estimated at at least 272 years—with an expanded DNA-maintenance repertoire, including three copies of RAD51 in a recent genome analysis. The pattern suggests unusually strong capacity for homologous repair across a very long life. It remains a genomic hypothesis until individual shark variants are tested, but it offers a focused set of candidates for studying how giant, ancient vertebrates maintain their chromosomes.
Mechanism: 81 duplicated genes forming DSB-repair GO-enriched STRING network; RAD51 in 3 copies (one intronless retrotranspositional); NF2 duplication; unique lysine insertion in p53 HKKEKE C-terminal motif predicted (AlphaFold3) to extend helix.
Achievements (effect sizes): Sahm 2024 bioRxiv (preprint): 6.45 Gb chromosome-level assembly; 22,634 genes; statistical enrichment p=0.029 (network), FDR=0.002 with TP53. Nielsen 2016 Science: lens radiocarbon dating → minimum ages 272 y. Nothing else — all predictions purely computational; no functional assay on GLS p53 variant; no mouse knock-in; no heterologous cell test; no tissue culture possible.
Highest Evidence Tier: T1 (genomic + in silico AlphaFold3 only)
Translational Gaps: Everything — expression/functional validation of GLS p53 variant; knock-in mouse; cell models.
Key References (DOIs): Sahm bioRxiv 2024 https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.09.09.611499 | Nielsen Science 2016 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Preprint; no expression/functional validation; p53 CTD structural prediction is low-confidence; RAD51 overexpression is oncogenic in mammals. "512-yr shark" = upper 95.4% CI bound; measured floor is ~272 y.

Manipulation: Gene therapy overexpression (AAV-delivered progranulin; the human disease direction is haploinsufficiency)
Narrative: Progranulin is a secreted growth factor that neurons and microglia rely on to keep lysosomes working. Losing one functional copy is enough to cause frontotemporal dementia in humans — GRN haploinsufficiency is one of the most common genetic causes — and losing both copies causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, a lysosomal storage disease. Mouse knockouts confirm the direction from the deficit side: complete Grn loss cut median lifespan by 32.5%. That makes progranulin unusual in this library — the enhancement direction (put more of it in) is precisely what three independent companies are already doing in humans. AviadoBio delivers AVB-101 into the thalamus, Prevail/Lilly delivers LY3884963, and Passage Bio delivers PBFT02, all AAV vectors carrying GRN, all in Phase 1/2 for FTD-GRN, with 18-35 participants each. Every one of those trials has adverse events as a primary endpoint, which is the honest read on where this stands: humans have received the gene, and nobody has yet shown it changes the course of the disease.
Short Description: A secreted factor keeps neuronal and microglial lysosomes clearing their contents, and losing one copy causes frontotemporal dementia. Three AAV gene therapies are dosing humans now — AVB-101, LY3884963 and PBFT02 — while mice lacking the gene entirely lost 32.5% of median lifespan. Mice with one copy removed lived slightly longer, so the mouse does not model the human deficit and the trials so far report safety, not efficacy.
Mechanism: Progranulin is a 593-residue secreted glycoprotein, cleaved by elastases into granulin peptides. It traffics to the lysosome via sortilin (SORT1) and prosaposin, where it supports the activity of lysosomal hydrolases including cathepsin D and glucocerebrosidase. Insufficiency produces lysosomal dysfunction, TDP-43 pathology, microglial over-activation and lipofuscin accumulation. The therapeutic logic is dose restoration rather than novel function: AAV-delivered GRN raises CSF and brain progranulin toward or above the normal range in carriers who have roughly half. Delivery route matters because progranulin is secreted and can cross-correct neighbouring cells — trials use intrathalamic or intracisternal administration to seed a diffusible supply rather than transduce every neuron.
Achievements (effect sizes): Human loss-of-function establishes the phenotype without ambiguity: GRN haploinsufficiency causes frontotemporal dementia; biallelic loss causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. Complete knockout in mice reduced median lifespan by 32.5%. Three separate AAV-GRN programmes have dosed humans in Phase 1/2 (AVB-101 intrathalamic, n=18, recruiting; LY3884963, n=35; PBFT02, n=30), establishing that the gene can be delivered to the human CNS.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human gene therapy administered in three independent Phase 1/2 trials with safety as primary endpoint and no published efficacy; supported by unambiguous human loss-of-function genetics and a mouse knockout lifespan deficit)
Translational Gaps: No trial has reported an efficacy result — all three are dose-escalation studies whose primary endpoints are adverse events, with CSF progranulin and neurofilament as biomarkers rather than clinical benefit. The mouse does not reproduce the human dose-sensitivity: heterozygous Grn mice lived slightly LONGER (+5.5% median), so the animal model cannot be used to titrate a human dose. Overshoot is a real and unquantified concern — progranulin is a growth factor with reported tumour-promoting activity in several cancers, and no trial has defined an upper safe CSF concentration. Whether restoring progranulin helps a brain that already has TDP-43 pathology, versus preventing it in a presymptomatic carrier, is untested.
Key References (DOIs): Ahmed 2011 Neurobiol Dis (10.1016/j.nbd.2011.08.029); Wils 2012 J Pathol (10.1002/path.4043); AVB-101 NCT06064890 (AviadoBio); LY3884963 NCT04408625 (Prevail Therapeutics); PBFT02 NCT04747431 (Passage Bio)
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: MOUSE-HUMAN MISMATCH: Grn+/- mice showed a 5.5% median lifespan INCREASE while Grn-/- mice lost 32.5% — the heterozygous state that causes human FTD is benign in the mouse. Do not present mouse data as dose guidance. CANCER: progranulin is a growth factor with documented tumour-promoting activity (breast, liver, ovarian); a therapy that pushes CSF and serum progranulin above normal has an unmeasured oncogenic ceiling. VECTOR MANAGEMENT: the Prevail protocol includes methylprednisolone with optional sirolimus and prednisone — the immune response to AAV in the CNS is being actively suppressed, which is itself a risk in an elderly population. DELIVERY IS NEUROSURGICAL: intrathalamic and intracisternal routes, not an injection. SCOPE: this is a disease-correction gene for a specific carrier population, not a general enhancement — a person with two working copies has no established deficit to correct.

Narrative:
A cell's chief chemical defence against oxidation is not an enzyme but a small molecule held in enormous quantity: glutathione, at millimolar concentrations, kept in its reduced form. Every time it neutralises something it is spent, oxidised to the disulphide GSSG. Glutathione reductase is the single enzyme that spends NADPH to convert it back. It is a recycling machine, and whether it is worth adding more of depends entirely on whether recycling is the step that runs out.

In C. elegans the answer was yes on both arms. Luersen and colleagues screened 67 glutathione-metabolism genes for tolerance to the pro-oxidant juglone and found gsr-1 was the only one absolutely essential — knocking it down dropped survival to about 3%. Knockdown also shortened mean lifespan by 14.5%, from 20.7 to 17.7 days, while worms carrying extra copies lived 18.0% longer, 16.4 to 19.4 days (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0060731).

In Drosophila the answer was conditional, and that conditionality is the honest core of this card. Mockett, Sohal and Orr made transgenic flies stably overexpressing glutathione reductase by up to 100% for their whole adult life. Under 100% oxygen the flies lived longer, accumulated fewer protein carbonyls and survived a semi-lethal oxygen dose far better. Under ordinary air, nothing: no change in longevity, protein carbonyls, or glutathione pools (https://doi.org/10.1096/fasebj.13.13.1733). The authors' own conclusion is that this enzyme is not rate-limiting for ageing in normal conditions and becomes limiting only when oxidative stress is high.
Short Description: Cells hold a large pool of glutathione as their main chemical reducing agent, and one flavoenzyme spends NADPH to recharge it after oxidative damage has used it up. Worms given extra copies lived 18.0% longer on average, 16.4 to 19.4 days, while knocking it down cost 14.5%. Flies with extra copies gained 19.6% mean survival in pure oxygen but just 2.6% in ordinary air, which was not significant, and no mammal has been tried.
Mechanism: GSR encodes a 522-residue homodimeric flavoenzyme of the pyridine-nucleotide-disulphide oxidoreductase family, with an FAD-binding domain, an NADPH-binding domain and a dimerisation interface; the active site lies at the subunit boundary so the dimer is obligate. Catalysis runs a ping-pong cycle: NADPH reduces FAD, the reduced flavin passes electrons to a redox-active cysteine pair, and that dithiol reduces the disulphide bond of GSSG to yield two GSH. The enzyme therefore converts NADPH reducing power, generated largely by the pentose phosphate pathway, into a maintained cytosolic and mitochondrial GSH:GSSG ratio, which in turn drives every glutathione peroxidase, glutaredoxin and glutathione S-transferase in the cell. Alternative first exons give cytosolic and mitochondrial forms from the same gene. Because it sits downstream of NADPH supply, its usefulness as an addition depends on whether the cell is limited by recycling capacity or by NADPH availability — which is exactly the pattern the fly hyperoxia experiment shows.
Achievements (effect sizes): C. elegans: extra genomic copies of gsr-1 gave +18.0% mean lifespan (16.4 to 19.4 days, significance_mean = 1) and RNAi knockdown gave -14.5% (20.7 to 17.7 days, significance_mean = 1). In a screen of 67 glutathione-metabolism genes, gsr-1 was the only one absolutely essential for survival under sub-lethal juglone stress, with a survival rate of 3.3 plus or minus 7.3% on knockdown (p < 0.001); the next-strongest hit, the omega-class glutathione S-transferase GSTO1, left 16.4 plus or minus 1.7% (Luersen 2013, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0060731). Drosophila: transgenic flies overexpressing glutathione reductase up to 100% throughout adult life gained +19.6% mean survival under 100% oxygen (3.72 to 4.45 days, significant) and a +371% median gain in the recovery experiment after a semi-lethal oxygen dose (14 to 66 days, significant), with reduced protein carbonyl accrual. Under normoxia the same flies gained only +2.6% median lifespan (70.0 to 71.8 days) with significance_median = 0, i.e. not significant, and one stress row went the other way at -22.7% median (Mockett 1999, https://doi.org/10.1096/fasebj.13.13.1733).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (bidirectional invertebrate in-vivo lifespan in C. elegans plus a conditional transgenic Drosophila result where the benefit appears only under hyperoxia; two independent laboratories and species, no mammalian lifespan test)
Translational Gaps: No mammal has been tested for lifespan or healthspan with raised glutathione reductase. The fly experiment is the strongest warning in this pack: a 100% increase in enzyme sustained across the whole adult lifespan produced no significant change in longevity, protein carbonyls, GSH or GSSG under ordinary air, so in an unstressed animal this enzyme is not the limiting step. That makes the plausible mammalian indication a stress-exposure one — hyperoxia, ischaemia-reperfusion, chemotherapy-induced oxidative injury — rather than general ageing. The enzyme also cannot work beyond the NADPH supplied to it, which is why the library's existing g6pd card, raising pentose-phosphate NADPH production, may be the more upstream intervention; adding recycling capacity without adding reducing power may do nothing. Human GSR deficiency is known and mild, which argues the pathway has reserve capacity in the normal direction.
Key References (DOIs): Luersen PLoS ONE 2013 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0060731 | Mockett FASEB Journal 1999 https://doi.org/10.1096/fasebj.13.13.1733
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Data-trap notes for this gene. The +371% figure in OpenGenes is a MEDIAN change in a post-hyperoxia recovery survival experiment (14 to 66 days), not a lifespan extension, and must never be used as a headline lifespan number; it is recorded here as a stress-recovery gene_testing row. The normoxia row carries significance_median = 0 and is reported as the negative row it is. One further fly row shows decreased survival under stress at -22.7% median with significance flagged, and is included. Overlap with the existing library: sod2 and mcat sit inside mitochondria on the superoxide-to-peroxide axis and g6pd supplies NADPH; GSR is the recycling step that consumes that NADPH, so it is the complementary node rather than a repeat — but the library reviewer should note that four oxidative-defence cards is already a crowded niche, which is part of why the recommendation is knowledge-base only. The worm overexpression strain background is LGIII/pha-1 e2123, a temperature-sensitive selection marker, not wild-type N2.

Narrative:
The Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalus, is the longest-lived vertebrate known. Radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei from 28 female sharks between 81 and 502 centimetres in total length revealed a lifespan of at least 272 years, with age at sexual maturity of at least 156 plus or minus 22 years and the largest animal, at 502 centimetres, dated to 392 plus or minus 120 years old (Nielsen 2016, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703). The exhibit record credits the species with negligible senescence past 400 years.

H1F0 encodes histone H1.0, a linker histone that binds at the point where DNA enters and exits the nucleosome and stabilises higher-order chromatin architecture. The hypothesis behind this entry is that shark-specific variants of the protein achieve enhanced chromatin compaction, which would reduce aberrant transcription and protect against the epigenetic drift that accumulates with age. It is an appealing idea because it proposes that extreme longevity is a problem of maintaining genomic order rather than of repairing damage, and because linker histones are among the most ancient and conserved proteins in the eukaryotic nucleus.

The honest position is that this is the least-evidenced entry in the Longevity and Genome category. The claims about shark H1F0 variants are genomic and transcriptomic correlations, not demonstrations of cause, and as set out in the notes below, the single reference the record carries is a genome paper for a different shark species.
Short Description: A Greenland-shark-inspired H1F0 programme proposes tighter chromatin as a way to suppress age-related transcriptional noise and keep dormant genomic regions quiet. In principle, linker histones could stabilise gene regulation across centuries of cell turnover. The shark's lifespan is firmly supported by radiocarbon dating, but H1F0 has not been shown to cause it, making this a provocative chromatin hypothesis rather than an established enhancement.
Mechanism: H1F0 encodes linker histone H1.0, which binds the nucleosome at the DNA entry and exit site and drives folding of the nucleosome array into compact higher-order chromatin. Compaction of that kind silences transposable elements and reduces transcriptional noise, both of which increase with age in most species examined. The mechanism proposed for this entry is that shark variants of the protein bind nucleosomes with higher affinity, which would produce tighter packaging and, in turn, suppressed age-related epigenetic drift and better-maintained heterochromatin integrity. The enhanced binding affinity is the proposed step; it is stated in the record as a property of the shark variants and no measurement of it appears in the reference the record cites.
Achievements (effect sizes):
What the record asserts, and what can be independently confirmed, need to be kept apart here.

The record states three findings: that Greenland sharks show negligible senescence markers past 400 years, that H1F0 expression remains stable across age cohorts, and that chromatin accessibility assays show tighter packaging in this species than in short-lived elasmobranchs. None of these three is reported in the single paper the record cites, which is the white shark genome (see notes), and I could not locate a source for any of them. They are preserved here as the record's claims, unattributed rather than falsely attributed.

What is independently verified is the longevity itself, from radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei in 28 female sharks (Nielsen 2016, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703), and the genomic groundwork that has since appeared. A chromosome-level Greenland shark genome assembly published in 2026 spans 5.9 gigabases with an N50 length of 233 megabases and a completeness score of 96.7 percent; analyses of gene family expansion and positive selection in that assembly recovered classical longevity-associated mechanisms including immune enhancement, cancer resistance and DNA repair (Yang 2026, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2601272123). The genome paper does not single out H1F0.

The reference the record carries is a 2019 paper by Marra and colleagues that reports the white shark genome and finds evidence of positive selection and gene-content enrichment for genome-stability genes across elasmobranchs (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1819778116). That is real evidence for elasmobranch genome-stability adaptations in general, but it concerns Carcharodon carcharias, not Somniosus microcephalus, and it is not about H1F0.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Nothing about this has been tested in a mammalian cell, so the first step is simply expressing a shark H1.0 variant in a human or mouse line and measuring whether chromatin compaction actually increases. Delivering a histone variant to post-mitotic cells is a genuine obstacle rather than a formality, because histones are normally deposited during replication and a non-dividing neuron or cardiomyocyte has no replication-coupled route to incorporate them. The long-term consequence of tighter packaging is the central unknown: gene expression plasticity depends on chromatin being openable, and an intervention that suppresses transcriptional noise by compaction will also suppress the induction of genes a cell needs later. Before any of that, the entry needs a source: the causal claim rests on correlational genomic and transcriptomic observations that the cited reference does not contain.
Key References (DOIs): Nielsen Science 2016 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703 | Yang Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2026 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2601272123 | Chiavacci Aging Cell 2026 https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.70505 | Marra Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2019 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1819778116
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
The longevity correlation is genomic and transcriptomic, not causal, and this entry has a citation problem that a reader should be told about directly.

The only reference the record carries is https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1819778116, published in 2019 by Marra and colleagues in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences under the title 'White shark genome reveals ancient elasmobranch adaptations associated with wound healing and the maintenance of genome stability'. It is a white shark genome paper. It does not concern the Greenland shark, and it makes no claim about H1F0, chromatin compaction in Somniosus microcephalus, nucleosome binding affinity, or senescence markers at any age. Three of the four statements in the record's achievements field therefore have no source in the record and none that I was able to find. I have preserved all three claims and marked them as unsourced rather than attaching a citation that does not support them.

A second point cuts against the entry's premise. A 2026 study of cardiac ageing in the Greenland shark found extensive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis throughout the ventricular myocardium, affecting both the compact and spongy layers in both sexes, together with extreme lipofuscin accumulation; the fibrotic pattern was absent in the comparison species, the deep-sea shark Etmopterus spinax and the short-lived killifish Nothobranchius furzeri, which suggests it is specific to Somniosus microcephalus (Chiavacci 2026, https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.70505). Fibrosis and lipofuscin are conventional senescence markers. Whatever the Greenland shark is doing to reach three centuries, 'negligible senescence' is too strong a description of its heart, and the exhibit should not claim otherwise.

The lifespan figure is also worth stating precisely. The radiocarbon study established at least 272 years, with the largest animal at 392 plus or minus 120 years (Nielsen 2016, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703); the 2026 genome paper quotes the estimated lifespan as 392 plus or minus 120 years (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2601272123). The record's 'over 400 years' sits inside the upper half of that confidence interval rather than being a measured value.

Narrative: Naked mole-rats live over 30 years and almost never get cancer — a scandal for a rodent. Their secret is a gooey, ultra-high-molecular-weight form of hyaluronic acid that makes their tissues feel springy under tweezers. In 2023, the Gorbunova-Seluanov lab put the mole-rat version of the gene that makes this molecule (nmrHas2) into ordinary mice. The result: median lifespan rose 4.4% (9% in females), maximum lifespan +12%, and cancer deaths in aged mice dropped from 83% to 49%. The mice aged more gracefully — better grip strength, less inflammation, younger-looking guts. It's the first time a single naked mole-rat gene has clearly extended a mammal's life. One caveat: in a xenograft tumor model, the same gene actually helped cancer grow — so context matters, and the effect is smaller than calorie restriction or rapamycin. Still, the first rodent longevity gene transfer that worked.
Short Description: Naked mole-rat HAS2 produces exceptionally large hyaluronic acid, creating a springy extracellular matrix linked to tissue resilience and cancer resistance. Mice carrying the naked mole-rat enzyme lived 4.4% longer on average and had fewer late-life cancer deaths in one cohort. Because the same matrix can support pancreatic tumour growth in another model, the exciting target is controlled, tissue-aware production rather than indiscriminate abundance.
Mechanism: NMR-specific Asn→Ser substitutions in catalytic loop produce high-molecular-mass HA (HMM-HA, >6.1 MDa, ~5× mouse/human); anti-inflammatory M2 polarization via CD44; reduced hyaluronidase in NMR tissues.
Achievements (effect sizes): Zhang 2023 Nature (conditional Tg C57BL/6, n=175): median lifespan +4.4% (♀ +9%), max +12.2% (♂ +16%). Spontaneous cancer mortality in old mice 83%→49%. Reduced DMBA/TPA papillomas. Lower frailty, preserved grip/rotarod, ↑bone connectivity (♀). Reduced plasma IL-12p40, MIP1α/β, CCL7 (aged ♀). BMDMs: ↓Il1b/Il6/Tnf, ↑Il10/Arg1 after LPS. Improved gut barrier; old intestinal organoids rescued by HMM-HA.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Human cell/in-vivo HMM-HA work not published; primate data; delivery; durable engineering in humans with high HYAL1/2 activity.
Key References (DOIs): Zhang Nature 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06463-0 | Tian Nature 2013 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12234 | Hadi Nature 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2410-x
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Tian 2015 AACR abstract — nmrHas2 and huHAS2 both PROMOTED AsPC1 pancreatic xenograft growth (context-dependent oncogenicity). (2) Maison 2025 preprint — nmrHas2 did NOT rescue age-related hearing loss (tissue-selective). (3) Hadi 2020 — NMR cells CAN be transformed at high oncogene dose (complicates cancer-resistance narrative); rebuttal exchange. (4) N→S residues shared with guinea pig/cetaceans — not unique to NMR. Single lab, single cohort, not independently replicated; effect smaller than rapamycin or CR; ceiling effect from mouse hyaluronidase.

Manipulation: haplotype introgression from a wild diploid relative
Narrative:
Salinity is one of the oldest ways to ruin farmland, and durum wheat — the pasta wheat — is unusually bad at surviving it. Bread wheat is hexaploid and carries a sodium-handling gene called Kna1 on the D genome it inherited from a wild grass. Durum is tetraploid, has no D genome, and therefore no Kna1. That single absence is much of the reason a durum field on saline soil yields badly while a bread wheat field beside it does not.

The fix came from an older, smaller wheat. Einkorn, Triticum monococcum, is a wild diploid that carries its own version of the transporter, and researchers at CSIRO and the University of Adelaide mapped it to a locus they named Nax2 and identified the causal gene as TmHKT1;5-A. Its position inside the plant is the whole story. The protein sits on the plasma membrane of the cells that wrap around the xylem vessels in the root — the pipes carrying sap upward. As sodium-laden sap moves past, the transporter pulls sodium back out of the stream and deposits it in the surrounding root tissue, so what arrives in the leaf is a diluted version of what the root absorbed. Uptake does not change; interception does.

They then crossed the locus into commercial durum and grew it in saline fields against near-isogenic lines that lacked it, which is the comparison that actually matters agronomically. The lines carrying Nax2 made a quarter more grain (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). This is the library's clearest example of an enhancement that is finished rather than promising: no transgene, no vector, no regulatory review, just a cross and a molecular marker. It is equally the clearest example of context-dependence. The same locus moved into bread wheat buys nothing at all, because the D genome already brought one, and the trait only addresses sodium toxicity — not the osmotic half of salt stress, which pulls water out of a root long before any sodium has accumulated in a leaf.
Short Description: The einkorn-wheat transporter TmHKT1;5-A pulls sodium out of the water stream before it reaches vulnerable leaves, allowing crops to keep growing in saline soil. Bred into durum wheat, the locus increased grain yield by 25% in salt-affected field trials. It is a mature example of resilience engineering: protect photosynthetic tissue by redirecting ions at the root-to-shoot boundary.
Mechanism: TmHKT1;5-A encodes a sodium-selective member of the HKT1 subfamily of high-affinity potassium transporters, a 517-amino-acid, 57.3 kDa membrane protein. Unlike the HKT2 subfamily, which runs sodium-potassium symport, HKT1-class proteins move sodium alone as a uniporter. The protein localises to the plasma membrane of the root cells that surround the xylem vessels, which places it exactly where the transpiration stream leaves the root for the shoot. From that position it retrieves sodium ions out of the xylem sap and unloads them into the neighbouring stelar parenchyma. The consequence is a lower sodium concentration in the leaf at unchanged sodium uptake by the root, so the trait is exclusion by interception rather than a refusal to absorb. Bread wheat carries a functionally equivalent HKT1;5 gene, Kna1, on its D genome; durum wheat, lacking that genome, has no counterpart, and that is the genetic reason durum is the salt-sensitive wheat.
Achievements (effect sizes): The headline result here is agronomic rather than physiological, which is rare in this library. The Nax2 locus from wild diploid einkorn wheat was crossed into the commercial durum cultivar Tamaroi by marker-assisted introgression, and the resulting lines were grown in saline field soil alongside near-isogenic lines lacking the locus — the same genetic background minus the transporter. Across those trials, “field trials on saline soils demonstrate that the presence of TmHKT1;5-A significantly reduces leaf [Na+] and increases durum wheat grain yield by 25% compared to near-isogenic lines without the Nax2 locus” (Munns 2012, https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). Two features make that sentence unusually strong evidence rather than a promising pot result. The endpoint is harvested grain in a field, not survival in a glasshouse, and the comparator is near-isogenic, so the 25% is attributable to the introgressed locus itself and not to whatever else a salt-tolerant landrace might carry along with it. The same work localised the transporter to the plasma membrane of the root cells surrounding the xylem, which ties the yield figure to a specific cell layer and a specific ion flux rather than to a vague tolerance phenotype (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (causal gene identified, mechanism localised to a specific cell layer, and validated by field trials against near-isogenic lines with a grain-yield endpoint; deployed by conventional breeding rather than as a transgene)
Translational Gaps: The 25% figure belongs to durum wheat on saline soil and nowhere else. The source reports no equivalent number for other cereals and none for non-saline conditions, and this record did not verify a non-saline control yield, so whether the locus costs anything in a good year is an open question rather than an answered one. No experimental structure of TmHKT1;5-A exists. Protein Data Bank entry 8W9T is TaHKT2;1 (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/8W9T), a member of the other HKT subfamily with different ion selectivity, and it must not be presented as this protein. Relevance to animals is nil in the strict sense: HKT transporters have no metazoan orthologue, so a human version of this card would have to borrow an entirely different protein family to achieve the same interception — and a human body has no xylem stream to intercept in the first place.
Key References (DOIs): Munns Nature Biotechnology 2012 https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Nomenclature is a trap here. The same protein appears in the literature as HKT8, as HKT1;5-A and as the Nax2 locus, and the UniProt entry A4ZGN5 is annotated under the older name HKT8 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A4ZGN5), so a visitor searching one name will miss papers filed under the others. The delivery route makes this the exhibit's most useful contrast: the enhancement was moved by crossing and marker selection rather than by transformation, which is why it sits in breeding pipelines rather than in a regulatory queue, unlike the transgenic and gene-edited cards in the same category (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). The work was carried out by CSIRO Plant Industry with the Australian Centre for Plant Functional Genomics at the University of Adelaide, which mapped the locus in Triticum monococcum, identified the causal gene, localised it in the root and ran the saline field trials (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). There are no clinical trials and no commercial human product; the commercial product is wheat. No contradictory replication surfaced in the literature searched for this record, but the card rests on a single quantified field result, so the 25% has not yet been independently reproduced in a separately published trial.

Narrative: Every animal has HSF1 — it's the master switch that turns on heat shock proteins when cells get stressed. But the sleeping chironomid did something unusual with it: over evolutionary time, P. vanderplanki rewired HSF1 to also activate desiccation-protection genes, including LEA proteins, trehalose synthesis enzymes, and thioredoxins. Mazin et al. (2018 PNAS) showed this cooption in detail: HSF1 in the midge activates not just classical heat-shock targets but an entire anhydrobiosis program. The key innovation is a double TCTAGAA motif upstream of the Hsf gene itself, creating a positive feedback loop — HSF1 activates its own transcription, amplifying the stress response. Knockdown of HSF1 in the Pv11 cell line suppressed trehalose-induced activation of multiple protective genes and reduced desiccation survival fivefold. The cooption works because the promoters of desiccation genes acquired HSF-binding sites, recruiting an existing regulatory network for a new purpose. This is not about the HSF1 protein being different — it's about rewiring the regulatory circuitry around a conserved transcription factor. The implication for engineering is tantalizing: you might not need novel alien proteins if you can teach human HSF1 to activate a broader protective program using synthetic promoter elements.
Short Description: A desert midge has rewired the universal stress regulator HSF1 into the conductor of a whole desiccation-survival orchestra, activating protective sugars, LEA proteins, antioxidants and heat-shock machinery together. Knocking HSF1 down cut cell survival after drying about fivefold, which shows the regulator is required in the midge; no mammalian construct has been built. The valuable design is its inducible feedback circuit, not leaving mammalian HSF1 permanently active.
Mechanism: Transcription factor cooption: P. vanderplanki desiccation genes acquired TCTAGAA HSF-binding motifs in their promoters. HSF1 auto-activates via double TCTAGAA upstream of its own gene. Drives LEA proteins, trehalose synthesis (TPS/TPP), thioredoxins, and heat shock proteins as a coordinated anhydrobiosis program.
Achievements (effect sizes): Mazin 2018 PNAS: HSF1 knockdown in Pv11 cells reduced desiccation survival ~5-fold; suppressed trehalose-induced activation of LEA, TPS, and thioredoxin genes. Promoter analysis: TCTAGAA motif enriched in desiccation-induced genes. Double HSF-binding site upstream of Hsf enables auto-amplification. Gusev 2011: HSP70/HSP90/HSP60/sHSP all upregulated during anhydrobiosis entry.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (Pv11 cell knockdown + transcriptomic analysis)
Translational Gaps: Regulatory rewiring rather than simple gene transfer — would require synthetic promoter engineering in mammalian cells; no mammalian proof-of-concept; HSF1 overexpression in mammals is oncogenic in some contexts (Dai 2007).
Key References (DOIs): Mazin PNAS 2018 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1719493115 | Gusev Cell Stress Chaperones 2010 https://doi.org/10.1007/s12192-010-0223-9 | Hiki BBRC 2026 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2026.153267
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CAUTION: HSF1 is a known oncogene in mammalian contexts — constitutive activation promotes tumor growth (Dai 2007 Cell). The chironomid cooption works because it is inducible and context-dependent, not constitutive. Simple HSF1 overexpression in human cells would likely cause problems. The engineering value is in the regulatory architecture (synthetic promoters), not in transplanting the midge HSF1 protein itself. Requires systems-level circuit design, not single-gene transfer.

Manipulation: Engineered point mutants in middle domain, overexpression
Narrative:
Yeast can do something your cells cannot. When heat or stress leaves its proteins tangled into aggregates, yeast deploys Hsp104, a hexameric ring that grips a polypeptide sticking out of an aggregate and drags it through a central pore using ATP, pulling molecules back out of the clump one chain at a time. Metazoa have no homolog of this protein at all - somewhere in animal evolution the disaggregase was lost, and animal cells got chaperones that prevent misfolding and proteolytic systems that destroy the aggregate, but nothing that reverses aggregation. Neurodegeneration is largely a disease of aggregates that have already formed, which makes the missing machine conspicuous.

James Shorter's laboratory at the University of Pennsylvania asked whether yeast Hsp104 could be pointed at human disease proteins. Wild-type Hsp104 barely touches them. But single missense mutations in the coiled-coil middle domain - most famously replacing alanine 503 - potentiate the enzyme, and the potentiated versions dissolve alpha-synuclein, TDP-43 and FUS, the aggregating proteins of Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.11.047). In a transgenic worm model they protected dopaminergic neurons that alpha-synuclein would otherwise have killed, and the effect was post-translational: the variants did not change how much alpha-synuclein the worm made, they changed what happened to it.

What makes this card honest is that the same paper measures the cost. Potentiation works by loosening how the enzyme chooses substrates, so the variant that dissolves a disease aggregate can also unfold a host protein that is merely metastable. At 37 degrees C - human body temperature - the A503V variant is toxic to yeast for exactly that reason (https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.016113). The programme since then has been about keeping the power while narrowing the aim (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.069).
Short Description: Engineered Hsp104 variants can grab proteins from existing aggregates and thread them apart, restoring a repair ability that animal cells lack. In a worm Parkinson's model, potentiated variants raised the fraction of animals retaining normal dopamine neurons from about 16% to 30–34%, while ordinary Hsp104 did not help. The next engineering goal is substrate precision, because the strongest variants can also unfold vulnerable host proteins at 37°C.
Mechanism: Hsp104 is a 908-amino-acid protein disaggregase from baker's yeast, a member of the AAA+ family of ATP-driven molecular machines (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities). Six copies assemble into a ring with two nucleotide-binding domains per subunit and a coiled-coil middle domain, and the ring threads polypeptides through its central channel using the energy of ATP hydrolysis, extracting individual monomers from disordered aggregates and from amyloid fibrils. Animals have no Hsp104 homolog, and the wild-type enzyme has only limited activity against human disease proteins.
