The reviewed UniProt accession used here, P20263, is the mouse Pou5f1 (OCT4) entry, matching the species of the experiments; the human Phase 1 uses the human orthologs of all three factors.

Manipulation: loss-of-function knockout, including tamoxifen-inducible deletion in 5-month-old adults
Narrative: Most attempts to get the longevity benefit of reduced growth signalling wreck the animal on the way, because they cut the hormone or its receptor and the mouse is born small. PAPP-A is the exception. It is a secreted zinc metalloprotease that sits in tissue, not in the bloodstream's control loop, and its job is to cut IGF-binding proteins so that locally trapped IGF-1 is released where it is needed. Delete it and circulating IGF-1 stays normal while local IGF action falls. Cheryl Conover's group at the Mayo Clinic followed PAPP-A knockout mice to the end of life and found mean and median lifespan up 27% and maximum up 35%, with a striking pathology signature: the knockouts got the same amount of cancer, but they got it later, and they had fewer degenerative changes in heart, brain, kidney, spleen, testes and thymus. Then they did the experiment that matters for an enhancement claim. Using tamoxifen-inducible Cre to delete the floxed gene in adult female mice at five months of age - after development is finished - median lifespan still rose 21%. The same group built a neutralising antibody against PAPP-A and gave it to adult mice; it reproduced the transcriptional signature, cut visceral adipocyte size 30-40% on a high-fat diet, and reduced bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis in aged mice. This is the rare node in the GH/IGF axis with an adult-onset route and an actual pharmacological handle.
Short Description: A secreted protease frees locally trapped IGF-1 in tissue; remove it and local growth signalling falls while blood IGF-1 stays normal. Knockout mice lived 27% longer at the mean and got their tumours later rather than less often, and deleting the gene in five-month-old adults still added 21% median lifespan. Knockouts have thinner tendons, shorter femurs and disorganised growth-plate cartilage.
Mechanism: PAPPA encodes a 1,627-amino-acid secreted zinc metalloproteinase that circulates and acts locally as a homodimer. Its substrates are IGF-binding proteins 4 and 5; cleaving them releases sequestered IGF-1 and IGF-2 to reach IGF1R at the cell surface. Because the protease works in the tissue microenvironment, deleting it lowers local IGF receptor activation without changing serum IGF-1 - the reason knockouts are only mildly small rather than dwarfed. Stanniocalcin-2 is the endogenous inhibitor of the same reaction. The cell type that matters most is the mesenchymal stromal cell: bone-marrow MSCs are the dominant source of PAPP-A, and antibody blockade collapses MSC number and system-wide extracellular-matrix gene expression, which is how one protease reaches bone, marrow fat, fibrosis and myelopoiesis at once.
Achievements (effect sizes): Conover 2010 (J Gerontol A): PAPP-A knockout mice had significantly increased mean (27%), median (27%) and maximum (35%) lifespan versus wild-type littermates. Neoplastic disease incidence was NOT significantly different between groups - tumours occurred at older ages in the knockouts - and knockouts were less likely to show degenerative changes of age, particularly in heart, testes, brain, kidney, spleen and thymus at scheduled 78/104/130-week pathology. OpenGenes records this cohort as +29% mean / +33% median (females, n=38 vs 50) and +25% mean / +20% median (males, n=40 vs 45). Conover 2017 (Aging Cell): tamoxifen-inducible deletion of floxed PAPP-A in female mice at 5 months of age extended median lifespan 21% (P = 0.005) with equivalent starting weight and weight gain - an adult-onset result. Conover 2020 (Endocrinology): a specific immunoneutralising monoclonal antibody (mAb-PA 1/41) in adult mice on a 15-week high-fat diet decreased visceral adipocyte size 30-40% with no effect on subcutaneous fat, and liver lipid also fell. Phillip 2021 (Aging Cell): the antibody reduced IGF signalling and extracellular-matrix gene expression system-wide and dramatically decreased bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cell number.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse germline and adult-onset inducible knockout, both with lifespan endpoints, plus a pharmacological antibody phenocopy in adult mice; no human exposure)
Translational Gaps: No human has received a PAPP-A inhibitor. The antibody work is preclinical and the compound is a research monoclonal, not a clinical candidate with an IND. The lifespan data come from one laboratory - Conover's at the Mayo Clinic - and no independent group has repeated the survival experiment. The adult-onset inducible study could only be run in females because of the breeding design, so there is no adult-onset male lifespan number. Circulating PAPP-A is used clinically as a first-trimester screening marker and as an acute-coronary-syndrome biomarker, so human reference ranges exist but human modulation data do not.
Key References (DOIs): Conover J Gerontol A 2010 https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glq032 | Conover Aging Cell 2017 https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.12624 | Conover Endocrinology 2020 https://doi.org/10.1210/endocr/bqaa160 | Phillip Aging Cell 2021 https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13313 | Bale Aging Biol 2024 https://doi.org/10.59368/agingbio.20240023
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
DIRECTION: the enhancement is loss of PAPP-A protease activity (less local IGF release). Overexpressing PAPPA is the pro-fibrotic, pro-tumour direction - PAPP-A is elevated in Ewing sarcoma and platinum-resistant ovarian cancer and correlates with IPF severity. CANCER: the knockouts were NOT cancer-free; incidence was statistically unchanged and only the age of onset shifted (https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glq032). Do not write this card as cancer protection. SKELETAL/CONNECTIVE TISSUE TRADEOFFS: PAPP-A knockout mice have reduced femur length and disorganised growth-plate chondrocyte columns (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-71062-6), and smaller tendon cross-sectional area with reduced fascicle stiffness and strength (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsb.2015.08.012). MARROW: antibody blockade reduces bone, marrow adiposity and myelopoiesis via loss of mesenchymal stromal cells (https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13313) - a haematopoietic reserve concern for chronic dosing. SINGLE-LAB: all lifespan data trace to the Conover group; independent replication is absent.

MANIPULATION DETAIL (moved from manipulation field, varchar(128) limit): loss-of-function knockout, including tamoxifen-inducible deletion in 5-month-old adults; pharmacologically phenocopied by a neutralising monoclonal antibody

Manipulation: Co-expression of the parietal-eye opsin pair (parietopsin + pinopsin) with Go-alpha in a single photoreceptor
Narrative: Many lizards carry a third eye. On top of the skull, under a translucent scale, sits the parietal eye: a small structure with a lens and a retina, wired to the pineal complex rather than to the visual brain, and incapable of forming an image. What it does instead is measure colour. Su and colleagues (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1123802) recorded in 2006 from single parietal-eye photoreceptors of the side-blotched lizard and found something no other vertebrate cell is known to do: the same cell answers green light by depolarizing and blue light by hyperpolarizing. Two opsins share one cell and pull its membrane potential in opposite directions, so the output is a ratio, the balance of blue against green overhead, rather than a count of photons. That ratio is exactly what swings at dawn and dusk, and an eye on the roof of the head is well placed to read it. The chemistry was pinned down in Osaka. Sakai and colleagues expressed lizard parietopsin in cultured cells, purified the pigment, and measured a green-sensitive absorption maximum at 522 nm, red-shifted relative to both rhodopsin and pinopsin, with a counterion arrangement closer to an invertebrate opsin than to a vertebrate one (https://doi.org/10.1021/bi2018283). Wada and colleagues then found the same 522 nm peak in iguana parietopsin, showing the tuning is a property of the molecule and not a quirk of one species (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0039003). For a body, this is a colour comparator you could wear on your forehead: not a picture, but an instant read-out of the spectral quality of the light above you, of the kind a lizard uses to know where it stands in the day. Nothing like it has been transferred to a mammal, and the obstacle is wiring rather than optics, because the cell speaks a G-protein language the vertebrate retina does not understand.
Short Description: Parietopsin and pinopsin give a lizard's parietal eye a striking colour-opponent sensor: one cell depolarizes to green light and hyperpolarizes to blue, reporting sky colour rather than brightness. Purified parietopsin peaks near 522 nm, a result reproduced in a second lizard species, while the paired pathways act in opposite electrical directions. Rebuilding it elsewhere requires both opsins, unusual G proteins, and a circuit able to interpret the bipolar signal.
Mechanism: The parietal-eye photoreceptor is the only vertebrate cell known to run two antagonistic phototransduction cascades at the same time. Green-sensitive parietopsin couples to Go-alpha, the alpha subunit of the Go class of heterotrimeric G proteins, and produces a depolarizing response, while blue-sensitive pinopsin couples to gustducin-alpha and produces a hyperpolarizing one. Neither rod nor cone transducin-alpha, the G protein that carries the signal in ordinary vertebrate photoreceptors, is present in the cell at all. Parietopsin's protonated retinal chromophore is stabilised by a counterion at Glu181 in the second extracellular loop, the arrangement typical of invertebrate opsins, rather than at the Glu113 position rhodopsin uses; Gln113 at that vacated site contributes to the pigment's red-shifted absorbance. Because both cascades converge on one membrane, the cell's voltage encodes the ratio of green to blue light instead of total intensity, which makes it a chromatic comparator rather than an intensity detector.
Achievements (effect sizes): Single-cell recordings from the parietal eye of the side-blotched lizard established that one photoreceptor can answer two colours in opposite directions, depolarizing to green light and hyperpolarizing to blue (Su 2006, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1123802). Recombinant work then measured the pigment itself. Lizard parietopsin expressed in cultured cells and purified showed an absorption maximum at 522 nm, which the authors single out as its noticeable characteristic, a red shift with respect to both rhodopsin and pinopsin (Sakai 2012, https://doi.org/10.1021/bi2018283). The same study asked how efficiently the pigment turns absorbed light into activation: photosensitivity at its 520 nm peak came to 0.69 +/- 0.02 of that of bovine rhodopsin at rhodopsin's own peak, and 0.63 +/- 0.02 when both pigments were compared at 500 nm. Its molar extinction coefficient, determined by acid denaturation against a bovine rhodopsin reference of 40600 M-1 cm-1, was 31700 +/- 500 M-1 cm-1 at 520 nm and 29000 +/- 500 M-1 cm-1 at 500 nm, so the pigment absorbs somewhat less strongly than rod pigment as well. An independent group repeating the measurement in a different lizard found iguana parietopsin peaking at 522 nm, almost identical to the side-blotched lizard's value, which makes the green tuning a property of the protein rather than of one animal (Wada 2012, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0039003).
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (native single-cell electrophysiology in lizard plus recombinant spectroscopy replicated in two lizard species and two laboratories; no mammalian transfer attempted)
Translational Gaps: No laboratory has yet expressed parietopsin, pinopsin and Go-alpha together in a mammalian photoreceptor or neuron and shown that the resulting cell answers two colours in opposite directions, so the central claim of this enhancement has never been tested outside a lizard. Parietal-eye photoreceptors also have a distinctive morphology of their own, and the intracellular messenger that carries the depolarizing arm of the cascade has not been fully identified, which means a builder would be copying a pathway whose middle step is still missing. Nobody knows whether a mammalian cell can hold two opposing opsin cascades without them cross-talking, and nobody knows what downstream circuit would interpret a bipolar voltage signal that no vertebrate visual pathway currently receives.
Key References (DOIs): Su Science 2006 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1123802 | Sakai Biochemistry 2012 https://doi.org/10.1021/bi2018283 | Wada PLoS ONE 2012 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0039003
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The founding electrophysiology paper (Su 2006, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1123802) is closed-access, so the spectroscopic numbers in this record come from two sources read in full text: Sakai 2012 (https://doi.org/10.1021/bi2018283) and Wada 2012 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0039003). One internal inconsistency deserves flagging. The Biochemistry paper (https://doi.org/10.1021/bi2018283) also reports 495 nm as a wild-type value inside a pH-7.0 mutant comparison, whereas its own summary statement of parietopsin's characteristic absorption maximum is 522 nm; 522 nm is the figure used here. There is no experimental crystal or cryo-EM structure of parietopsin or of pinopsin, although AlphaFold models exist for lizard parietopsin (UniProt Q1L4C8, https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q1L4C8) and for pinopsin from the same species (UniProt Q1L4C7, https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q1L4C7). The trait has no commercial or clinical existence: no company and no registered trial. Bistable pineal opsins from this same family are being examined as optogenetic actuators, which is the most plausible near-term route by which these cascades would first reach a mammalian neuron.

Narrative: Heart disease is the world's top killer, and its chief accomplice is LDL cholesterol. For decades, statins have been the answer — but they require daily pills for life, and many patients stop taking them. Nature, however, has already solved the compliance problem. In 2006, Hobbs and Cohen discovered that roughly 3% of African Americans carry loss-of-function mutations in PCSK9, a liver enzyme that destroys LDL receptors. These carriers had LDL levels 28% lower and an 88% reduction in coronary heart disease — with no apparent downside. In 2021, Verve Therapeutics used lipid nanoparticle-delivered adenine base editing to knock out PCSK9 in cynomolgus monkeys with a single intravenous infusion: LDL dropped 59% and stayed down for over a year with no booster. In 2025, their phase Ib human trial (VERVE-102) showed durable 39–55% LDL reductions in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia patients already on maximally tolerated therapy. One injection, permanent cholesterol lowering, no daily pills. The catch: liver base editing is irreversible — any off-target edits in hepatocytes are permanent, and the long-term cancer risk of widespread somatic editing remains theoretical but unquantified.
Short Description: Disabling PCSK9 lets liver cells keep more LDL receptors and continuously clear cholesterol from blood. People born with inactive copies have about 28% lower LDL and 88% less coronary disease, while one-shot liver base editing has produced durable 39–55% LDL reductions in early human testing. The benefit could replace lifelong dosing, but the edit is permanent, so liver targeting and off-target surveillance must be exceptionally rigorous.
Mechanism: Adenine base editor (ABE) delivered via LNP to hepatocytes; introduces A→G transition creating splice-site disruption in PCSK9 exon 1; loss of functional PCSK9 protein → LDL receptors on hepatocyte surface persist instead of being degraded → increased LDL-C clearance from plasma.
Achievements (effect sizes): Cohen 2006 NEJM: PCSK9 LOF carriers — LDL −28%, CHD risk −88% (15-year follow-up, n=3363 Black participants). Musunuru 2021 Nature (monkey, n=4): single LNP-ABE dose → PCSK9 protein −90%, LDL-C −59% at 8 months, stable. VERVE-102 2025 (phase Ib, n=12 HeFH): LDL reductions 39–55% at highest dose, durable through 180 days; no serious liver events.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Phase III efficacy/safety (MACE endpoints); long-term off-target somatic editing surveillance; immunogenicity of LNP on repeat dosing (if ever needed); applicability beyond FH to general population; liver cancer risk from widespread base editing.
Key References (DOIs): Cohen NEJM 2006 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa054013 | Musunuru Nature 2021 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03534-y | Vafai New England Journal of Medicine 2026 https://doi.org/10.1056/nejmoa2601283
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: PCSK9-null humans (compound LOF homozygotes) are healthy, supporting safety — but sample size is tiny (2 reported individuals). LNP tropism is liver-dominant but not liver-exclusive; low-level editing in other organs is possible. Base editing off-targets are harder to detect than CRISPR indels. Cohen 2006 CHD reduction (88%) may overestimate causal effect due to lifelong exposure vs mid-life intervention. Verve trials use next-gen LNP (GalNAc-targeted) to improve hepatocyte specificity. COMMERCIAL STATUS: Verve Therapeutics (https://www.vervetx.com/), developer of VERVE-101/102, was acquired by Eli Lilly in June 2025, signalling major-pharma confidence in the approach. This is a regulated clinical program, not an alternative-jurisdiction therapy. The base-editing platform is not commercially available outside clinical trials.

Manipulation: Two-gene pathway transfer (neofunctionalised pyruvate decarboxylase + muscle alcohol dehydrogenase)
Narrative:
In northern Europe, shallow ponds freeze over and the water beneath the ice runs out of oxygen completely for months. Almost nothing with a spine survives that. Crucian carp not only survive it, they stay active - and unlike the anoxia-tolerant freshwater turtles, which go still and wait, the fish keeps swimming (https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.00979). The reason is that its muscle ferments glucose to ethanol rather than to lactate, and the ethanol simply diffuses out of the gills into the pond. Because the anaerobic end product leaves the body as a neutral molecule instead of piling up as acid, glycolysis can run indefinitely without the lactic acidosis that kills other vertebrates in minutes.

In 2017 a group at the University of Oslo worked out the machinery (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4). A whole-genome duplication in the genus Carassius left spare copies of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and one pair of E1 subunits was repurposed into a pyruvate decarboxylase - the first ever described in a vertebrate, performing the same chemistry brewer's yeast uses. A single amino-acid change, betaD319N, breaks the salt bridge that would normally dock that subunit onto the complex core, so it works detached and releases acetaldehyde instead of feeding acetyl-CoA into respiration. A muscle-specific alcohol dehydrogenase, ADH8a, then reduces the acetaldehyde to ethanol. The fish gets away with it because tetraploidy let it keep an intact, normally functioning complex encoded on the other gene copy, and because it confines the whole arrangement to skeletal muscle.

The uncomfortable detail is that betaD319N is the substitution associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase complex dysfunction in human cells. What is an elegant solution in a tetraploid fish with gills is, in a diploid land animal, a metabolic disease allele plus ethanol with nowhere to leave.
Short Description: Crucian carp stay active for four to five months without oxygen by converting pyruvate into ethanol instead of accumulating acidifying lactate. A repurposed pyruvate-dehydrogenase pair makes acetaldehyde and muscle ADH8a finishes the ethanol route, with pathway transcripts enriched more than 60-fold in ethanol-producing muscle. The fish can release ethanol through its gills; a land animal would need a safe outlet while preserving normal aerobic metabolism.
Mechanism: A whole-genome duplication in the genus Carassius left spare copies of the subunits of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH complex), the mitochondrial machine that normally converts pyruvate into acetyl-coenzyme A for aerobic respiration. One pair of E1 paralogs, E1alpha3 together with E1beta2, neofunctionalised into a pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC) - the first described in any vertebrate and analogous to the enzyme brewer's yeast uses - which releases acetaldehyde from pyruvate instead of channelling it into acetyl-CoA. The enabling change is the substitution betaD319N in E1beta2, absent from the E1beta1 copy, which abolishes a salt bridge to lysine residues on the E2 core of the complex so that the E1 unit operates physically detached from it. A muscle-specific alcohol dehydrogenase, ADH8a, then reduces the acetaldehyde to ethanol, and the ethanol diffuses freely across the gills into the surrounding water. Because the terminal product of anaerobic glycolysis leaves the body as a neutral small molecule rather than accumulating as lactate, glycolysis can continue indefinitely without lactic acidosis.
Achievements (effect sizes): Transcript profiling across crucian carp tissues showed that in red and white skeletal muscles, total E1:E2 and E1:E3 transcript ratios were significantly higher by a factor greater than 60 compared to all other, non-ethanol producing tissues such as brain, heart and liver - the evidence that a free, complex-independent E1 exists specifically in the muscle that makes ethanol (Fagernes 2017, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4). The same study identified the enabling mutation and showed why it works: the amino acid substitution betaD319N, which molecular modelling places at a salt bridge between betaD319 and lysine 362 on the E2 core, produces a greater than 100-fold increase in the dissociation constant between E1 and E2 and a concomitant decrease in in vitro pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity, and the substitution appears to be unique to the ethanol-producing goldfish and crucian carp and is not found in any other species investigated. That substitution was independently confirmed in the sequence databases, where E1beta2 carries asparagine at position 319 (UniProt A0A288DUG2, https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A288DUG2) while E1beta1 carries aspartate there (UniProt A0A288DSR4, https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A288DSR4). The physiological magnitude is large and sustained: the fish reaches elevated tissue ethanol concentrations reaching up to 7 micromol/g in red muscle during anoxia for up to 4-5 months of the year (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4), and it survives for months in completely oxygen-deprived freshwater habitats, also tolerating a few days of anoxia at room temperature and, unlike anoxia-tolerant freshwater turtles, remaining physically active while anoxic (Nilsson & Renshaw 2004, https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.00979).
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (comparative genomics, transcript quantification and structural modelling in the native species; no heterologous reconstitution of the two-gene pathway)
Translational Gaps: Nobody has transferred the two genes into a heterologous animal and measured anoxic survival, so the gain-of-function claim rests entirely on comparative evidence: Carassius has the pathway and survives months of anoxia, while common carp lacks it and dies within hours (Fagernes 2017, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4). Reconstituting it would require more than putting two genes into a host, because the pathway depends on tissue-restricted expression at a more than 60-fold excess of E1 over the E2 and E3 core components in muscle alone; expressing the decarboxylase everywhere would compromise aerobic pyruvate oxidation in every tissue that got it. There is also no route for the product. A carp voids ethanol across its gills into open water, and a terrestrial body has no comparable diffusive sink, so the recipient would have to clear months of continuous ethanol through the liver instead. No experimental structure exists for the carp subunits; only predicted models are available.
Key References (DOIs): Fagernes Scientific Reports 2017 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4 | Nilsson Journal of Experimental Biology 2004 https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.00979
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The natural negative control is stated in the same paper and is unusually clean: common carp tolerates severe hypoxia but dies within hours of anoxia, apparently because lactate accumulates in the absence of any ethanol route (Fagernes 2017, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4). The accessions were checked directly against UniProt for this entry - A0A288DSR4 (E1beta1, 359 amino acids) carries aspartate at position 319 while A0A288DUG2 (E1beta2, 360 amino acids) carries asparagine (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A288DUG2). There are no clinical trials, no registry records and no products; the authors instead propose Carassius as a model organism for chronic ethanol exposure and for hypoxia and ischaemia research (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-07385-4). Note the direction of the human literature on betaD319N: in people the same substitution is discussed as a cause of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex dysfunction, so a change that reads as an enhancement in a fish is catalogued as pathology in a human, and this card should be read as a species-specific solution rather than a portable upgrade. Within this library it does not overlap EPAS1, which blunts the hypoxia-inducible factor response to thin air and concerns oxygen delivery; here oxygen is absent altogether and what changes is the end product of fermentation.

Manipulation: Overexpression restricted to intestinal stem cells and enteroblasts (tissue-restricted; ubiquitous overexpression is harmful)
Narrative:
Every cell decides how much mitochondrial machinery to build, and one transcriptional coactivator makes that decision. PGC-1alpha does not bind DNA itself; it docks onto nuclear receptors and transcription factors already sitting at promoters and recruits the acetyltransferase and mediator complexes that turn them on, switching whole programmes of mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism at once. Its level rises with exercise and cold and falls with age.

The longevity result that matters here is not a whole-body one. Rera and colleagues at the Buck Institute overexpressed the Drosophila homolog spargel and asked where it had to act. Driven everywhere with da-GAL4 the flies did worse, losing about 10-11% of median lifespan at 200% and 5900% expression. Driven in the digestive tract with TIGS-2 the flies gained 33% of mean lifespan and 37% of maximum lifespan in females, and driven specifically in intestinal stem cells and their immediate daughters with esg-GAL4 the same construct raised mean survival by 41% in males and 49% in females (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2011.09.013). Old guts in these flies did not undergo the usual burst of stem-cell over-proliferation and mis-differentiation; the tissue simply aged more slowly.

The mammalian story is where care is needed. The most-cited mouse ageing paper on muscle PGC-1alpha, Wenz 2009 in PNAS, was RETRACTED in 2016 (retraction notice: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1619713114), so it cannot be used as evidence. What survives is that muscle-restricted PGC-1alpha overexpression drives a genuine fibre-type and mitochondrial shift in mice (https://doi.org/10.1038/nature00904) and that cardiac-restricted overexpression causes uncontrolled mitochondrial proliferation and a cardiomyopathy (https://doi.org/10.1161/01.res.0000117088.36577.eb). Dose and tissue are the entire finding in both species.
Short Description: One coactivator protein tells a cell how many mitochondria to build and how hard to run them, and its level falls in ageing muscle and gut lining. Driving it up only in fly intestinal stem cells raised mean survival 49%, while driving it everywhere at 59-fold expression shortened median lifespan 11%. The mammalian gene is the same gene, but the 2009 mouse ageing paper was retracted in 2016 and cardiac overexpression drives runaway mitochondrial proliferation.
Mechanism: PPARGC1A encodes a 798-residue, largely intrinsically disordered transcriptional coactivator (34% of the chain is annotated disordered in UniProt Q9UBK2). It carries an N-terminal activation domain that binds CBP/p300 and the mediator subunit MED1, an LXXLL nuclear-receptor box, a central repression region, and a C-terminal RNA-recognition motif and RS domain that couple transcription to splicing. It has no DNA-binding domain of its own: it is recruited by PPARs, ERRalpha, NRF1 and FOXO1, and once docked it converts a poised promoter into an active one. Through NRF1 and NRF2 it drives TFAM and thereby mitochondrial DNA replication, so raising it raises mitochondrial number and respiratory capacity. In the fly gut, raising spargel in intestinal stem cells and enteroblasts increases mitochondrial activity in those cells and suppresses the age-associated over-proliferation and mis-differentiation of the intestinal epithelium; the lifespan effect tracks the tissue effect, not a systemic metabolic change.
Achievements (effect sizes): In Drosophila, RU486-induced dPGC-1 expression in the digestive tract with the TIGS-2 driver gave a 33% increase in mean lifespan and a 37% increase in maximum lifespan in females; OpenGenes records the matching row as +33.0% mean (significance flag 1) with median rising 40 to 53 days. Constitutive esg-GAL4 expression in intestinal stem cells and enteroblasts gave +41.0% mean in males (median 45 to 65 days) and +49.0% mean in females (median 39 to 59 days), both flagged significant. The inducible S1106 fat-body/gut driver gave a smaller +11.0% mean (median 69 to 76 days). The direction reverses with ubiquitous expression: da-GAL4 at 200% expression cost 10% of median lifespan in females and at 5900% cost 11% in males, both significant. The paper reports 19% and 17% mean-survival gains for the 5961GS driver induced through development-plus-adulthood and adulthood only. Flies did not pay for this in reproduction or global stress resistance, but did show lower whole-fly triglyceride and modestly raised free glucose (Rera 2011, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2011.09.013).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (invertebrate in-vivo lifespan with a tissue-restriction experiment and an internal dose reversal; the mammalian ageing anchor for this gene was retracted, and no mouse lifespan cohort supports it)
Translational Gaps: There is no mammalian lifespan experiment for PGC-1alpha overexpression that can be cited: the paper that would have served, Wenz 2009 PNAS on muscle PGC-1alpha in ageing, was retracted in 2016 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1619713114), and this card must not be built on it. The fly result is tissue-restricted by construction — the same construct driven ubiquitously shortened life — so any mammalian test must be a conditional, tissue-restricted one rather than systemic delivery. Cardiac overexpression in mice causes uncontrolled mitochondrial proliferation and cardiomyopathy (https://doi.org/10.1161/01.res.0000117088.36577.eb), which sets a hard ceiling on dose. The intestinal-stem-cell compartment that carries the fly effect is not the same tissue architecture as the mammalian crypt, and no one has tested crypt-restricted Ppargc1a overexpression on mouse lifespan. The protein is 798 residues and largely disordered, so it is a coactivator to be induced rather than a druggable enzyme.
Key References (DOIs): Rera Cell Metabolism 2011 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2011.09.013 | Lin Nature 2002 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature00904 | Russell Circulation Research 2004 https://doi.org/10.1161/01.res.0000117088.36577.eb | Retraction of Wenz 2009 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1619713114
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: IMPORTANT provenance note for future curators: the obvious mammalian citation for this gene, Wenz et al. 2009 PNAS 'Increased muscle PGC-1alpha expression protects from sarcopenia and metabolic disease during aging' (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0911570106), carries an erratum in 2014 and a RETRACTION in 2016 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1619713114). Crossref returns its title prefixed 'RETRACTED:'. It must not be cited as evidence anywhere in this library. The OpenGenes rows for PPARGC1A are all from a single Drosophila study and all six are internally consistent with the published figures. Note the direction trap: two of the six rows are lifespan DECREASES from the same gain-of-function construct at high ubiquitous expression, so the gene is not simply 'more is better'. The human protein has 45 PDB entries but they are fragments and peptide complexes; there is no full-length structure, consistent with 34% annotated disorder.

Narrative: You feel a feather brush against your skin because of PIEZO2 — a colossal ion channel shaped like a three-bladed propeller that converts mechanical force into electrical signals. Ardem Patapoutian won the 2021 Nobel Prize for discovering it. PIEZO2 sits in the tips of Merkel cell–neurite complexes in your skin and in proprioceptive neurons throughout your body. When tissue deforms, the channel opens and cations rush in, firing the sensory nerve. Humans with loss-of-function mutations in PIEZO2 lose the ability to feel light touch and proprioception — they cannot sense where their limbs are without looking. The protein is enormous: 2,752 amino acids forming a homotrimeric dome that curves the cell membrane and acts as its own force sensor. Woo and colleagues showed in 2014 that conditional knockout of Piezo2 in mouse Merkel cells completely abolished gentle-touch mechanosensitivity. The inverse experiment — overexpression to lower activation thresholds — has not been published, but the biophysics suggest that increasing PIEZO2 density could create tactile hypersensitivity comparable to the star-nosed mole. The main translational concern is that PIEZO2 gain-of-function mutations in humans cause distal arthrogryposis — excess mechanosensitivity can lock joints. A tissue-targeted overexpression strategy, restricted to skin Merkel cells, would be essential.
Short Description: PIEZO2 is the giant propeller-shaped channel that turns skin deformation into the electrical language of touch and gives the brain a map of limb position. Removing it from mouse Merkel cells abolishes gentle-touch responses, while human genetics confirms its essential role in fine touch and proprioception. Greater activity could sharpen tactile sensitivity, but known gain-of-function variants can produce prenatal joint contractures, making tissue-specific control essential.
Mechanism: PIEZO2 forms a homotrimeric propeller-shaped mechanically-activated cation channel (~2,800 kDa complex). The curved transmembrane dome acts as an area spring that flattens under membrane tension, gating the central pore. Ca²⁺ and Na⁺ influx depolarizes Merkel cells and sensory neurons, initiating touch and proprioceptive signaling.
Achievements (effect sizes): Woo 2014 Nature: conditional Piezo2 KO in mouse Merkel cells completely abolished gentle-touch mechanosensitivity. Delle Vedove 2016: human PIEZO2 LOF causes loss of proprioception and discriminative touch. Coste 2010 Science: identification of Piezo channels as first molecularly-defined mechanically-activated ion channels. 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (Patapoutian).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse conditional KO, multiple labs) + T7 (human genetic validation)
Translational Gaps: Gain-of-function overexpression not yet tested — only LOF phenotypes characterized. Need tissue-specific promoters restricting expression to Merkel cells to avoid systemic effects. No AAV/LNP delivery to cutaneous Merkel cells demonstrated.
Key References (DOIs): Coste Science 2010 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1193270 | Woo Nature 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13251 | Delle Vedove Am J Hum Genet 2016 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajhg.2016.09.019
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CAUTION: Human gain-of-function mutations in PIEZO2 (e.g., E2727del) cause Gordon syndrome / distal arthrogryposis type 5 — excess mechanosensitivity causing prenatal joint contractures. Any enhancement strategy must restrict expression to cutaneous mechanoreceptors, not muscle or joint proprioceptors. The therapeutic window between enhanced touch and pathological mechanosensitivity is unknown.

Narrative: The iridescence of a pearl is a mechanical structure, not a pigment, and it is assembled under genetic control. Nacre consists of stacked aragonite tablets held in a biopolymer matrix, all with their crystallographic c-axes pointing the same way, and that geometry makes the composite roughly 3,000 times more fracture-resistant than the aragonite it is made of, because cracks are forced to deflect around thousands of tablet interfaces instead of running straight through the mineral. Pif is the protein that directs the assembly. The akoya pearl oyster Pinctada fucata secretes it as a 1,007-amino-acid precursor, which is then cleaved into two functional pieces: Pif97, which anchors to the chitin framework, and Pif80, which nucleates aragonite and sets its orientation. Suzuki and colleagues found the protein through a calcium carbonate-binding assay and established its necessity by knocking it down with RNA interference, which disrupted nacre formation (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1173793); CRISPR-Cas9 work in molluscs subsequently confirmed that Pif plays a significant role in structured nacre crystal growth (https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12640). The biomimetic appeal is obvious: nacre-like composites could reinforce bone, coat implants or armour a surface that heals its own microcracks. In a human osteoblast, Pif-directed mineralisation would in principle produce bone composite with nacre-like fracture resistance. What stands in the way is not delivery but chemistry and system complexity. Nacre is not a protein product; it is the output of a controlled crystallisation process needing a chitin scaffold, tightly held supersaturation, and dozens of matrix proteins acting together, and the mineral it deposits is not the one human bone uses.
Short Description: Pif directs pearl-oyster cells to assemble nacre: one fragment anchors to chitin while another nucleates and aligns aragonite tablets into a crack-deflecting composite. Knocking it down disrupts nacre formation, and the finished material is estimated to be roughly 3,000 times more fracture-resistant than pure aragonite. Its strongest near-term promise is engineered materials, because vertebrate bone uses hydroxyapatite and lacks nacre's chitin scaffold and supporting protein network.
Mechanism: The Pif precursor, 1,007 amino acids in Pinctada fucata, is cleaved after translation into two proteins that remain functionally coupled. Pif97 carries a von Willebrand factor type A domain, a protein module used across biology for binding structural polymers, and here it binds the chitin framework of the shell's organic matrix; it is the anchor that fixes the complex to the scaffold. Pif80 is strongly acidic, and its dense negative charge binds calcium ions and the growing crystal face, which is how it both nucleates aragonite and constrains its orientation. Because one half is attached to the scaffold and the other half templates the mineral, the pair converts a scaffold geometry into a crystal geometry, which is what produces uniformly oriented aragonite tablets rather than randomly arranged crystals. Repeating that cycle layer by layer builds nacre's brick-and-mortar nanoarchitecture, with mineral bricks separated by organic mortar. The orientation control is the functionally critical part, since it is the alignment of the tablets and the compliant interfaces between them, rather than the mineral's own strength, that gives nacre its fracture toughness (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1173793).
Achievements (effect sizes): Suzuki and colleagues identified Pif in the pearl oyster Pinctada fucata using a calcium carbonate-binding assay that selected for proteins binding specifically to aragonite crystals, cloned the complementary DNA and showed that it encodes a precursor which is post-translationally cleaved into Pif97 and Pif80. Three independent lines of evidence then established the protein's role in nacre formation: immunolocalisation placing it at the mineralisation front, an RNA interference knockdown experiment that disrupted nacre deposition, and in-vitro calcium carbonate crystallisation studies (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1173793). Clark and colleagues, reviewing the genetic basis of mollusc shell production, report that RNA interference and CRISPR-Cas9 experiments have provided proof of concept for functional investigation of mollusc gene sequences, showing specifically that the aragonite-binding Pif protein plays a significant role in structured nacre crystal growth (https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12640). Mantle transcriptome work in the related pearl oyster Pinctada martensii has catalogued the wider set of biomineralisation genes that accompany Pif (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10126-012-9476-x). The mechanical prize the system delivers is a fracture toughness roughly 3,000 times that of pure aragonite.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (pearl oyster in-vivo RNAi + CRISPR)
Translational Gaps: No vertebrate has been made to express Pif, and the obstacles are chemical rather than merely technical. Nacre formation requires the coordinated action of more than 30 matrix proteins, so Pif is necessary but nowhere near sufficient (https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12640). The chitin scaffold that Pif97's von Willebrand A domain grips does not exist in vertebrate bone, which removes the anchor the mechanism depends on. Most fundamentally, the mineral is wrong: vertebrate bone mineralises with hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate, whereas Pif80 nucleates and orients aragonite, a calcium carbonate polymorph, and Pif-directed mineralisation has never been tested in a hydroxyapatite system, so it is unknown whether the acidic domain would nucleate anything useful there or simply bind calcium unproductively. There are no registered clinical trials.
Key References (DOIs): Suzuki Science 2009 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1173793 | Clark Biological Reviews 2020 https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12640 | Shi Marine Biotechnology 2013 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10126-012-9476-x
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Nacre formation is a system-level phenomenon, and that is the central caveat rather than a hedge. Pif is necessary, demonstrated by knockdown, but more than 30 matrix proteins have been identified in the process, and the mineral architecture also depends on physical conditions such as controlled supersaturation that no gene supplies (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1173793, https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12640). The aragonite-versus-hydroxyapatite mismatch is a fundamental barrier rather than an engineering detail: human bone uses an entirely different mineral system, so a protein whose acidic domain evolved to template calcium carbonate has no established function in a calcium phosphate environment. Taken together, these constraints suggest that the realistic application of Pif is biomimetic materials engineering, where the chitin scaffold and crystallisation conditions can be supplied in a reactor, rather than genetic enhancement of a human skeleton. One bookkeeping note: the record's DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10126-012-9476-x resolves in Crossref to a paper published in 2013 by Shi and colleagues, not 2012 as the entry previously stated, and it concerns the Pinctada martensii mantle transcriptome rather than Pif specifically (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10126-012-9476-x).

Manipulation: CAR T cell therapy (anti-uPAR scFv-CD28-CD3z); targets the gene product, not overexpression
Narrative:
Senescent cells are the body's retired workforce that refuses to leave the building. They stop dividing but do not die, and they leak inflammatory signals that degrade the tissue around them. Clearing them rejuvenates old mice. The problem has always been how: small-molecule senolytics kill by nudging stressed cells over an apoptotic threshold, which means dosing again and again as new senescent cells accumulate.

Corina Amor, working in Scott Lowe's laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering with the CAR T pioneer Michel Sadelain, asked a different question: what if senescent cells have a surface marker, and the immune system could be taught to read it? They found one — the urokinase plasminogen activator surface receptor, a protein tethered to the outside of the membrane that turns up on senescent cells whatever pushed them into senescence. Then they built the standard oncology tool against it: a second-generation chimeric antigen receptor, an antibody fragment fused to signalling domains, installed in T cells that thereafter kill anything wearing the marker.

The first paper (Amor 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9) showed this clears senescent cells from liver and reduces fibrosis. The follow-up (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5) asked what happens in an animal that is simply old. Twenty-month-old mice got one infusion. Their fasting glucose fell, they handled a sugar bolus better than untreated controls for over two hours, and most of them ran longer on a treadmill than they had before treatment — two and a half months after the single dose. Young mice showed no glucose effect, which is the right control: the therapy removes an age-specific burden rather than improving metabolism generally. Because CAR T cells expand and persist — the authors report persistence beyond 15 months — one dose buys surveillance instead of a pulse. An independent group has since done the same thing with a different receptor in aged monkeys. The unsolved part is not biology. It is that manufacturing an autologous cell product, and preceding it with lymphodepleting chemotherapy, is a great deal to ask of someone whose only complaint is being old.
Short Description: Anti-uPAR CAR T cells turn the immune system into long-lived surveillance against many senescent cells. One infusion in 20-month-old mice improved fasting glucose, glucose handling, and later treadmill performance, while uPAR marked 67–90% of senescent cells in aged liver and engineered cells can persist beyond 15 months. Translation must narrow the target and simplify treatment because uPAR is not senescence-exclusive and current protocols use lymphodepletion.
Mechanism: The urokinase plasminogen activator surface receptor (uPAR, encoded by PLAUR, 335 amino acids, anchored to the outer face of the plasma membrane by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol tail) is broadly upregulated on senescent cells regardless of what triggered the senescence, and Plaur is a component of the SenMayo senescence gene signature. The therapeutic agent is not the gene itself but a receptor aimed at it: a second-generation chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) built from an anti-uPAR single-chain variable fragment fused to a CD28 costimulatory domain and a CD3ζ signalling domain. Installed in T cells, it redirects them to lyse uPAR-positive cells through the perforin and granzyme pathway, with antigen-specific release of granzyme B and interferon gamma on engagement. The pharmacological distinction from small-molecule senolytics matters: because CAR T cells expand on antigen contact and persist afterwards, one infusion establishes durable immune surveillance of the senescent compartment rather than the transient kill-and-clear that repeated small-molecule dosing produces.
Achievements (effect sizes): Single-cell RNA sequencing of uPAR-positive and uPAR-negative cells sorted from 20-month-old mice established that the marker actually covers the population it needs to: uPAR-positive cells constituted 67–90% of the senescent cell burden in liver, 92–66% in adipose tissue and 76–63% in pancreas (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5). Treating aged mice with a single infusion of the anti-uPAR CAR, against both untransduced T cells and an irrelevant CAR as controls, significantly decreased fasting glucose, and after an intraperitoneal bolus of 2 g glucose per kg body weight the treated animals held significantly lower plasma glucose than controls for over 2 hours; most also showed improvements in exercise capacity 2.5 months after treatment compared with their own pretreatment levels (n = 7 untransduced, n = 8 irrelevant CAR, n = 8 anti-uPAR CAR for exercise testing), while young mice showed no such glucose effect (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5). The original demonstration was in liver: in an NRAS-G12V oncogene-induced senescence model, livers of CAR-treated mice had significantly reduced numbers of NRAS-positive (p<0.01) and senescence-associated beta-galactosidase-positive cells (p<0.001) versus controls, and in established liver fibrosis the treated livers showed fewer senescent cells and less fibrosis by senescence-associated beta-galactosidase and Sirius red staining (p<0.001) at 20 days, with under 2% of the CAR T cells displaying a triple-marker exhaustion phenotype at day 15 (Amor 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse cell therapy across oncogene-induced, fibrotic, aged and high-fat-diet models in two papers from the same group, with independent confirmation of the approach using a different antigen; no human senolytic CAR trial)
Translational Gaps: No registered clinical trial of a senolytic CAR T cell exists. Searching the registry for uPAR CAR and for senolytic CAR T returns nothing; the only record that combines CAR engineering with senescence language is INT2104 from Kite/Gilead (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06539338), an in vivo lentiviral CD20 CAR for B-cell malignancies, which targets a different antigen in an oncology indication and is noted here only to document that the direction check was run and came back negative. Two practical barriers stand in the way. Manufacturing an autologous cell product for each patient is expensive and slow, and it has so far only been justified for fatal cancers rather than for ageing. The protocol also requires cyclophosphamide preconditioning, so a recipient takes lymphodepleting chemotherapy before receiving the cells. The authors additionally state that it remains undetermined which uPAR-positive populations actually drive the metabolic benefit, which means a safer, narrower antigen cannot yet be substituted for the broad one (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5).
Key References (DOIs): Amor Nature 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9 | Amor Nature Aging 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5 | Yang Science Translational Medicine 2023 https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.add1951
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: An independent group reached the same conclusion through a different antigen, which is the strongest available evidence that the approach and not the specific receptor is what works: NKG2D-targeting CAR T cells eliminated senescent cells in aged mice and in aged nonhuman primates without observed adverse effects (Yang 2023, https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.add1951). Durability is real — the 2024 paper reports CAR T cells persisting and expanding for over 15 months (https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5). Two cautions belong on the record. uPAR is not senescence-exclusive: the same receptor sits on activated immune cells and on invasive tumour cells, and the 2020 paper had to establish specifically that anti-uPAR CAR T cells do not attack normal tissue (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9). And senescence is itself tumour-suppressive and promotes wound healing, so clearing it systemically removes a genuine brake on premalignant expansion. The 2020 Nature paper carries an author correction (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07197-3). Commercially, nothing is available: the closest clinical senolytics are small molecules — dasatinib combined with quercetin, and fisetin — which kill by a different mechanism and must be dosed repeatedly.

Narrative: Turritopsis dohrnii, a grape-sized jellyfish, can reverse its life cycle: a damaged adult collapses into a cyst and re-emerges as a juvenile polyp, resetting its biological age. It is the only animal known to do this reliably. In 2022, Carlos López-Otín's group sequenced its genome and identified a variant of POT1 — a human telomere-protection gene — predicted to release the brake on telomerase. When they put the G272N jellyfish mutation into the human POT1 protein, it bound telomeric DNA much less tightly in a test tube. That's the entire experimental result. No cell phenotype, no telomere-length measurement, no mammalian model. More worryingly, reduced POT1 binding in humans causes cancer — familial melanoma, leukemia, glioma. The paper has two formal Corrections and a published critique. Transdifferentiation is a whole-organism phenomenon; reducing it to a single shelterin variant is almost certainly too simple. The jellyfish is doing something astonishing, and nobody yet knows what.
Short Description: Turritopsis jellyfish can reverse from an adult medusa into a juvenile polyp, and its altered telomere-maintenance network is one intriguing part of that reset. A jellyfish-style G272N change introduced into human POT1 weakened binding to telomeric DNA in a biochemical assay, showing that the variant changes shelterin behaviour. That is a precise molecular clue, not yet a rejuvenation mechanism, and reduced POT1 binding in people is associated with cancer predisposition.
Mechanism: POT1 shelterin variant (G272N) predicted to reduce telomerase inhibition; SIRT3 mitoprotection; RTEL1 telomere helicase; GAR1 duplicated.
Achievements (effect sizes): Pascual-Torner 2022 PNAS: whole-genome T. dohrnii vs mortal T. rubra; identified expansions/variants. ONLY WET RESULT: introduced jellyfish-style G272N into recombinant human POT1, EMSA with 3×TTAGGG oligo → reduced ssDNA binding. No cell phenotype, no telomerase activity measured. Matsumoto/Miglietta 2025 bioRxiv: life-cycle-reversal transcriptome — SIRT3 peaks in cyst; RTEL1/HSP70/90 dynamic; POU/Sox/Klf/Myc detected. No functional tests. No gene editing in T. dohrnii; no mammalian transfer.
Highest Evidence Tier: T2–T3 for POT1 biochemistry on human-backbone protein; T1 for everything else
Translational Gaps: T. dohrnii POT1 in mammalian cells; telomere-length/cell phenotype; transdifferentiation never recapitulated in a mammal.
Key References (DOIs): Pascual-Torner PNAS 2022 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2118763119
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: MAJOR CAVEAT: reduced POT1–ssDNA binding in humans = CANCER PREDISPOSITION. POT1 loss-of-function causes familial melanoma, CLL, glioma, pulmonary fibrosis (L259S, H266L). Pascual-Torner 2022 has TWO formal PNAS Corrections + a published critique by Miglietta 2023 PNAS. Annotation reliability for non-model organisms questioned. Binding ≠ function; 3×TTAGGG oligo is a minimal substrate.

Manipulation: Human common-variant knock-in (Pro12Ala, PPARγ2 isoform; homozygous Ala/Ala)
Narrative: PPARγ is the master switch for fat-cell formation and the receptor the glitazone diabetes drugs bind. Pro12Ala is a common human coding variant in the γ2 isoform, carried by a substantial minority of people, and it has been argued about for two decades — small, inconsistent effects on diabetes risk across cohorts. Heikkinen et al. settled part of the argument by putting the human variant into the mouse genome. On ordinary chow, homozygous Ala/Ala mice were leaner, more insulin-sensitive, had better plasma lipids, and lived longer. Then they fed the same mice a high-fat diet and every benefit disappeared — adiposity, lipids and insulin sensitivity all reverted. The variant is not an upgrade; it is a conditional upgrade whose value is set entirely by what the animal eats. That is the honest card here, and it explains why the human association literature was so noisy: the effect exists only in one dietary context.
Short Description: A single amino-acid swap in the fat-cell master regulator makes adipose tissue store less and respond to insulin better. Knock-in mice carrying the human variant gained 13.0% mean lifespan in males, leaner and more insulin-sensitive, and the allele occurs naturally in people whose PPARγ is already a licensed drug target. High-fat feeding erased every benefit in the mice, and no one has delivered this allele to a person.
Mechanism: PPARG encodes a nuclear receptor that heterodimerises with RXR to drive the adipogenic and insulin-sensitising transcriptional programme. The Pro12Ala substitution sits in the γ2-isoform-specific N-terminal extension and modestly reduces transactivation, shifting cofactor interactions and raising adiponectin signalling. In the knock-in mouse this produced lower adiposity, improved insulin sensitivity and a favourable plasma lipid profile on chow. Loss-of-function controls in the same gene run the other way: whole-gene reduction in white adipose tissue shortened median lifespan by 14.5% and Pparg2 isoform knockout by 9.0%, confirming that this is a fine-tuning variant on an essential gene rather than a hypomorph that happens to help.
Achievements (effect sizes): Human common variant validated by knock-in: Ala/Ala mice leaner, more insulin-sensitive, better plasma lipids, and longer-lived (+13.0% mean, +12.5% median in males). Gene-environment interaction demonstrated directly — high-fat feeding eliminated the benefits on adiposity, lipids and insulin sensitivity. Mechanism traced to cofactor interaction and adiponectin signalling. Loss-of-function controls in the same gene shorten lifespan, bracketing the dose direction.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human common variant knocked into mice with lifespan, metabolic and mechanistic endpoints plus an explicit diet-interaction arm, single laboratory; the allele is naturally present in humans with a widely-studied but inconsistent metabolic phenotype, and no allele-delivery has been attempted in a person)
Translational Gaps: The mouse benefit is chow-only and vanishes on a high-fat diet — the diet most people in the relevant populations actually eat, which likely explains why human association studies disagree. No human lifespan data exist for carriers, and the human literature on Pro12Ala and type 2 diabetes risk is inconsistent across cohorts. Nobody has delivered this allele: it would be a base-editing target in adipose tissue, and adipose is not a solved editing target. The mouse experiment is a germline homozygous knock-in, whereas most human carriers are heterozygous.
Key References (DOIs): Heikkinen S et al. Cell Metab 2009;9:88-98 (10.1016/j.cmet.2008.11.007); Argmann 2009 PLoS Genet (10.1371/journal.pgen.1000752)
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: DIET-CONDITIONAL: high-fat feeding eliminated the beneficial effects on adiposity, plasma lipids and insulin sensitivity. This is the defining caveat and must stay on the card, not just in the details panel. GENE IS ESSENTIAL AND DOSE-SENSITIVE DOWNWARD: reducing Pparg expression in white adipose tissue cost 14.5% of median lifespan and Pparg2 isoform knockout 9.0% — this is not a gene to knock down. DRUG-CLASS TRADEOFFS: pharmacological PPARγ agonism (rosiglitazone, pioglitazone) causes fluid retention, weight gain, heart-failure exacerbation and bone loss, and rosiglitazone carried a cardiovascular warning. A variant that mildly REDUCES transactivation is not the same intervention as an agonist, but it is the same receptor and the class history belongs in the record. ONCOLOGY LINK: the PAX8-PPARγ fusion drives a thyroid carcinoma subtype (its own Phase 2 trial, NCT01655719) — the locus is transformation-relevant. HETEROZYGOSITY: mouse data are homozygous Ala/Ala; most human carriers are heterozygous and the dose-response is unmapped.

Narrative:
Deinococcus radiodurans survives 5,000 Gy, roughly 1000 times the lethal human dose for a whole organism. It does this not by preventing damage but by tolerating it: the genome shatters, and the cell stitches it back together within hours. The reassembly is coordinated by a single master-switch protein called PprI, also known as IrrE.

Shi and colleagues produced recombinant PprI in Pichia pastoris yeast and tested it on mammalian systems. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells given the protein before 4 Gy of gamma rays showed markedly fewer gamma-H2AX foci, the standard marker of double-strand breaks, at 1, 2, 4 and 8 hours after irradiation, along with higher survival, better antioxidant capacity and less apoptosis. In the same paper, BALB/c mice given PprI around a 6 Gy whole-body dose had their 30-day mortality fall from 50% to 20%, with improved white blood cell and platelet counts, better bone marrow colony formation and reduced pathological injury across several organs (2016, https://doi.org/10.1038/srep26664).

That is one of the cleanest demonstrations of bacterial radioresistance machinery working in a mammal. The cautions are substantial. The mammalian work comes essentially from one group and has not been independently replicated. The protein is bacterial and therefore likely immunogenic. And the full Deinococcus phenotype does not rest on any single gene: Daly and colleagues showed that the organism's resistance depends heavily on small-molecule manganese antioxidant complexes that shield the proteome from oxidative damage, so that the repair enzymes survive the dose and remain able to work (2010, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0012570).
Short Description: PprI recruits a coordinated stress response from one of nature's most radiation-resistant bacteria, helping damaged cells preserve DNA repair, antioxidant capacity, and blood-forming tissue. In cultured human endothelial cells it roughly halved radiation-damage foci, and after 6 Gy whole-body exposure mouse mortality fell from 50% to 20%. The mammalian target is still unknown and the main efficacy studies come from one group, making independent replication the key next test.
Mechanism:
PprI, also called IrrE, is a manganese-dependent zinc metalloprotease that acts as the top of a regulatory cascade rather than as a repair enzyme itself. Under normal conditions the transcriptional repressor DdrO holds the radiation-response regulon shut. After irradiation, PprI cleaves DdrO, derepressing the regulon and driving expression of RecA, PprA and single-stranded DNA-binding protein, alongside induction of antioxidant defences including catalases. The result is that a single protease event converts radiation damage into a coordinated, genome-wide repair programme.

PprA is one of the downstream effectors and is specific to Deinococcus. It binds DNA ends and nicks, stimulates DNA ligase activity, and interacts with gyrase and topoisomerase IB, which is consistent with a role in holding shattered fragments in a ligatable configuration during reassembly.
Achievements (effect sizes):
Gao and colleagues expressed IrrE in Escherichia coli and obtained approximately 1.6-fold higher survival after gamma irradiation at 50 and 100 Gy, with upregulation of RecA and the catalase KatG (2003, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dnarep.2003.08.012).

Pan and colleagues showed that IrrE, the global regulator of extreme radiation resistance in Deinococcus radiodurans, also confers salt, oxidative and thermal tolerance when transferred into Escherichia coli and Brassica napus (2009, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0004422).

Shi and colleagues carried out the pivotal mammalian work. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells were pretreated with 4 micrograms per millilitre of Pichia-produced PprI six hours before irradiation. Clonogenic survival analysis gave a mean lethal dose D0 of 1.5837 Gy for the control group versus 1.6597 Gy with PprI, which the older record rounds to a shift from 1.58 to 1.66 Gy, and a quasi-threshold dose Dq of 0.9936 versus 1.5430, rounded to 0.99 rising to 1.54; the larger shoulder indicates an increased capacity to absorb sublethal damage. Treated cells showed markedly reduced gamma-H2AX foci at 1, 2, 4 and 8 hours after irradiation, roughly half the control level, reduced apoptosis and increased RAD51. In the same paper, male BALB/c mice, eight weeks old and ten per group, received intraperitoneal PprI at 100 micrograms per kilogram one hour before, one hour after and 24 hours after a 6 Gy dose from a cobalt-60 source. In the saline control group five of ten mice died within 15 days, a 50% mortality rate, while only two of ten died in the treated group, a 20% rate. Treated mice also showed improved white blood cell and platelet counts, better bone marrow clonogenic survival, and reduced lung fibrosis and hepatic and renal damage (2016, https://doi.org/10.1038/srep26664).

Chen and colleagues used in vivo electroporation of a pprI-carrying plasmid in mice before a 6 Gy dose and likewise reduced mortality, an improvement of around 30 percentage points (2016, https://doi.org/10.18632/oncotarget.13893). This record carries that paper under the surname Zhang and the year 2017. Crossref gives the first author as Chen and dates the online publication to 10 December of 2016, with the print issue following two months later in 2017, which is where the 2017 in the old record came from.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (PprI mouse, single lab) + T6 (HUVECs)
Translational Gaps: Independent replication is the first requirement, because the mammalian efficacy data rest essentially on a single group. Long-term safety has not been examined at all, which matters for an agent whose mechanism includes suppressing apoptosis in irradiated cells, since apoptosis is also how a body disposes of cells carrying unrepairable damage. Delivery needs to move away from bolus injection of a bacterial protein toward a humanised or PEGylated construct, or messenger RNA delivery, before repeated dosing is plausible.
Key References (DOIs): Gao DNA Repair 2003 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dnarep.2003.08.012 | Pan PLoS ONE 2009 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0004422 | Shi Scientific Reports 2016 https://doi.org/10.1038/srep26664 | Chen Oncotarget 2016 https://doi.org/10.18632/oncotarget.13893 | Daly PLoS ONE 2010 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0012570 | Daly Science 2004 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1103185
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
The mechanistic story does not transfer cleanly. PprI's known substrate, the repressor DdrO, is absent in mammals, so whatever PprI does in a human cell it is not doing by cleaving DdrO and derepressing a Deinococcus regulon. The observed effects in human cells, increased antioxidant capacity and elevated RAD51, are therefore indirect and the actual mammalian target is unidentified. This is the central unresolved problem with the gene: it works, and nobody has shown how.

The magnitude of the transferable effect is also far smaller than the organism's reputation suggests. Deinococcus itself is roughly 1000 times more radiation-resistant than a human cell, but moving IrrE into Escherichia coli bought only about 1.6-fold (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dnarep.2003.08.012), and the HUVEC D0 shifted from 1.5837 to 1.6597 Gy, that is from 1.58 to 1.66 Gy, a change of under 5%, while the Dq shoulder widened from 0.99 to 1.54. The larger Dq shoulder is the more meaningful cellular effect, and the mouse mortality change is the most impressive number in the record, but none of these approach the native phenotype.

Daly's work argues that Deinococcus resistance is primarily a matter of small-molecule manganese antioxidant complexes shielding the proteome, rather than of PprI or PprA acting alone (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0012570; see also Daly 2004, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1103185, on manganese accumulation facilitating gamma-radiation resistance). If the protective principle is manganese chemistry, then transferring the regulator without the manganese chemistry transfers the smaller half of the mechanism.

Bolus protein dosing is not translation-ready, and immunogenicity against a bacterial protein is a foreseeable obstacle to repeated administration. PprA, despite being included in this entry, has no robust standalone mammalian in vivo evidence at all; the mammalian case rests on PprI.

Narrative:
Proteorhodopsin was found in the ocean before it was found in an organism. A shotgun-sequencing survey of surface seawater turned up a rhodopsin gene on a bacterial DNA fragment catalogued as EBAC31A08, belonging to the SAR86 clade — a group of gammaproteobacteria nobody had ever grown in culture. The gene existed as a database entry before anyone could hold the cell that carried it, and what it encodes is a light-driven proton pump that lets an ordinary heterotroph run part of its energy budget on sunlight without performing photosynthesis at all.

What the protein does is mechanically simple and biologically radical. A seven-helix opsin holds a molecule of vitamin A aldehyde, all-trans-retinal, buried in the middle of the membrane. A green photon bends the retinal, the protein flexes through a conformational cycle, and one proton is carried from the inside of the cell to the outside. Do that continuously and you have a proton gradient — the same electrochemical currency the respiratory chain builds, and one that can be spent directly on adenosine triphosphate synthesis or on spinning a flagellum.

The experiment that proved the point, done in the Liphardt laboratory at Berkeley, is memorable for its brutality. Escherichia coli carrying the gene were poisoned with sodium azide, which shuts down the respiratory chain, and then put in sunlight. Cells with the pump and its retinal cofactor kept swimming and kept forming colonies; cells with the pump but no retinal did worse than cells with nothing at all, because an opsin without its chromophore is a piece of membrane hardware that does nothing (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104). That control is the honest heart of this card. In the dark, or on a vitamin-A-poor diet, the enhancement is not neutral — it is a liability. And because the pump absorbs green light, which is among the worst wavelengths for getting through tissue, a body-scale version would need a light source inside it.
Short Description: Proteorhodopsin is a compact green-light-driven proton pump that lets cells convert photons directly into membrane energy without photosynthesis. When respiration was poisoned, engineered E. coli with both the pump and retinal restored flagellar power and achieved 11% survival versus 1% in comparison cells. Animal energy support is conceivable with related pumps, but this protein needs retinal and illumination, and green light penetrates tissue poorly.
Mechanism: Proteorhodopsin is a 249-amino-acid, 27.3 kDa seven-transmembrane opsin. It binds all-trans-retinal, the aldehyde form of vitamin A, through a Schiff base to a lysine residue on its seventh helix, which buries the chromophore in the middle of the lipid bilayer. Absorption of a green photon isomerises that retinal to its 13-cis form, and the strained chromophore drives a cycle of conformational changes in the protein during which one proton is translocated vectorially across the membrane. The gradient this builds — the proton-motive force — is the identical currency produced by the respiratory electron transport chain, which is why it can power the flagellar motor and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase directly, with no electron transport, no oxygen and no quinone pool. The variant on this card is the green-light-absorbing form; a blue-absorbing relative from deeper water differs at a small number of residues that retune its absorption maximum, so the family as a whole reads as a depth gauge for the sunlit ocean.
Achievements (effect sizes): The decisive experiment poisoned respiration and asked whether light could replace it. Escherichia coli were exposed to 30 mM sodium azide for 30 minutes in sunlight under four conditions — with and without proteorhodopsin, with and without exogenous all-trans-retinal — and then plated for colony counts: “the cells lacking retinal were most sensitive to azide; no colonies were recovered after plating the azide exposed cells. The cells lacking PR but having retinal were slightly more azide resistant; 1% of cells survived. The cells with both PR and retinal were significantly more azide resistant than in all three other conditions (11% of cells survived; P < 0.005, Mann-Whitney U test)” (Walter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104). A single-cell version of the same logic measured proton-motive force directly, by watching one tethered bacterium's flagellum turn across an azide titration from 0 to 110 mM: “the pmf dropped to 50% of its original value at an azide concentration of 55 mM... When the cells were illuminated with intense green light, their rotation rate was restored to the speed of cells with an unimpaired respiratory system”, and the same work estimated the pump's Michaelis-Menten constant at 10^3 photons per second/nm2 (Walter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (heterologous gain-of-function in bacteria with single-cell biophysics and survival endpoints; related mitochondrially targeted proton pumps validated in Drosophila and C. elegans by independent laboratories)
Translational Gaps: In an animal this class of pump has only ever been used inside mitochondria, never at the plasma membrane, and never as proteorhodopsin itself. Imai and colleagues targeted delta-rhodopsin from the archaeon Haloterrigena turkmenica to Drosophila mitochondria and recovered mitochondrial membrane potential and motor behaviour in a CHCHD2 model of Parkinson's disease (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0674-1). Berry and colleagues targeted a light-driven proton pump to the mitochondria of Caenorhabditis elegans and extended lifespan (https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00340-7). Both experiments depend on feeding the animal retinal, because neither the fly nor the worm can synthesise it, and neither used the marine proteorhodopsin of this card. No mammalian in vivo work exists at all. Nobody has measured whether a human cell tolerates a light-gated proton leak in its plasma membrane, and nobody has solved the optical problem: green light penetrates tissue poorly, so a body-scale version would need either an implanted illuminator or a red-shifted pump that has not been built.
Key References (DOIs): Walter Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2007 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104 | Imai Communications Biology 2019 https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0674-1 | Berry Nature Aging 2022 https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00340-7
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This gene is a good exhibit for how sequencing changed biology. It was found by environmental shotgun sequencing of seawater rather than by culturing an organism, so the sequence was in a database before anyone had the bacterium; the host is recorded simply as gamma-proteobacterium EBAC31A08 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q9F7P4). Structures exist at three levels and can be shown side by side: a solution nuclear magnetic resonance structure of the green-absorbing pump (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/2L6X), a cryo-electron microscopy structure of the same protein (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7B03), and crystal structures of the blue-absorbing variant that occupies a different depth in the water column (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4KLY and https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4KNF), which lets the display show spectral tuning against ocean depth. There are no clinical trials and no commercial product for proteorhodopsin. The one clearly negative result in the record deserves to stay on the wall rather than be quietly dropped: cells expressing the opsin without retinal were the worst of the four conditions tested, not merely equivalent to untreated cells (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104). Finally, the mitochondrially targeted animal work uses different rhodopsins from different archaea and should not be read as validation of this particular gene (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0674-1, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00340-7).

Narrative: Bats and dolphins both hear well into the ultrasonic range — frequencies far above anything a human or mouse can detect — and they evolved this ability independently. The molecular centerpiece is prestin, a motor protein in cochlear hair cells that physically contracts in response to voltage, amplifying faint sounds. Echolocating bats and dolphins carry the exact same amino-acid substitutions in prestin, a textbook example of convergent molecular evolution, and those substitutions change the protein's electrical properties when measured in human HEK293 cells. This is where the press ran ahead of the data. Yalin Li's lab showed in 2022 that prestin-knockout mice still hear above 40 kHz — prestin amplifies loudness but doesn't determine frequency range. Tian 2021 found that prestin's electrical parameters don't actually correlate with how high an animal can hear. Nobody has yet put bat prestin into a mouse and extended its hearing. The convergent evolution is beautiful; the functional story is shakier than it first looked.
Short Description: Prestin is the voltage-driven motor in outer hair cells, physically amplifying faint cochlear vibrations before sensory cells report them to the brain. Echolocating dolphins and bats evolved convergent substitutions that shift its electrical behaviour, and dolphin prestin shows visible electromotility in cultured human cells. The protein clearly boosts sensitivity, but mice without it still detect frequencies above 40 kHz, so prestin alone does not set ultrasonic range.
Mechanism: Outer hair cell voltage-driven piezoelectric motor protein; non-linear capacitance (NLC) parameters Qmax/Clin, V½, 1/α.
Achievements (effect sizes): Liu 2014 MBE: 7 species' prestins in HEK293, whole-cell NLC. 1/α significantly increased in all echolocators (N7T attributed); V½ depolarized in dolphin and Stoliczka's trident bat (I384T attributed). Bavi/Santos-Sacchi 2021–2023 dolphin prestin HEK293: V½ −61 mV, 1/α 37 mV; visible electromotility. No knock-in mouse carrying bat/dolphin prestin has been published. Prestin-KO mice: ~50 dB threshold elevation high-freq; Cheatham 2012 V499G/Y501H KI: ~34% residual charge, defective high-freq amplification.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (HEK293 NLC, multiple labs)
Translational Gaps: No bat/dolphin prestin-KI mouse gain-of-function; mouse hearing range not extended.
Key References (DOIs): Liu Curr Biol 2010 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2009.11.058 | Liu MBE 2014 https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msu194
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Li 2022 Neurosci Bull — prestin-KO mice RETAIN >40 kHz hearing — prestin amplifies amplitude, is NOT the ultrasonic selectivity determinant. (2) Tian 2021 Front Cell Dev Biol — NLC parameters DO NOT correlate with species Fmax — direct challenge to the "prestin drives ultrasonic hearing" narrative. (3) Shen 2012 — Pteronotus CF bat lacks rhinolophid adaptive signature — convergence incomplete.
