HEK293 ≠ cochlear micromechanics; Qmax depends on expression; site-direction on common backbone ≠ full-length.

Manipulation: loss-of-function germline knockout of the RII-beta regulatory subunit (lowers PKA activity in brain and fat)
Narrative: Reducing protein kinase A activity extends lifespan in yeast, and the mammalian test of that idea has an unusually specific handle. PKA is a holoenzyme of catalytic and regulatory subunits, and the RII-beta regulatory subunit is expressed mainly in brain and adipose tissue rather than everywhere - so deleting it lowers PKA activity in the two tissues that set energy balance while leaving the kinase intact elsewhere. Enns and colleagues had a strong prior: RII-beta-null mice were already known to be lean and insulin sensitive, protected on a high-fat high-carbohydrate diet against weight gain, hyperinsulinemia, fatty liver and insulin resistance. They ran 40 mutants against 40 wild-type littermates with equal numbers of each sex to lifespan. Male knockouts gained on both survival measures: median lifespan rose from 884 to 1005 days and the 80% lifespan from 941 to 1073 days. Females gained nothing on either. The healthspan data are where the interest is. Wild-type mice of both sexes became increasingly obese with age while mutants held their lean phenotype into old age; wild types lost 8% (males) and 15% (females) of body weight in their final month while mutant males kept lean mass to end of life. Old mutant males stayed insulin sensitive throughout, resisted age-induced fatty liver, and at necropsy showed lower tumour incidence, better renal lesion scores in three of ten graded categories, and a trend toward less cardiac pathology - splenic tumours appeared in all wild-type mice but only about 40% of mutants. The authors' own reading is that the lifespan effect tracks decreased body fat rather than insulin sensitivity.
Short Description: Losing one regulatory subunit of protein kinase A leaves mice lean and insulin sensitive for life instead of fattening with age. Male knockouts reached a median lifespan of 1005 days against 884 for littermates (P=0.006), with fewer spleen tumours, less age-related fatty liver and better kidney scores. Females got nothing at all, and the entire cohort was 20 animals per sex in a single laboratory.
Mechanism: PRKAR2B encodes a 418-residue, 46.3 kDa regulatory subunit of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A. Two regulatory subunits bind two catalytic subunits to hold the kinase inactive until cAMP binds the regulatory pair and releases the catalytic subunits. RII-beta expression is concentrated in brain and adipose tissue, so its loss lowers PKA signalling selectively in those compartments, with compensatory subunit substitution altering rather than abolishing kinase output. The metabolic consequence is a lean phenotype resistant to diet-induced obesity, hyperinsulinemia, fatty liver and insulin resistance, with lower serum glucose and cholesterol and improved glucose dispersal - a profile the authors explicitly compare to caloric restriction. The survival correlation was with adiposity, not insulin sensitivity: 50% of male mice in the 30-35 g range (roughly 5% body fat) reached 1000 days regardless of genotype, and no male outside that weight range did.
Achievements (effect sizes): Enns 2009 (PLoS ONE): in a cohort of 40 RII-beta-null mice against 40 wild-type littermates with equal numbers of each sex, male knockouts had median lifespan increased from 884 to 1005 days (+13.7%, log-rank P=0.006) and 80% lifespan from 941 to 1073 days (+14.0%, Wang-Allison P=0.004). OpenGenes records the male row as +7.9% median (+10.4% maximum) and the female row as -9.7% median. There was no difference in either median or 80% lifespan for females. Healthspan: wild-type mice of both sexes became increasingly obese with age while mutants stayed lean into old age; mutant males maintained lean body mass to end of life whereas wild types lost 8% (male) and 15% (female) of body weight in their final month; old mutant males were insulin sensitive throughout life; both sexes had modestly lower blood glucose; mutant males resisted age-induced fatty liver. End-of-life pathology in males: decreased tumour incidence with splenic tumours in 100% of wild-type versus roughly 40% of mutants, significantly better scores in 3 of 10 graded renal lesion categories including tubular degeneration and interstitial and pelvic inflammation, and a trend toward less age-related cardiac pathology.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse germline-knockout lifespan cohort with both sexes powered equally, two survival statistics, longitudinal body-composition and insulin-sensitivity phenotyping and systematic end-of-life pathology across kidney, liver, spleen and heart; one laboratory, 20 animals per sex per genotype, no human intervention)
Translational Gaps: The lifespan benefit is male-only and the female data are not merely null - the OpenGenes female row records -9.7% median, so this gene has an opposite-direction sex effect rather than a sex-limited one, and the paper confirms no difference in either female survival statistic. That is a harder constraint than the female-only pattern seen in the library's S6K1 card. Cohort size is 20 animals per sex per genotype from one laboratory, never replicated. The authors' own preliminary interpretation weakens the mechanism claim: they attribute the survival gain to decreased body fat rather than to insulin sensitivity or to PKA signalling as such, and the strongest single predictor in their data is body weight in the 30-35 g window irrespective of genotype - which means the intervention may be a route to leanness rather than an aging pathway. No human has had PKA RII-beta reduced. PRKAR2B has no solved PDB structure, and the clinically relevant PKA regulatory-subunit disease in humans is the opposite lesion: inactivating PRKAR1A mutations cause Carney complex with multiple tumours, so the PKA regulatory subunits are not a family where reduced function is assumed safe.
Key References (DOIs): Enns PLoS ONE 2009 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0005963
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: STATISTIC: 884 -> 1005 days is MEDIAN lifespan in MALES and recomputes to +13.7%; the 941 -> 1073 day figure is the 80% lifespan (Wang-Allison), +14.0%. OpenGenes records +7.9% median for the male row - the pack quotes the paper's own day values and flags the discrepancy. The OpenGenes _min for the male row is -9.0%, i.e. NEGATIVE, which is another reason the minimum-lifespan column must never be used as an effect size. SEX EFFECT IS OPPOSITE-SIGNED, not just absent: female row is -9.7% median in OpenGenes and the paper reports no difference in either female survival measure. This must survive into card copy. MECHANISM CAVEAT FROM THE AUTHORS: they attribute the lifespan effect to decreased body fat, NOT to insulin sensitivity - do not write this card as an insulin-signalling story. NO STRUCTURE: PRKAR2B has zero PDB entries (verified this session); AlphaFold only. FAMILY CAUTION: inactivating PRKAR1A mutations cause Carney complex in humans - reduced PKA regulatory-subunit function is not a safe-by-default direction.

Manipulation: gain of function - one additional genomic copy of the gene (systemic, modest overexpression across all tissues)
Narrative: Almost every intervention in this pathway works by removing something: a receptor, a kinase, a protease. PTEN is the one that works by adding. It is the phosphatase that undoes PI3K's work, stripping the phosphate off PIP3 and shutting the AKT growth signal down - and it is one of the most frequently lost tumour suppressors in human cancer. Manuel Serrano's group at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre built mice carrying additional genomic copies, so the whole animal expresses modestly more PTEN from the start. Those mice were protected from cancer, which was expected, and they lived longer - and the survival benefit held even after accounting for their lower cancer incidence, which was not. The mechanism turned out to be metabolic rather than purely anti-proliferative: the extra-PTEN mice had increased energy expenditure, carried less fat, and their brown adipose tissue was hyperactive with high levels of the uncoupling protein UCP1, which the group showed is a FOXO1 target. A synthetic PI3K inhibitor reproduced the raised energy expenditure and the brown-fat activation in ordinary mice, so the effect is pathway-level, not an artefact of the transgene. The direction of this card is the important part. PTEN is one of the very few nodes in the GH/IGF axis where more of the gene is the enhancement, which makes it deliverable in principle by the same overexpression toolkit the rest of the library uses. What kills the simple story is what happens with less: tissue-restricted Pten knockout in melanocytes cut median lifespan 92%, because losing PTEN is how melanoma starts.
Short Description: An extra copy of the phosphatase that shuts off the PI3K growth signal makes brown fat burn harder and keeps the body leaner. Mice with additional copies lived 18% longer at the mean in males and were markedly protected from cancer, with raised energy expenditure rather than reduced food intake. PTEN loss drives many human tumours, so the dose window is bounded on one side by cancer and on the other by the fact that no delivery to a person exists.
Mechanism: PTEN encodes a 403-amino-acid lipid phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3 to PIP2, directly reversing class I PI3K and thereby lowering AKT activation. Reduced AKT signalling keeps FOXO transcription factors nuclear; the Serrano work identified UCP1 as a FOXO1 target, linking extra PTEN to uncoupled respiration in brown adipocytes and a genuinely raised metabolic rate rather than reduced intake. Extra PTEN also promotes oxidative phosphorylation and decreases glycolysis, opposing the metabolic reprogramming cancer cells depend on - one proposed reason the cancer protection and the longevity effect are partly separable. Dosage is the whole story for this gene: modest systemic elevation is protective, while loss of even one allele is tumour-permissive.
Achievements (effect sizes): Ortega-Molina 2012 (Cell Metabolism): Pten transgenic mice carrying additional genomic copies of Pten were protected from cancer and presented a significant extension of lifespan that was independent of their lower cancer incidence, with increased energy expenditure and protection from metabolic pathologies. Brown adipose tissue was hyperactive with high UCP1, shown to be a FOXO1 target, and a synthetic PI3K inhibitor reproduced the increased energy expenditure and brown-fat hyperactivation in wild-type mice and in isolated brown adipocytes. OpenGenes records the lifespan cohorts as +18% mean / +11% median in males (n=21 vs 42 control) and +11% mean / +18% median in females (n=19 vs 52 control), both significant, with a documented 100% increase in target gene expression and improvements recorded in DNA metabolism, carcinogenesis, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, body composition and INS/IGF pathway signalling. The same record contains the opposing direction: melanocyte- and Trp2-neuron-restricted Pten knockout decreased median lifespan 92% in homozygotes and 13% in heterozygotes.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse germline transgenic with lifespan endpoints in both sexes plus a small-molecule pathway phenocopy; no human genetic or therapeutic gain-of-function exists)
Translational Gaps: There is no way to give a human an extra PTEN copy. No PTEN gene therapy has entered human trials, and the human PTEN clinical literature runs the opposite direction - PTEN loss defines Cowden syndrome and PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome, and PTEN status is used to select patients for PI3K/AKT inhibitors in oncology. The mouse lifespan data come from a single laboratory and have not been independently replicated with a survival endpoint. The dosage window has not been mapped: the transgenic mice carry roughly doubled expression, and no experiment defines how much extra PTEN becomes harmful, or what happens if expression is uneven across tissues after vector delivery.
Key References (DOIs): Ortega-Molina Cell Metabolism 2012 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2012.02.001 | Ortega-Molina Trends Endocrinol Metab 2013 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tem.2012.11.002 | Inoue-Narita Cancer Research 2008 https://doi.org/10.1158/0008-5472.can-08-0889
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: DIRECTION: this is the rare add-a-copy card in the GH/IGF axis - the enhancement is MORE PTEN. All clinical activity around the symbol concerns PTEN LOSS (Cowden syndrome, PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome, PI3K-inhibitor patient selection in oncology), so any registry search on this symbol returns the opposite direction and must be filtered. CANCER: the negative rows are not hypothetical - melanocyte-restricted Pten knockout cut median lifespan 92% (https://doi.org/10.1158/0008-5472.can-08-0889). This asymmetry is the card's core fact: extra copies protect, missing copies kill. DOSAGE UNKNOWN: no experiment defines the upper safe bound of PTEN overexpression, and unlike the knockdown cards there is no partial-inhibition dial - vector-delivered overexpression would be uneven across tissues. SINGLE LAB: lifespan data are from the Serrano group only. TRAIT CHOICE: the brown-fat/UCP1 metabolic mechanism overlaps the existing fgf21_stgfbr2 'Metabolic Reset' card, which is why that existing trait was reused rather than minting a new one.

Manipulation: overexpression of a stabilised decuple variant (PtUGT1stable)
Narrative:
Indigo is the oldest blue humans have, and it has always been a chemically awkward one. The pigment is insoluble, so to get it into cloth you must first destroy it: a traditional vat reduces indigo to its soluble leuco form with harsh reducing agents in strongly alkaline water, soaks the yarn, then lets air oxidise the dye back to blue inside the fibre. Denim is dyed this way at a scale of tens of thousands of tonnes a year, and the reducing agents and alkali are the reason blue jeans have an environmental reputation.

The dyer's knotweed of Japan solves the same problem from the other direction. Rather than making indigo and then having to un-make it, the plant makes indoxyl, the reactive monomer, and immediately caps it with a sugar. The product, indican, is colourless, water-soluble and stable, and it stays that way until the cap comes off. Break the leaf, or add a beta-glucosidase, or simply shine light on it, and free indoxyl is released, dimerises, oxidises in air and becomes indigo. This is a pigment stored as a loaded spring, and it is the basis of fermentation indigo dyeing as practised for centuries.

The enzyme doing the capping, PtUGT1, is a perfectly good plant enzyme and a poor industrial one: at the indoxyl concentrations bulk production needs, it inactivates. A protein-engineering campaign fixed exactly that, combining ten stabilising substitutions into a single variant that melts 13.1 degrees Celsius higher without losing wild-type activity, and then ran the whole process through both a techno-economic model and a life-cycle assessment (Bidart 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). The result is honest in a way such papers often are not. Dyeing with indican is dramatically cleaner than the conventional vat, but producing indican is very slightly dirtier than producing indigo, and the whole case rests on a yield figure sitting one percentage point from break-even. For an enhancement library the interest is the chemistry itself: colour held in reserve, colourless until something opens it.
Short Description: PtUGT1 stores blue as a molecular surprise: it caps reactive indoxyl with sugar to make colourless, water-soluble indican, which releases indigo when light or an enzyme removes the cap. A ten-mutation engineered enzyme kept full activity, gained 13.1 °C in thermal stability, and converted 65% of a 100 mM substrate batch. This cleaner dye route is demonstrated at laboratory scale, with large-scale cofactor recycling still to prove.
Mechanism: PtUGT1 is a uridine-diphosphate-dependent glucosyltransferase (UGT) that transfers glucose onto indoxyl to make indican, that is indoxyl-beta-glucoside, a stable, colourless, water-soluble storage form of the pigment precursor. Removing the glucose again, either enzymatically with a beta-glucosidase or photolytically under light, releases free indoxyl, which spontaneously dimerises and oxidises in air to indigo, the pigment itself. The plant uses this as a precursor-storage strategy, keeping the reactive indoxyl capped and inert until it is needed. Industrially the same chemistry replaces the conventional indigo vat, which needs harsh reducing agents and strongly alkaline conditions to solubilise pre-formed indigo, because with indican the dye is generated inside the yarn under mild conditions instead. The wild-type enzyme suffers severe substrate inactivation at the indoxyl titres bulk production requires, and it was this inactivation, rather than catalytic rate, that the stabilising engineering was designed to overcome.
Achievements (effect sizes): The engineering result is a stability gain with no activity penalty. Mutations with a favourable effect on melting temperature were combined into a decatuple variant designated PtUGT1stable, which showed a Delta Tm of +13.1 degrees C (+13.8 kcal/mol) while retaining wildtype activity (Bidart 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). That stability translated into process performance: the variant achieved 65% conversion of 100 mM indoxyl in an inexpensive phosphate-citrate buffer, against a techno-economic viability threshold the authors had set at 60% conversion of at least 100 mM indoxyl with uridine-diphosphate-glucose recycling and replacement of the HEPES buffer by a pH stat (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). A cradle-to-factory-gate life-cycle assessment then compared indican dyeing against the conventional indigo vat and found that photolytic, light-driven release would reduce the environmental impact of blue denim dyeing with 73%, compared to a 92% reduction offered by enzymatic dyeing, and that indican dyeing has the potential to reduce human lifetime loss, biodiversity loss and financial loss from resource depletion to 9, 10 and 6% respectively of conventional-dyeing losses (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). The same assessment declines to overclaim: producing indican rather than conventional indigo at 65% yield carries a 1.2% increase, which can be monetarized to 21.0 USD/kg versus 20.7 USD/kg, and the authors note that raising the yield from 65 to 66% would make the two equal, while the dyeing step itself costs 1.5-fold conventional, or 0.08-0.14 USD per pair of jeans at scale (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (engineered enzyme characterised in vitro, demonstrated dyeing process, plus techno-economic and life-cycle assessment; not yet at industrial scale)
Translational Gaps: Everything demonstrated here happened in a test tube and a dye bath. The work established an in vitro enzymatic process and a laboratory-scale dyeing protocol, and nobody has expressed the engineered enzyme in a plant or an animal host or run the process at industrial scale, so the card's body framing is an extrapolation from plant chemistry rather than a reported phenotype. The techno-economic case also depends on recycling uridine-diphosphate-glucose efficiently at scale, and the authors model that recycling rather than demonstrating it in an industrial reactor. The life-cycle numbers carry a similar caveat: they were computed against the current European electricity grid mix, and the authors state that a fully renewable energy input would change them substantially. Because the margin is thin, small process losses matter more than they would in a mature route.
Key References (DOIs): Bidart Nature Communications 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Two closely related UniProt accessions cover this enzyme family in Persicaria tinctoria and it is easy to cite the wrong one. A0A2Z5UHQ8 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A2Z5UHQ8) is annotated as indican synthase 2 at 497 amino acids, while A0A2R2JFJ4 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A2R2JFJ4) is 478 amino acids and is the accession cross-referenced by Protein Data Bank entry 5NLM (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/5NLM), a 2.14 angstrom structure titled as a complex between a UDP-glucosyltransferase from Polygonum tinctorium capable of glucosylating indoxyl; Polygonum tinctorium is the older synonym for Persicaria tinctoria, so the two species names in the literature refer to one plant. Both accessions have AlphaFold models. On availability, the engineered enzyme is not a product: plant-derived indican and indigo from Persicaria tinctoria and Isatis tinctoria are sold today as natural dyes, but the PtUGT1stable route remains pre-commercial and has no clinical dimension at all (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). Two caveats on the environmental claim deserve recording rather than smoothing over. Marine eutrophication is reported as getting worse under the indican route, and human toxicity and mineral resource scarcity rise because of the sodium phosphate manufactured for the dyeing buffer, so the 73% and 92% headline reductions describe the dyeing step and not the whole supply chain. The authors also report a viability floor: below 53% conversion the process ceases to be economically viable, which sits uncomfortably close to the 65% achieved. This entry also fills the plant kingdom, previously absent from the database entirely.

Narrative: The sleeping chironomid Polypedilum vanderplanki is the only insect that can dry out completely and come back to life — its larvae survive total water loss in African rock pools for years. A major part of its trick is a family of 27 Late Embryogenesis Abundant (LEA) proteins, intrinsically disordered molecules that form protective glass-like matrices as water leaves the cell. The 2014 genome project by Gusev and colleagues found these genes massively expanded and clustered on Chromosome 4 — an evolutionary hotspot for desiccation innovations. LEA proteins from anhydrobiotic organisms have been expressed in mammalian cells: independent groups showed LEA fusions localize to cytoplasm and mitochondria in HepG2 hepatoma cells and sheep fibroblasts, protecting against acute desiccation damage. Gusev's team confirmed PvLEA localization in mammalian and insect (Sf9) cells, though GFP-fusion localization varied between constructs and cell lines. The mechanism is distinct from tardigrade CAHS proteins: while CAHS D forms reversible gel-like fibers, LEA proteins act through vitrification — forming an amorphous solid that physically immobilizes biomolecules. The limitation is real: LEA glass formation requires very low water content, and human cells don't naturally dehydrate that far. Still, for biopreservation of cells, tissues, or organs, LEA engineering is one of the most-studied routes.
Short Description: PvLEA proteins help the sleeping chironomid survive years of near-total drying by forming a glass-like matrix that immobilizes and shields membranes, proteins, and enzymes until water returns. Its genome carries 27 LEA copies, and related proteins have protected cultured mammalian cells and isolated biomolecules during dehydration. The strongest opportunity is preserving cells, tissues, and organs, where drying conditions can be engineered alongside trehalose.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered proteins that undergo vitrification (glass-state transition) at low water activity; physically immobilize and shield biomolecules and membranes during desiccation. Reinforced by trehalose-based glassy matrix. 27 paralogues in P. vanderplanki clustered on Chromosome 4.
Achievements (effect sizes): Gusev 2014 Nat Commun: genome revealed 27 PvLEA genes massively upregulated during anhydrobiosis. A group 3 LEA protein from Artemia has been reported to protect human HepG2 cells from desiccation and maintain membrane integrity; the primary source for this specific result could not be verified and the claim is retained without attribution pending confirmation. Marunde 2013: AfrLEA3m protected sheep fibroblasts during air-drying. Kondratyeva 2022: PvLEA-GFP fusions localized to cytoplasm/mitochondria in mammalian and Sf9 cells. In vitro: LEA proteins protect LDH, citrate synthase, and liposomes from dehydration-induced damage.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (mammalian cell expression, localization confirmed) + T3 (cross-species functional protection)
Translational Gaps: No stable mammalian transgenic; no in-vivo drying survival demonstrated; vitrification requires near-complete dehydration beyond physiological range; GFP-fusion localization inconsistent between constructs.
Key References (DOIs): Gusev Nat Commun 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5784 | Kondratyeva Biology 2022 https://doi.org/10.3390/biology11040487 | Yoshida NAR Genomics 2022 https://doi.org/10.1093/nargab/lqac029
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: LEA vitrification requires very low water content — human cells do not naturally reach this state. GFP-fusion artifacts: localization differed between N-terminal and C-terminal fusions (Kondratyeva 2022). LEA proteins are highly redundant — 27 paralogues raises the question of which are essential vs. vestigial. Overlap with CAHS D: both protect against desiccation but through different physical mechanisms (glass vs. gel). Biopreservation is the realistic use case, not whole-organism desiccation tolerance.

Narrative: Bdelloid rotifers (Adineta vaga) survive complete desiccation for decades — losing virtually all body water and reviving when rehydrated. PvLiL (LEA-like protein from bdelloid rotifers) is a Late Embryogenesis Abundant protein that forms a protective glass-like matrix around cellular components during drying, preventing protein aggregation and membrane fusion. This molecular vitrification shield preserves life without water.
Short Description: Bdelloid rotifers can dry almost completely, remain dormant for more than nine years, and revive when water returns. PvLiL is a LEA-like protein proposed to form a reversible glassy shield around membranes and proteins, limiting aggregation and tearing during water loss. In cultured mammalian cells it contributes to desiccation protection alongside other stress proteins, pointing toward preservation systems built from several cooperating safeguards.
Mechanism: PvLiL is an intrinsically disordered protein that transitions to an alpha-helical glass-like state upon dehydration. It coats membranes and proteins, preventing deleterious interactions during water loss. Upon rehydration, it dissolves back to its disordered state, releasing protected components intact.
Achievements (effect sizes): Bdelloid rotifers survive complete desiccation for 9+ years. Heterologous LEA protein expression protects mammalian cells from desiccation damage. LEA proteins from related organisms stabilize enzymes and liposomes during drying.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Bdelloid rotifer-specific LEA proteins are less characterized than Polypedilum vanderplanki PvLEA. Full desiccation tolerance likely requires multiple protective proteins working in concert.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Complements existing PvLEA (sleeping chironomid) and CAHS D (tardigrade) desiccation genes. Bdelloid rotifers represent a distinct evolutionary solution. SOURCING GAP flagged for review: this record previously carried a single reference, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43075-8, which is Nicolas 2023 on horizontal acquisition of a DNA ligase improving DNA damage tolerance in eukaryotes and does not describe a rotifer desiccation protein. Searches of Crossref and PubMed found no publication describing a bdelloid rotifer gene named PvLiL; the Pv prefix belongs to Polypedilum vanderplanki, the sleeping chironomid behind the separate pvlea record. The gene identity here is unverified and the row should either be re-sourced to a specific Adineta vaga publication or withdrawn. The general claims about bdelloid rotifer desiccation survival and heterologous LEA protection are supported in the wider literature but are not attributable to this gene as named.

Narrative: Proteins accumulate damage over time — one of the most common lesions is the spontaneous conversion of aspartate and asparagine residues into isoaspartate, which kinks the backbone and kills function. Every organism has at least one enzyme to fix this: protein L-isoaspartate methyltransferase (PIMT). Humans have one copy. The sleeping chironomid has fourteen. Gusev's 2014 genome project revealed this dramatic gene expansion, and later work showed PIMTs are among the most overexpressed genes during both desiccation and ionizing radiation exposure — the molecular repair crew works overtime whenever proteins get beaten up. Deviatiiarov 2020 characterized the family in detail: only PIMT1 and PIMT2 retain classical enzymatic activity; the others appear to have acquired novel functions through subfunctionalization. Shaikhutdinov 2023 found that the closely related P. pembai (which is also desiccation-tolerant) independently amplified PIMTs to 6 copies with radical structural changes, suggesting strong positive selection on protein repair. The human orthologue PCMT1 is well studied — PCMT1-knockout mice die within 42 days of seizures and brain damage. Overexpression of PCMT1 in Drosophila extends lifespan under heat stress. The chironomid's solution is simple brute force: more copies, more repair, more survival.
Short Description: PIMT repairs isoaspartate, a spontaneous backbone kink that accumulates in proteins during age, heat, radiation, and drying. The sleeping chironomid expanded this repair family to 14 copies, while flies with extra PIMT lived about 30% longer under heat stress and mice lacking their sole copy die young with seizures. The next question is which active chironomid paralogue adds useful repair, since only two retain the classical enzyme activity.
Mechanism: SAM-dependent methyltransferase that converts L-isoaspartate back to L-aspartate via a methyl ester intermediate. 14 paralogous copies in P. vanderplanki (vs. 1 in most insects/mammals). Subfunctionalized: only PIMT1/PIMT2 retain canonical enzymatic activity; others may have acquired novel repair or regulatory roles.
Achievements (effect sizes): Gusev 2014: 14 PIMT paralogues identified, among most upregulated genes during anhydrobiosis. Deviatiiarov 2020: expression profiling across 5 clusters; only PIMT1/2 enzymatically active. Shaikhutdinov 2023: P. pembai independently amplified PIMTs to 6 copies with radical structural changes under positive selection. Kim 2002: PCMT1-knockout mice die by day 42 (seizures). Chavous 2001: Drosophila PCMT overexpression extends lifespan ~30% under heat stress.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (P. vanderplanki expression/functional data) + T3 (Drosophila/mouse orthologue studies)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian PIMT overexpression study; unclear which of the 14 paralogues are most protective; subfunctionalized copies may not all transfer useful activity; human PCMT1 is essential but whether more is better is unknown.
Key References (DOIs): Gusev Nat Commun 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5784 | Deviatiiarov Insects 2020 https://doi.org/10.3390/insects11090634 | Shaikhutdinov GBE 2023 https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evad169 | Chavous PNAS 2001 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.251446498
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Amplification strategy assumes more copies = more repair, but subfunctionalization means many paralogues have diverged in function. PCMT1-null mice die young — the enzyme is essential, but the dose-response curve for overexpression is unstudied in mammals. P. pembai shows a completely different PIMT architecture, suggesting there is no single optimal solution even among chironomids. No direct cross-species expression in mammalian cells yet.

Narrative: Hibernating ground squirrels cool their bodies to near freezing for months — yet their brains emerge unscathed. When a human brain drops below 33°C during cardiac arrest, neurons die from failed synapse regeneration. The difference comes down to RBM3, a cold-shock RNA-binding protein that orchestrates synapse rebuilding during rewarming. Peretti and colleagues published a landmark study in Nature in 2015 showing that RBM3 is the key mediator of cooling-induced neuroprotection. In both prion-infected and Alzheimer's (5XFAD) mouse models, the capacity to regenerate synapses after cooling declined in parallel with loss of RBM3 induction. When they overexpressed RBM3 via lentivirus in the hippocampus — without any cooling — the results were dramatic: restored synapse reassembly, prevented behavioral deficits, prevented neuronal loss, and significantly prolonged survival in both disease models. Follow-up work mapped the signaling pathway: TrkB-PLCγ1-pCREB activates RBM3 transcription, and RTN3 is the downstream effector promoting synapse formation. The human RBM3 gene exists and is functional — it's just not strongly cold-induced in adult humans the way it is in hibernators. Overexpression could bring the benefits of therapeutic hypothermia without the hypothermia.
Short Description: RBM3 is a cold-shock RNA-binding protein that helps neurons rebuild synapses, offering part of therapeutic hypothermia's benefit without requiring cooling. Lentiviral expression in mouse hippocampus restored synapse reassembly, prevented neuronal loss and behavioural decline, and extended survival in both prion and Alzheimer's models. The survival evidence is strong but comes from one laboratory, and RBM3's broad control of messenger RNA calls for careful dosing.
Mechanism: RBM3 is a 157-aa RNA-binding protein with an N-terminal RNA recognition motif (RRM) and glycine-rich C-terminal domain. Upregulated during hypothermia via TrkB-PLCγ1-pCREB signaling. Promotes synapse reassembly through downstream effector RTN3, facilitating neurite outgrowth and synapse formation. Also broadly stabilizes mRNAs at low temperature.
Achievements (effect sizes): Peretti 2015 Nature: lentiviral RBM3 overexpression in mouse hippocampus restored synapse reassembly, prevented behavioral deficits and neuronal loss, significantly extended survival in both prion (RML) and Alzheimer's (5XFAD) models — without cooling. Peretti 2021: TrkB agonism induces RBM3 without cooling. Bastide 2017: RTN3 identified as downstream neuroprotective effector.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse in-vivo overexpression with survival endpoint in two disease models)
Translational Gaps: Single laboratory (MRC Prion Unit) — not independently replicated. Effect demonstrated in disease rescue, not healthy brain enhancement. AAV delivery to human hippocampus is invasive. Long-term effects of constitutive overexpression unknown. RBM3 affects global mRNA stability — transcriptome-wide side effects possible.
Key References (DOIs): Peretti Nature 2015 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14142 | Peretti Life Sci Alliance 2021 https://doi.org/10.26508/lsa.202000884 | Bastide Curr Biol 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2017.01.047
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Published in Nature with robust survival data, but all key experiments from one laboratory (the Mallucci group at the MRC Prion Unit; first author Peretti, senior author Giovanna R. Mallucci, https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14142). Independent replication critical. Effect is disease rescue, not enhancement above normal — the 'hibernation in a bottle' framing is attractive but unvalidated. RBM3 is a global RNA chaperone; constitutive overexpression may have unintended transcriptome effects. TrkB agonism (pharmacological RBM3 induction without cooling) may be more attractive than direct gene delivery.

Narrative: Cuttlefish and octopuses change color in milliseconds by telling reflectin proteins inside special skin cells to reorganize. Reflectin is weirdly rich in methionine and arginine and self-assembles into stacked layers that act as tunable mirrors. In 2020, Alon Gorodetsky's group at UC Irvine stably expressed squid reflectin in human HEK293T cells; the protein condensed into intracellular nanoparticles, and when researchers changed the salt concentration outside the cells, the reflectin condensates reversibly swelled and shrank, modulating how the cells scattered light. Media outlets called it 'invisible human cells,' which overstates a genuinely cool result: what changed was the cells' refractive index by a few percent, not their transparency to the naked eye. Cephalopod skin also needs chromatophore organs — pigmented sacs under fine neural control — that simply don't exist in mammals. Reflectin, by itself, is a promising biomaterial with medical-imaging potential; adaptive camouflage for humans is not in the cards.
Short Description: Reflectin self-assembles into tunable optical particles, giving cephalopod skin its ability to change how strongly it scatters and reflects light. In stable human-cell cultures, reflectin condensates reversibly swelled and shrank with salt, moving their refractive index from about 1.4 toward the 1.33–1.38 range of cytoplasm. This proves controllable optics in mammalian cells, though organism-scale camouflage also needs layered tissues and neural control.
Mechanism: Reflectins (~20–60% Met/Tyr/Arg) self-assemble into membrane-bound lamellar Bragg stacks; phosphorylation-controlled hydration tunes reflectance.
Achievements (effect sizes): Kramer 2007 Nat Mater: recombinant squid reflectin in E. coli forms films/gratings/fibers; ammonia/acid triggers visible spectrum shifts. Chatterjee 2020 Nat Commun: stable HEK293T lines expressing D. opalescens reflectin A1 — condensed into intracellular nanoparticles; quantitative phase microscopy showed leucophore-like contrast; NaCl osmotic challenge REVERSIBLY modulated light scattering (refractive index n≈1.4 vs cytoplasm 1.33–1.38); tens of percent transmittance changes across visible/NIR. Gorodetsky lab reflectin-coated films: tens of percent reversible IR reflectance with stretch — MATERIALS, not tissue.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (HEK293T in vitro) + T3 (E. coli films)
Translational Gaps: No in-vivo mammal; no tissue-level camouflage; requires innervated chromatophores in native animal.
Key References (DOIs): Kramer Nat Mater 2007 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat1930 | Chatterjee Nat Commun 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-16151-6
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Press framing ("invisible human cells") OVERSTATES result: effect is refractive-index modulation only, not perceptible transparency. Structural biology of reflectin contested (IDP, no crystal structure). No mouse/zebrafish demonstration.

Narrative: A flea jumps 150 times its own body length because its legs contain resilin — nature's most efficient rubber. This elastomeric protein stores and returns 92–97% of mechanical energy, outperforming any synthetic rubber. Insects use it for high-frequency wing hinges, jumping pads, and sound-producing tymbals. Resilin was first described by Torkel Weis-Fogh in 1960, and the gene was identified in Drosophila melanogaster as CG15920. The protein is largely intrinsically disordered (~94%), gaining its extraordinary elasticity from entropic recoil — stretched resilin spontaneously recoils because the disordered chains seek maximum entropy, like a rubber band. Cross-linking occurs in vivo via dityrosine bridges catalyzed by peroxidase. Qin and colleagues showed in 2011 that recombinant resilin from Drosophila exon 1, expressed in E. coli and photo-cross-linked, formed solid biomaterials with ~90% resilience and high extensibility. Resilin-like polypeptides are actively pursued for tissue engineering: cardiovascular grafts, cartilage repair, and vocal fold reconstruction. In human tissue, resilin expression in tendons, ligaments, or vocal cords could confer insect-level elastic energy storage and fatigue resistance — imagine tendons that never degrade from repetitive strain.
Short Description: Resilin is nature's near-perfect biological spring, returning about 92–97% of stored mechanical energy in insect wing hinges, jumping pads, and sound organs. Recombinant Drosophila resilin formed cross-linked biomaterials with roughly 90% resilience and high extensibility, inspiring elastic grafts and tissue scaffolds. Building the same performance into living vertebrate tissue requires precise dityrosine cross-linking and integration with the local extracellular matrix.
Mechanism: Resilin is an intrinsically disordered protein that achieves near-perfect elasticity through entropic recoil. Predominantly glycine/proline-rich chains lack stable secondary structure and behave as freely-jointed polymer chains. Cross-linking via dityrosine bonds (catalyzed by peroxidase) creates a covalent elastomeric network with 92–97% energy return efficiency.
Achievements (effect sizes): Qin 2011: recombinant Drosophila resilin exon 1 formed biomaterial with ~90% resilience after photo-cross-linking. Qin 2009: full-length resilin expressed, chitin-binding domain characterized, cross-linked materials showed excellent elastomeric properties. Weis-Fogh 1960: measured 97% resilience in locust wing hinge.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (recombinant expression in E. coli, biomaterial characterization) + T4 (insect in-vivo)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian tissue expression. Dityrosine cross-linking requires controlled enzyme activity — uncontrolled cross-linking could damage tissue. Integration into existing extracellular matrix unknown. Mechanical loading differs between insect cuticle and mammalian tendon.
Key References (DOIs): Qin Biomaterials 2011 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biomaterials.2011.06.010 | Qin Biomacromolecules 2009 https://doi.org/10.1021/bm900735g | van Eldijk Top Curr Chem 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/128_2011_205
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: No study has expressed resilin in any vertebrate tissue. The 620-aa Drosophila pro-resilin includes a signal peptide (17 aa) and a chitin-binding domain (exon 2) not relevant for human expression — typically only exon 1 (elastic repeats) is used. The path from E. coli expression to in-vivo tendon enhancement is long. Resilin-like polypeptides (RLPs) are among the most promising protein biomaterials but remain pre-clinical.

Narrative:
Reverse gyrase is the closest thing molecular biology has to a diagnostic signature. It is the only protein found exclusively and universally in hyperthermophiles — the organisms that live above 80 C in hydrothermal vents and hot springs — and its presence in a genome is used as the definitive marker for that lifestyle. Structurally it is a fusion of two familiar parts: a topoisomerase IA domain welded to a helicase-like ATPase. Functionally it does something no other enzyme does, introducing positive supercoils into closed circular DNA, tightening the helix rather than relaxing it as bacterial gyrase does.

For years the supercoiling was assumed to be the point, on the reasonable theory that overwinding a helix would resist thermal melting. The more interesting answer turned out to be mechanical. Reverse gyrase recognises nicked DNA, recruits a cooperative coat of protein onto the lesion, and holds the strands in register so a single-strand nick cannot propagate into a double-strand break; it also keeps denatured regions from tangling and helps them re-anneal correctly. This chaperone-like protection needs neither ATP hydrolysis nor any supercoiling activity, which means the enzyme has a second job entirely separable from the one it was named for — it is a splint, not a winch (https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683).

The literature then produced a beautiful apparent contradiction. One paper is titled to say reverse gyrase is not a prerequisite for hyperthermophilic life; another says it is essential for microbial growth at 95 C. Both are right. Knock the gene out of Thermococcus kodakaraensis and the organism still grows at 90 C, merely more slowly as the temperature rises (https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004). Delete it from Pyrococcus furiosus, which prefers 100 C, and growth at 95 C and above stops outright (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). Together the two papers bracket a threshold near 90 C, above which the splint becomes non-negotiable. That threshold is also this card's hardest limitation, because a human being does not live anywhere near it.
Short Description: Reverse gyrase acts as a molecular splint for DNA at extreme heat, coating nicked strands so they stay aligned instead of breaking apart. Purified enzyme reduced double-strand breakage about eightfold at 90 °C, and Pyrococcus cannot grow at 95–100 °C without it. The capability is spectacular but temperature-gated: at body temperature its positive supercoiling could interfere with the DNA topology needed for transcription and replication.
Mechanism: Reverse gyrase is a topoisomerase IA domain fused to a helicase-like adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) domain, 1,214 amino acids and about 140 kDa in Pyrococcus furiosus. Its namesake activity is the introduction of POSITIVE supercoils into closed circular DNA, the opposite of what bacterial gyrase does. The thermoprotective function, however, is separable from supercoiling. The enzyme recognises nicked DNA, recruits a cooperative coat of protein molecules onto the lesion, and then acts as a physical splint that stops a single-strand nick from propagating into a double-strand break; at the same time it prevents denatured stretches of DNA from aggregating inappropriately and promotes their correct re-annealing. This chaperone-like protection requires no ATP hydrolysis and is independent of the positive-supercoiling activity, so the two functions can be uncoupled experimentally. Nothing in this description is repair: no base is excised, no phosphodiester bond is remade to restore a lost nucleotide. The enzyme prevents damage from getting worse rather than reversing damage already done.
Achievements (effect sizes): The mechanistic result is a straight in vitro measurement. Purified reverse gyrase incubated with DNA at 90 C “reduces the rate of double-stranded DNA breakage approximately 8-fold at 90 degrees C” relative to a protein-free control, and the authors report that this activity does not require ATP hydrolysis and is independent of the enzyme's positive-supercoiling activity (Kampmann 2004, https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683). Genetics in living archaea then bracketed when the protection actually matters. Deleting the gene from Pyrococcus furiosus, an organism whose optimal growth temperature is 100 C, showed that “the gene is required for growth at 95 degrees C, as well as at 100 degrees C”, leading the authors to conclude that a temperature threshold above 90 C exists above which reverse gyrase is absolutely necessary (Lipscomb 2017, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). The boundary condition comes from a different genus: in Thermococcus kodakaraensis KOD1, whose optimum is 85 C, “the disruption of the reverse gyrase gene did not lead to a lethal phenotype at 90 degrees C”, although positive-supercoiling activity present in the host strain was absent from the disruptant and growth retardation became more striking as temperature rose (Atomi 2004, https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004). Opposite direction, for bounding only — a third laboratory, a third organism and a third method showed the enzyme is required under chemical DNA damage (this establishes necessity, not benefit from overexpression): knocking down topR1 by endogenous type III-B CRISPR-Cas messenger-RNA interference in the thermoacidophilic crenarchaeon Sulfolobus islandicus and challenging the cells with the alkylating agent methyl methanesulfonate showed that “the survival rate of pKD-topR1/E233S1 was about four times lower than pSeSD1/E233S1 during 1.3 and 2 mM MMS treatment and about 90 times lower during 2.6 mM MMS treatment” (Han 2017, https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340).
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (in vitro biochemistry plus loss-of-function genetics in three archaeal species from independent laboratories; no heterologous gain-of-function in any eukaryote)
Translational Gaps: Every quantified result in this record is either purified-enzyme biochemistry or loss of function in an archaeon. Nobody has expressed reverse gyrase in a mesophilic eukaryote and then measured thermotolerance, so the gain-of-function direction this card frames has never been tested in the direction it is framed. Delivery is a second obstacle with a hard number attached: the protein is 1,214 amino acids in Pyrococcus furiosus and 1,711 in Thermococcus kodakarensis, which puts its coding sequence near the practical ceiling for packaging into a single adeno-associated viral vector. There is also a plausible mechanistic conflict that has not been experimentally examined: human topoisomerases maintain negative supercoiling to support transcription and replication, and an enzyme that adds positive supercoils would be working against them. Whether a human cell tolerates that has not been measured in any system.
Key References (DOIs): Kampmann Nucleic Acids Research 2004 https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683 | Lipscomb Extremophiles 2017 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z | Atomi Journal of Bacteriology 2004 https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004 | Han International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2017 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The apparent contradiction in the titles is real and worth putting on the wall rather than smoothing over. One paper is titled to say reverse gyrase is not a prerequisite for hyperthermophilic life (https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004) and another that it is essential for microbial growth at 95 C (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). Both conclusions hold, because they were reached in different organisms at different temperatures, and read together they define a threshold near 90 C: disrupting the gene in Thermococcus kodakaraensis is survivable at 90 C, whereas the Pyrococcus furiosus gene is required at 95 C and 100 C. Structural depiction requires care. The deposited structures 4DDT (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4DDT), 3P4X (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3P4X) and 3OIY (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3OIY) are all of the Thermotoga maritima homologue, UniProt O51934 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O51934); no experimental structure of the Pyrococcus enzyme (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P95479) exists, so any image of it is an AlphaFold prediction and should be labelled as one. There are no clinical trials and no commercial product. The enzyme's practical uses today are as a research reagent and as the definitive phylogenetic marker for hyperthermophily. Supporting loss-of-function evidence now spans three archaeal genera and three independent methods — gene disruption in Thermococcus, deletion in Pyrococcus, and CRISPR interference in Sulfolobus (https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340) — which is unusually broad for a gene with no eukaryotic data at all.

Narrative: The silver spinyfin (Diretmus argenteus) has the most complex visual system of any vertebrate — 38 rod opsin genes where most fish have one. By expressing multiple tuned rhodopsins in its retina, each absorbing a slightly different wavelength, the spinyfin can distinguish colors in the near-total darkness of the deep ocean using only rod photoreceptors. This breaks the textbook rule that rod cells cannot do color vision.
Short Description: A many-pigment rod system could add color discrimination to vision in deep-sea darkness, overturning the textbook idea that rods see only in monochrome. The silver spinyfin expresses 14 of its 38 RH1 copies in the adult retina, spanning roughly 444–519 nm; 444 nm is the most blue-shifted rod pigment known. Realizing the capability requires retinal circuitry able to keep those rod signals distinct.
Mechanism: Through tandem duplication of the RH1 (rhodopsin) gene, the spinyfin expresses 14+ rod opsins tuned to wavelengths from 444-519 nm. Key spectral tuning sites (including positions 83, 122, 261, 292) carry substitutions that shift absorption peaks. Co-expression of differently tuned opsins in separate rod populations enables wavelength discrimination without cone cells.
Achievements (effect sizes): The most blue-shifted rod photopigment known (RH1-1, ~444 nm) was characterized from spinyfin. 14 of 38 RH1 genes are expressed in adult retina. Three independent deep-sea fish lineages evolved expanded RH1 repertoires convergently.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Rod opsin engineering for human therapy is speculative. Retinal gene therapy for single genes is feasible (Luxturna), but multi-opsin systems are far more complex. Basic science value is primary.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav4632
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Breaks the vertebrate 'one rod opsin' rule. Three independent evolutionary origins of multi-RH1 systems in deep-sea fish.

Manipulation: loss-of-function knockout (whole-body germline; also liver-specific and myeloid-specific deletion in the inflammation work)
Narrative: Caloric restriction extends life in mice, and for decades the question was which molecular limb carries the signal. Dominic Withers and colleagues cut one specific limb: S6 kinase 1, the kinase mTORC1 phosphorylates to switch on ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis. Deleting it in mice extended lifespan and, more usefully for anyone thinking about human enhancement, produced a healthspan signature rather than just a survival curve - resistance to age-related bone, immune and motor dysfunction, and protection from the loss of insulin sensitivity. The transcriptional profile of the knockouts resembled caloric restriction and pharmacological AMPK activation. The number that matters is female-specific: +20.4% mean and +18.5% median lifespan. Males got almost nothing, +5% mean and +0.6% median, and the median change in males was not significant. A 2024 follow-up from the same group found the mechanism is at least partly inflammatory rather than purely anabolic: S6K1 deletion does not reduce senescent-cell burden in aged liver, it dampens what those cells secrete, cutting IRF3 activation, IL-1-beta production and immune infiltration. That effect was hepatocyte-intrinsic and reproduced with liver-specific and myeloid-specific knockouts, which is what makes a tissue-restricted intervention imaginable instead of a whole-body kinase knockout.
Short Description: Deleting the kinase mTOR uses to switch on protein synthesis reproduces much of what caloric restriction does to a mouse: better bone, immune and motor function into old age. Female knockouts gained 19% median lifespan with a gene-expression signature resembling restricted animals, and insulin sensitivity improved. Males got the healthspan without the lifespan, and no human has ever received an S6K1 intervention.
Mechanism: RPS6KB1 encodes a 525-amino-acid serine/threonine kinase, the principal effector of mTORC1's anabolic arm. mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K1 at Thr389; active S6K1 phosphorylates ribosomal protein S6 and eIF4B to drive ribosome biogenesis and cap-dependent translation, and phosphorylates IRS1 on inhibitory serines to close the insulin feedback loop. Deleting S6K1 therefore lowers translational output and simultaneously relieves that negative feedback, which is why the knockouts keep insulin sensitivity instead of losing it the way chronic mTORC1 inhibition can. The knockouts' expression profile overlaps caloric restriction and AMPK activation. A separate, tissue-autonomous arm runs through inflammation: in aged liver, S6K1 loss reduces IRF3 activation and IL-1-beta production, lowering immune infiltration without changing senescent-cell number.
Achievements (effect sizes): Selman 2009 (Science): S6K1 deletion in mice increased lifespan and conferred resistance to age-related pathologies - bone, immune and motor dysfunction and loss of insulin sensitivity - with a gene-expression signature resembling caloric restriction or pharmacological AMPK activation. OpenGenes records the female cohort (n=29 vs 23 control) at +20.4% mean and +18.5% median lifespan, the pooled cohort (n=48 vs 49) at +1.4% mean and +9.3% median, and the male cohort (n=19 vs 26) at +5.0% mean and +0.6% median with the median change not significant. Barinda 2024 (Nature Aging): S6K1 deletion reduced inflammation in aged mouse liver without reducing senescent-cell burden, via reduced IRF3 activation, impaired IL-1-beta production and reduced immune infiltration; liver-specific and myeloid-specific knockouts showed the effect is hepatocyte-intrinsic. A German gene-based association study reports RPS6KB1 variants rs201316437 and rs1051424 associated with human longevity.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse germline knockout with lifespan and multi-organ healthspan endpoints, female-restricted effect) + T7 (single unreplicated human gene-based longevity association)
Translational Gaps: The lifespan benefit is essentially female-only: male mean lifespan rose 5% and male median 0.6%, which was not significant. No selective S6K1 inhibitor has reached human trials - the clinical assets touching this node are mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin, everolimus, RTB101) that hit the whole complex, not S6K1 alone, and their human results are evidence for MTOR rather than for this gene. The human genetics is one gene-based association study in a German cohort, not a replicated locus. Whole-body S6K1 loss reduces body size, so an adult tissue-restricted approach - liver or myeloid, as in the 2024 inflammation work - is the only version that avoids paying for the benefit with growth.
Key References (DOIs): Selman Science 2009 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1177221 | Barinda Nature Aging 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-024-00695-z | Sanese J Gerontol A 2021 https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glab023
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: DIRECTION: enhancement is loss of S6K1 activity; activating S6K1 is the pro-growth, pro-inflammatory direction. SEX EFFECT: this is the dominant caveat and must survive into any card copy - female +20.4% mean, male +5.0% mean with a non-significant median. Do not quote a single sex-averaged number as the headline; the pooled cohort was only +1.4% mean. GROWTH: whole-body S6K1 knockout mice are smaller and S6K1 is required for normal ribosome biogenesis, so systemic inhibition carries an anabolic-capacity cost - relevant to muscle maintenance in older adults, where this pathway is the one deliberately stimulated by resistance training and protein intake. IMMUNE: the mechanism runs partly through blunting IL-1-beta and immune infiltration, which helps inflammaging and does not help pathogen defence; the mTOR-inhibitor trial record shows this axis cuts both ways. NO DRUG: verified this session - there is no selective S6K1 inhibitor in human trials; card copy must not imply the rapamycin trials are evidence for this gene.

Narrative: Deer antlers are the fastest-growing bone in the animal kingdom — up to 2 cm per day. S100A10 (annexin A2 ligand) is a calcium-binding protein highly enriched in the antler growth zone that accelerates osteoblast proliferation and bone mineralization. Stanford researchers showed that antler progenitor cells can stimulate bone repair in mice, with S100A10 as a key driver of this extraordinary growth rate.
Short Description: S100A10 helps bone-forming cells coordinate calcium signaling, matrix deposition, and mineralization, making it an intriguing component of rapid skeletal repair. Deer antlers can grow up to 2 cm per day, and antler progenitor cells accelerated fracture healing after implantation in mice. The protein is one contributor within a larger regenerative niche rather than the whole antler-growth program.
Mechanism: S100A10 forms a complex with annexin A2 on osteoblast surfaces, enhancing calcium signaling and plasminogen activation. In antler periosteum, it is dramatically upregulated during the rapid growth phase, promoting progenitor cell proliferation, extracellular matrix deposition, and accelerated mineralization through enhanced calcium flux.
Achievements (effect sizes): Antler-derived progenitor cells implanted in mice accelerated bone fracture healing. S100A10 is among the most differentially expressed genes in antler growth zones. Deer antlers regenerate 20+ kg of bone annually with zero cancer risk.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Antler growth involves a complex niche of progenitor cells, growth factors, and vascular networks. S100A10 alone may be insufficient. Cancer risk from stimulating rapid bone growth in humans needs evaluation.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add0488
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Paired with UHRF1 (epigenetic regulator) from same Stanford deer antler study.

Narrative:
Syntrichia caninervis is a desert moss and probably the toughest multicellular organism in this library. Li and colleagues reported in 2024 that it recovers photosynthetic and physiological activity within seconds of rehydration after losing more than 98% of its cellular water, regenerates after three or five years at -80 degrees C and after 15 or 30 days in liquid nitrogen, has an estimated gamma-radiation LD50/1h of about 5,000 Gy in the dry state against about 2,000 Gy when hydrated, and survives simulated Mars conditions with its capacity to regenerate intact (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657). None of that is attributed to this gene, and the honest version of the story keeps the organism and the enzyme apart.

What the gene does is narrower and much better measured. Every one of those insults - drying, salinity, ionising radiation - peroxidises membrane lipids, and peroxidised lipids break down into reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal that then attack proteins and DNA. ScALDH21 is a single-copy aldehyde dehydrogenase from a family found only in mosses, and it oxidises those aldehydes to their corresponding acids. A group at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography in Urumqi cloned it, put it into tobacco (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001), then into upland cotton, and took the cotton all the way to a field trial under water withholding, where the transgenic plants outyielded controls without losing fibre quality (https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2).

This is the least theatrical kind of stress resistance and possibly the most useful. It is not a shield and not a radical scavenger: it is a mop for the damage products that get past both, which is why it works on drought, salt and oxidative stress with the same chemistry. In a human body the same logic would apply to any tissue that peroxidises its own membranes under load - and so would the complication that the aldehyde being mopped up is also a messenger.
Short Description: ScALDH21 acts as a chemical cleanup enzyme, oxidizing reactive aldehydes that continue damaging proteins and DNA after drought, salt, or oxidative stress injures membranes. Transgenic cotton retained photosynthesis, formed larger bolls, and produced more fiber under drought without reduced fiber quality; tobacco showed matching stress protection. Its broad value is damage-product clearance, though excessive clearance could also mute useful stress signals.
Mechanism: ScALDH21 is an aldehyde dehydrogenase of 483 amino acids and roughly 53 kDa that depends on the oxidised nicotinamide cofactor NAD(P)+, and it belongs to aldehyde dehydrogenase family 21 - a family unique to mosses and represented there by a single-copy gene. When drought, high salinity or ionising radiation peroxidise membrane lipids, the damaged lipids release reactive electrophilic aldehydes: malondialdehyde (MDA), 4-hydroxynonenal and related lipid-derived carbonyls, all of which form covalent adducts with proteins and with DNA. The enzyme oxidises these aldehydes to their corresponding carboxylic acids, removing the electrophile and regenerating the reduced cofactor NAD(P)H. That places it downstream of the antioxidant enzymes rather than alongside them: it is chemical detoxification of a damage product, not radical scavenging and not physical shielding, so it clears the damaging species that survive after superoxide dismutases, catalases and peroxidases have already acted.
Achievements (effect sizes): Aldehyde dehydrogenase 21 from the desert moss Syntrichia caninervis was first moved into tobacco, where transgenic plants challenged with drought and salt stress displayed higher germination ratios, higher root lengths, greater fresh weight, higher proline accumulation, lower malondialdehyde (MDA) contents and stronger photosynthetic capacities, as well as higher activities of antioxidant enzymes, and detached leaves from those plants lost water more slowly than non-transgenic leaves (Yang 2015, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001). In upland cotton the same transgene produced an agronomic result rather than a purely physiological one: transgenic cotton accumulated approximately 11.8-304% more proline than did non-transgenic cotton under drought stress, made a lower concentration of lipid-peroxidation-derived reactive aldehydes, kept higher peroxidase activity under oxidative stress and lost less of its net photosynthetic rate. Under field conditions the transgenic cotton showed greater plant height, larger bolls, and greater cotton fiber yield than non-transgenic cotton, but no significant difference in fiber quality, which led the authors to conclude that overexpression can greatly improve drought tolerance without costing yield or quality (Yang 2016, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2). A salt-stress time course on the transgenic line L96 confirmed the underlying chemistry, since hydrogen peroxide and MDA contents were decreased in the L96 line compared to non-transgenic cotton at all time points across 0, 2 and 5 days of 150 mM sodium chloride, while proline content and phenylalanine ammonia-lyase activity ran significantly higher (Yang 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms24065822).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (transgenic gain-of-function in two crop species with field-scale agronomic endpoints; single primary lab lineage)
Translational Gaps: Every gain-of-function experiment is in a plant - tobacco and cotton - and no animal or mammalian cell has ever expressed this enzyme, so nothing is known about how a high-capacity moss aldehyde dehydrogenase behaves in a tissue that already runs a full complement of human aldehyde dehydrogenases. The primary work also comes from one laboratory lineage, so independent replication is still owed. A second gap is attributional rather than experimental: the source organism's spectacular tolerances, including the roughly 5,000 Gy dry-state gamma LD50/1h, the regeneration after five years at -80 degrees C and the survival of simulated Mars conditions, are properties of the whole moss and are not credited to this gene by the paper that reports them (Li 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657), so a visitor buying this card is buying the measured aldehyde-clearance phenotype and not the moss.
Key References (DOIs): Yang Molecular Biology Reports 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11033-011-1017-6 | Yang Plant Physiology and Biochemistry 2015 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001 | Yang Molecular Breeding 2016 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2 | Yang International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2023 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms24065822 | Li The Innovation 2024 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The sequence identifier needs a caveat: no UniProt entry maps cleanly onto ScALDH21, and the protein is deposited in GenBank instead, as ACT10822 and ACT10823 at 483 amino acids from Syntrichia caninervis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/ACT10823), consistent with the 483-amino-acid, 53 kDa protein reported when the gene was cloned (Yang 2012, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11033-011-1017-6). No experimental structure exists. Commercially, transgenic ScALDH21 cotton has been through greenhouse and field trials in China as a drought-tolerance trait, but no commercial cultivar release has been reported, and there is no clinical relevance and no registered trial of any kind. The organism-level numbers reported by Li 2024 are verified in that paper's full text and belong to the moss rather than to the transgene (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657); mixing the two would be the easiest way to overstate this card. Within this library the entry is deliberately distinct from the desiccation genes such as CAHS D, PvLEA and trehalose synthase, which work by physically vitrifying or gelling the cytoplasm - this one is an enzyme that destroys a chemical, with no shielding role at all.

Narrative: The electric eel generates 860 volts by stacking thousands of modified muscle cells — electrocytes — that discharge in unison. The molecular machinery is a teleost-specific duplicate of the muscle sodium channel, scn4aa, which lost its original job in muscle and was repurposed to fire on demand inside the electric organ. It's a beautiful case of evolutionary tinkering. In 2018, Harold Zakon's group took five amino-acid changes from an Apteronotus knifefish and engineered them into a human cardiac sodium channel expressed in frog eggs. The resulting human channel generated a large, physiologically relevant persistent sodium current without needing the usual accessory proteins. But the 860-volt discharge isn't a protein — it's an anatomical design, the electrical equivalent of batteries wired in series across five thousand cells. No mammalian cell or mouse makes its own electricity. The hydrogel 'artificial electric organs' that periodically make the press are pure materials science: zero genes, 110 volts, impressive engineering, no biology.
Short Description: Repurposed sodium channels let electric-fish electrocytes fire powerful, synchronized currents instead of contracting as muscle. Five knifefish substitutions placed into a human sodium-channel backbone created a large persistent current in frog oocytes, demonstrating that the electrical gating changes are portable. The eel's spectacular discharge—more than 860 volts—also depends on thousands of electrocytes stacked like batteries.
Mechanism: Teleost-WGD Nav paralog; lost muscle expression, compartmentalized to electrocytes; positively selected substitutions in inactivation gate / S4–S5 linker; electric organ voltage arises from STACKED series of electrocytes firing via Nav channels.
Achievements (effect sizes): Zakon 2006 PNAS: convergent muscle-expression loss + positive selection. Gallant 2014 Science: eel genome + muscle-vs-EO transcriptomics. Traeger 2015 BMC Genomics: Nav isoform quantification. Thompson 2018 PLoS Biol: Apteronotid 5-residue D4 S4–S5 linker substitutions engineered into HUMAN hNav1.5 backbone, expressed in Xenopus oocytes → large persistent Na+ current (INaP) gain-of-function, independent of auxiliary beta-subunits. Native eel protein was NOT expressed in mammalian cells. Whole-animal E. voltai >860 V is ANATOMICAL (stacked electrocytes). Schroeder 2017 Nature "artificial electric organ" is hydrogel (110 V, ~27 mW/m2), zero genetic content.
Highest Evidence Tier: T2–T3 (Xenopus oocyte on human backbone)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian cell/mouse bioelectrogenesis; electrocyte developmental program un-transferred.
Key References (DOIs): Zakon PNAS 2006 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0600160103 | Thompson PLoS Biol 2018 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.2004892 | Schroeder Nature 2017 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature24670
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Voltage = MULTICELLULAR ARCHITECTURE, not single gene. Channel identity is actually scn4ab1 in Apteronotids (not scn4aa) — complicating "universal electric-organ gene" narrative. Apteronotids retain muscle scn4aa. Artificial organs (Schroeder 2017) sidestep biology entirely.

Manipulation: Overexpression (brain-restricted transgene, PRNP promoter; DMH/LH-predominant activity)
Narrative: SIRT1 is the gene the resveratrol and NAD literature was built on, and the mouse data do not say what the popular story says. Two transgenic experiments matter. Satoh et al. built BRASTO mice — Sirt1 overexpressed under a prion-protein promoter, giving high levels in brain including the dorsomedial and lateral hypothalamus — and these mice lived significantly longer: ~16% median in females, ~9% in males, ~11% pooled, with maximal lifespan also extended. The mechanism is neural, not metabolic-cell-autonomous: Sirt1 partners with Nkx2-1 to raise orexin type 2 receptor expression in the DMH/LH, and knocking down Sirt1, Nkx2-1 or Ox2r in those nuclei removes the phenotype. Separately, Herranz et al. made whole-body Sirt1 transgenics and found NORMAL lifespan — survival curves indistinguishable from wild type in a cohort powered to detect >10% differences — with protection against metabolic-syndrome-associated cancer but no longevity. So the honest claim is narrow and tissue-specific: this is a hypothalamic circuit intervention that happens to use a deacetylase, not a systemic anti-aging gene.
Short Description: A deacetylase dialled up in the hypothalamus keeps the orexin-receptor circuit that drives night-time activity and metabolic tone from fading with age. Brain-restricted overexpression gave female mice 16.4% more median lifespan and males 9%; whole-body overexpression, by contrast, did not extend life at all. The location is the entire finding, and no brain-targeted human delivery of this gene exists.
Mechanism: SIRT1 is an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase. The lifespan-relevant activity localises to the DMH and LH, where SIRT1 complexes with the transcription factor Nkx2-1 at the Ox2r promoter and raises orexin type 2 receptor expression, enhancing neural activity in those nuclei. That signal maintains age-sensitive systemic outputs — skeletal muscle tone, nocturnal physical activity, body temperature, oxygen consumption. DMH/LH-restricted knockdown of Sirt1, Nkx2-1 or Ox2r abolishes the phenotype, and DMH-specific Sirt1 overexpression alone reproduces part of it. Because the dependency is on a hypothalamic circuit, raising SIRT1 in peripheral tissues does not deliver the lifespan effect.
Achievements (effect sizes): Brain-restricted transgenics: median lifespan +16% (females), +9% (males), ~+11% pooled, with statistically significant maximal-lifespan extension. Delayed age-related decline in skeletal muscle and nocturnal activity. Mechanism mapped to a specific Sirt1/Nkx2-1/Ox2r axis in two hypothalamic nuclei with knockdown and region-specific rescue. Four independent human candidate-gene longevity associations (rs12778366 Dutch; rs7896005 American/Caucasian; rs4746720 Japanese).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (two independent mouse transgenic lifespan cohorts with OPPOSING results — brain-restricted extends, whole-body does not — plus region-specific knockdown/rescue mechanism, and four human candidate-gene longevity associations; no human SIRT1 gene therapy, and the small-molecule 'SIRT1 activator' literature is contested on target)
Translational Gaps: The lifespan effect requires overexpression in specific hypothalamic nuclei; whole-body overexpression produced a normal lifespan curve, so a systemically delivered SIRT1 gene therapy would most likely reproduce the null result. No adult-onset or vector-delivered hypothalamic Sirt1 experiment has been reported. The human evidence is candidate-gene SNP association only — no human has received SIRT1 as a gene or protein, and resveratrol/NAD-precursor trials do not test SIRT1 dose. Whether SIRT1 is the direct target of the reported small-molecule activators remains disputed.
Key References (DOIs): Satoh A et al. Cell Metab 2013;18:416-430 (10.1016/j.cmet.2013.07.013); Herranz D et al. Nat Commun 2010;1:3 (10.1038/ncomms1001); Kuningas 2013 PLoS ONE (10.1371/journal.pone.0058636); Kilpelainen 2011 Biogerontology (10.1007/s10522-011-9360-5); Kim 2018 J Gerontol A (10.1093/gerona/glx247)
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: DOSE IS NON-MONOTONIC: within the same brain-transgenic paper, the +14-copy line extended lifespan while the +16-copy line did not (females lost 7.9% median lifespan, males +2.1% mean/-0.3% median). More is not better. TISSUE SPECIFICITY IS THE WHOLE STORY: whole-body Sirt1-tg mice had indistinguishable survival curves from wild type in a cohort powered for >10% differences (Herranz 2010) — that paper's contribution is cancer protection, not longevity. POPULAR-CLAIM MISMATCH: resveratrol and NAD-precursor supplementation are widely sold on this gene's name; those compounds' human trials measure mitochondrial and vascular endpoints, not lifespan, and several do not establish SIRT1 as the mediated target. Do not let card copy inherit the supplement narrative. DELIVERY: the mouse route is a germline promoter, not an injectable; hypothalamic targeting in a human is a stereotaxic brain procedure. HUMAN GENETICS: all four association rows are candidate-gene studies, not GWAS — a weaker design, and they cap primary confidence rather than raising it.

Manipulation: Overexpression (fat body / adipose-restricted; ubiquitous is dose-sensitive and can reverse)
Narrative:
The seven mammalian sirtuins are usually described as deacetylases, but SIRT4 barely deacetylates anything. Its real catalytic activities are lipoamidase — stripping the lipoyl group off the E2 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase, which switches that complex off — plus ADP-ribosylation of glutamate dehydrogenase, which shuts down glutamine entry into the citric acid cycle. It sits in the mitochondrial matrix and its function is to say no: to stop a cell burning fuel it should be conserving.

Wood and colleagues asked what happens when you change the dose of the single fly Sirt4 in either direction. Knockouts were short-lived across seven independent cohorts, losing 19.0 to 33.3% of mean lifespan, and were sensitive to starvation, less fertile, less active, and unable to mobilise long-chain fatty acids from their energy stores. Overexpression went the other way: driven in the fat body with ppl-GAL4 the flies gained up to 22.8% of mean lifespan, and driven ubiquitously with da-GAL4 up to 20.7% (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1720673115). The bidirectional design is what makes this record worth a card — most invertebrate longevity claims have only one arm.

The caution is in the same dataset. One Tubulin-GAL4 overexpression cohort lost 5.0% of mean lifespan while three others gained 3.0 to 14.0%, so the benefit is driver- and dose-dependent even inside a single paper.
Short Description: A mitochondrial enzyme strips lipoyl and acyl groups off metabolic machinery, throttling how fast a cell burns pyruvate and glutamine when food runs short. Extra copies in fly fat body raised mean lifespan up to 22.8%, while deleting the gene cost 19.0 to 33.3% and left flies starvation-sensitive and less fertile. No mouse lifespan test exists, and in flies the gain is driver-dependent: one ubiquitous line lost 5% instead of gaining.
Mechanism: SIRT4 is a 314-residue NAD-dependent mitochondrial matrix enzyme with a mitochondrial targeting sequence and the canonical sirtuin Rossmann fold, but with a catalytic pocket that favours bulkier acyl groups over acetyl.
